10001-apocolocyntosis:
Seneca's Apocolocyntosis is a short Roman satire on the death of the emperor Claudius and his supposed rise to godhood. Its very title jokes that Claudius was turned not into a god but into a pumpkin, and the piece mocks the solemn business of making emperors divine.

This edition, with an English translation by W. H. D. Rouse published in 1920, gives the Latin text with notes on its long history, from its first printing in Rome in 1513. Readers get ancient political humor at its sharpest, and a glimpse of how Romans laughed at their rulers.
10114-the-great-events-by-famous-histori:
Volume two of The Great Events by Famous Historians continues the series' plan. It offers a comprehensive, readable account of world history, emphasizing the more important events, told as complete narratives in the master-words of the most eminent historians.

The volume is non-sectarian, non-partisan, and non-sectional, with brief introductions by specialists to connect and explain the celebrated narratives, arranged in order of time, with indices, bibliographies, and chronologies. Readers get ancient and early history from writers who shaped its telling, in a browsable, well-planned volume. It suits readers who like history in stories, not summaries.
10119-adonais:
Shelley's Adonais, edited by William Michael Rossetti in 1891 for the Clarendon Press Series, is the poet's great elegy on the death of John Keats. Rossetti calls it a poem of convenient length, neither short nor decidedly long, and the one Shelley work best suited to such an edition.

The poem mourns Keats as Adonais, a beautiful youth cut down young, and turns grief into a vision of poetry's lasting life. Rossetti's introduction and notes, with a memoir of Shelley, guide readers. Students get Shelley's most musical elegy, with a scholarly editor to explain it.
1045-venus-and-adonis:
Venus, goddess of love, finds the young hunter Adonis in the woods and begs him to leave the hunt for her arms. He resists, keen only for the chase, and the poem follows their long, witty, and sad debate until a boar's tusk ends it. William Shakespeare wrote this narrative poem early in his career.

The verse is lush and playful, full of animal images and sharp reversals, as the goddess who rules desire meets a boy who will not be ruled. Adonis dies, Venus mourns, and love itself seems both comic and cruel. The poem was a bestseller in its age and still shows Shakespeare's hand before the great plays.
10723-betty-s-bright-idea-deacon-pitkin-:
Harriet Beecher Stowe, author of Uncle Tom's Cabin, published this trio of Christmas stories in 1875, with illustrations. "Betty's Bright Idea" opens in New York at Christmas, as shops and streets fill with festive trade and the holy season settles over the city's noise. "Deacon Pitkin's Farm" and "The First Christmas of New England" complete the volume.

Stowe writes of giving, faith, and family feeling, with the moral warmth her readers expected. The stories mix city Christmas bustle with old New England scenes. Readers looking for gentle, old-fashioned holiday tales will find here a charming set from a famous American author.
11550-squash-tennis:
Richard C. Squires, writing in March 1968, presents squash tennis as a game for anyone who loves tennis, squash racquets, or platform tennis and has good reflexes. It lacks the endurance of squash racquets, he says, but offers powerfully hit strokes, split-second racquet work, and graceful footwork.

Chapters cover who can play, strategy, fundamental strokes, shot-making, and the history of the game, with court specs, equipment, official rules, and national champions. The green ball rebounds off as many as five walls, and the player must charge forward at once for a sharp cross-court shot.
1170-anabasis:
Xenophon, an Athenian soldier and pupil of Socrates, tells how ten thousand Greek mercenaries, hired by a Persian prince who then died in battle, marched home through hostile Asia. The Anabasis follows their retreat across rivers, mountains, and snow, under generals chosen on the march.

The cry "Thalatta! Thalatta!" when they first see the sea crowns the tale. Xenophon writes as both actor and historian, plain and vivid. The book has served soldiers and students for two thousand years, and it remains the great story of a fighting retreat. The march has taught soldiers and students for two thousand years.
12010-the-fourth-dimensional-reaches-of-:
Cora Lenore Williams's 1915 book The Fourth-Dimensional Reaches of the Exposition treats the San Francisco exposition of that year as a doorway to higher space. Published by Paul Elder and Company, it is dedicated to her father and mother. It includes lines on fourth-dimensional insight by Ormeida Curtis Harrison and an essay on a fourteenth-century legend.

Williams, author of As If and essays on involution, reads the fair's courts, towers, and crowds as signs of a dimension beyond ordinary sight. Where Bragdon argued the fourth dimension philosophically, Williams finds it in a particular place and year. The exposition becomes a test case for a theory that fascinated early twentieth-century readers.
12699-the-works-of-aristotle-the-famous-:
This complete edition, with engravings, of the Works of Aristotle the Famous Philosopher gathers his Complete Masterpiece and Family Physician, his Experienced Midwife, his Book of Problems and his Remarks on Physiognomy. A Midwife's Vade-Mecum follows, with particular directions for midwives and nurses, genuine recipes for speedy delivery, and approved directions for nurses.

Part one, book one, The Masterpiece, treats marriage, at what age young men and virgins are capable of it, and why they desire it so much. Marriage, the text says, is honourable to all, ordained in Paradise, without which no man or woman can honestly be in a capacity for family life. The book is pseudo-Aristotle, popular medicine and morals, not the philosopher's genuine work.
13387-shakespeare-his-life-art-and-chara:
The Rev. H. N. Hudson's fourth revised edition, volume one, joins a life of Shakespeare to a history of English drama. Miracle plays, moral plays, comedy, and tragedy trace the stage from its religious roots to Shakespeare's contemporaries, with Hudson writing from Boston in 1872 and dedicating the work to Joseph Burnett.

Hudson argues that art at its best interprets truth and feels the soul of nature, seeing things as they are. When art glorifies its own powers instead, it turns sickly and joyless. His readings of heroines who stoop from their height to act a man's part show his care for modesty, motive, and self-command. The volume serves students who want life, stage history, and criticism in one place.
13545-mary-at-the-farm-and-book-of-recip:
Edith M. Thomas spent time among the Pennsylvania Germans and gathered their cookery into Mary at the Farm, published in 1915. The book opens with a song to Pennsylvania, grand old Keystone State, land of rivers and rock-ribbed mountains, and dedicates itself to friends for many helpful kindnesses.

Recipes sit beside farm stories: boys trick Fritz with a burlap and barrel-hoop bag, a lighted candle, and a club to hunt the Elbadritchel, then drive home leaving him alone. Croquettes, made the day before and kept cold before frying, and stewed rabbit, washed and left overnight in salted water, show the practical core. Thomas preserves a regional kitchen with affection and detail.
14130-the-outdoor-chums-on-the-gulf-or-r:
Captain Quincy Allen's 1911 boys' adventure sends the Outdoor Chums south under sealed orders toward the Gulf. Fire traps, swamp fugitives, and a Florida sheriff open the chase. Will slips through a great swamp with a local guide, wisely hiding that sheriff and bloodhounds passed that morning, until the boys reach their tied-up motorboat in triumph.

Fishing, fog, and balloonists fill the later chapters. Jerry, sportsman to his fingertips, hauls cavalli aboard until his fingers ache, landing five before giving up. A cry across a lagoon, a mysterious sharpie, an oyster bar, and a message from the air lead to a dash upon the Gulf. Sealed packets, northers, and big-game ambushes keep the pace brisk. Boys who loved boats, camps, and rescues found here a full summer in one volume.
1451-the-art-of-lawn-tennis:
William T. Tilden, the great American tennis champion known as Big Bill, writes on the art of lawn tennis, from strokes and footwork to tactics and temperament. Tilden dominated the game in the 1920s. Tilden won seven United States singles titles, a record that stood for decades.

He explains serve, volley, and ground strokes, and he stresses thought and placement over mere power. The book remains a classic of tennis instruction, valued for its clarity and for the mind of a champion. His advice on the mental game, staying calm under pressure, still helps club players.
1496-massacre-at-paris:
Christopher Marlowe's Massacre at Paris dramatises the French Wars of Religion, from the marriage of Navarre and Margaret to the St Bartholomew's Day Massacre of 1572. Kings, queens, Guises, and admirals crowd the stage, and the play moves swiftly from court intrigue to street murder and revenge.

Marlowe's verse is fierce and his action is unflinching, with scenes of scholars, soldiers, and Protestants with books kneeling before their killers. The play survives in a rough text, but its power is clear. It is a stark, early history play about faith, power, and the cost of religious hatred.
15093-phyllis:
Maria Thompson Daviess's 1914 novel follows Phyllis, a young Southern girl whose garden path, friends, and family scrapes fill the story. Illustrations by Percy Johnson show her flying down paths, laughing with Roxanne, and facing a colonel with a medal. The tone is bright, funny, and full of country charm.

Phyllis narrates much of the tale herself, with a child's eye for grown-ups, dogs, and small disasters. Her father's face, a shed explosion, and a doorway laugh all become set pieces. Readers who enjoy old-fashioned girls' stories will find Phyllis warm, mischievous, and easy to like.
15446-vocal-mastery-talks-with-master-si:
Harriette Brower, author of books on piano mastery, gathered these talks with master singers and teachers, published by Frederick A. Stokes in 1920. Twenty portraits illustrate the volume, and the opening pages carry a signed note from Enrico Caruso. Each talk takes one singer's name and one working rule.

Caruso speaks on the value of work, Geraldine Farrar on will, Victor Maurel on mind, and Galli-Curci on self-teaching. Later talks cover Tetrazzini on coloratura voice, Scotti on training American singers, and Homer on what a musical career demands. Students get practical counsel, not gossip: practice, patience, criticism of oneself, and steady effort. The book preserves opera's great voices in their own advice.
1559-a-distinguished-provincial-at-paris:
A Distinguished Provincial at Paris, part two of Balzac's Lost Illusions, follows Lucien Chardon to the capital, where his provincial poems meet the harsh world of Parisian journalism, theatre, and salon politics. Lucien, dazzled and desperate, sells his pen to rival papers and his heart to an actress and a marquise.

Through garrets, newspaper offices, and first nights, Balzac shows a young writer corrupted by the very city he worshipped. The novel is a masterpiece of literary satire. It remains the classic portrait of ambition, journalism, and illusion in nineteenth-century Paris.
1579-lysis:
Plato's Lysis, translated by Benjamin Jowett, asks what friendship is, just as the Charmides asks what temperance is, and gives no final answer. Socrates talks with young Lysis and his friends in a wrestling school, and the talk turns on love, likeness, and the good that friends seek in each other.

The dialogue is rich in Greek life and youthful beauty, and its puzzles are gentle rather than fierce. It ends, like many early dialogues, in friendly perplexity. The Lysis is a short, graceful introduction to Plato on friendship, and to Socratic questioning itself.
15850-iphigenia-in-tauris:
Goethe's classical drama Iphigenia in Tauris, in Anna Swanwick's translation, issued by Arthur Hinds and Company in New York. The Handy Literal Translations series aimed at students who needed a faithful English text. Persons of the drama are Iphigenia, Thoas king of the Taurians, Orestes, Pylades, and Arkas. The scene is a grove before Diana's temple.

Iphigenia, priestess in a foreign land, longs for home and shrinks from human sacrifice. Her brother Orestes arrives, unrecognised, with his friend Pylades. Truth, pity, and the gods' will decide their fate. Goethe's verse, in Swanwick's plain rendering, gives students a noble entry to Greek myth remade by a German master.
16207-ade-le-dubois:
Published in Boston in 1865 by A. K. Loring, Adele Dubois tells a story of the lovely Miramichi Valley in New Brunswick. Its first chapter, The Dubois House, brings Mr. Norton to a curiously carved old armchair before a blazing hearth, in a home that surprises him in so wild a region. Everything is agreeable and tidy, he notes, yet unlike a Yankee home, an Elim in the desert with goodly palms and abundant water.

From that hospitable house grows a romance of valley life, family, and love in colonial Canada. The book's setting, French-named and river-bound, gives it a flavor of its own among American novels of the day. Readers who like regional romance will enjoy its warm, old-fashioned charm.
16322-luther-examined-and-reexamined-a-r:
W. H. T. Dau, a professor at Concordia Seminary in St. Louis, answers Catholic attacks on Martin Luther in this 1917 review. He works through charge after charge: Luther worship, Luther hatred, his birth, his monk years, his Bible work, his Rome visit, and his teaching on faith and works. Each point gets a rebuttal and a plea for a fairer reading.

Dau writes with open partisanship, as a Lutheran scholar defending his church's founder. The chapters are short and pointed, easy to dip into by topic. The book stands as a clear sample of early twentieth-century confessional debate, sharp in tone but orderly in form.
16339-the-passenger-from-calais:
Arthur Griffiths's The Passenger from Calais, published in Boston by L. C. Page in 1906, tells Colonel Annesley's story of a Channel crossing gone strange. The crossing from Dover had been rough, with drizzling rain and most passengers below, on a Sunday in late July when a strong stream toward Central Europe might be expected. The narrator's place was booked through in the Lucerne sleeping car of the Engadine express.

Room on the train de luxe surprises him, and from that quiet start grows a tale of travel, identity, and pursuit across Europe. Griffiths, author of The Rome Express, writes railway mystery with a practiced hand. Readers who like Edwardian train thrillers will enjoy this brisk, atmospheric novel.
16518-a-day-s-tour-a-journey-through-fra:
Percy Fitzgerald's 1887 trifle proves that a short, unpretending trip can entertain more than a grand tour. The preface recalls the tale Eyes and No Eyes, where one boy saw much on a walk and his fellow saw nothing. Fitzgerald's day runs from London by Dover and the packet to Calais, Tournay, Douai, Arras, Lille, Ypres, Bergues, and St. Omer.

The book opens on a bright, sultry August day in London, with flags scorching underfoot and provincials gazing in awe. Sketches lighten the text. The volume suits travelers who like small places seen slowly, and it still charms as a lesson in looking closely.
16627-angelic-wisdom-concerning-the-divi:
Emanuel Swedenborg first put this work out in Latin at Amsterdam in 1763, and the first English version came in 1794. The Swedenborg Foundation text here is William Rotella's revised standard edition. It sets out his view of divine love and divine wisdom as the twin roots of all life, with love as the life of man.

Swedenborg argues in numbered parts, moving from love known in plain speech to how love and wisdom join in God, in angels, and in men. He uses plain cases: a king and his folk, a husband and wife, a mother and child. The book is dense but orderly, and it rewards slow reading by those who want his thought in his own system, not in summary.
16741-aunt-phillis-s-cabin-or-southern-l:
Mary H. Eastman wrote this 1852 Philadelphia novel as a pro-slavery reply to Uncle Tom's Cabin, presenting southern life as its title claims it is. Her preface traces slavery to the Bible, holding that God gave laws for his own institution, and that history and philosophy must back Scripture. Lippincott, Grambo issued the book.

Eastman portrays enslaved people as content under kind masters, a view modern readers will read as propaganda for slavery, not as fact. The novel's value today is as evidence: it shows how slavery's defenders answered abolitionist fiction in print. Readers should approach it as a historical document of a cruel defense, not as a true picture of enslaved life.
16763-say-fellows-fifty-practical-talks-:
Wade C. Smith wrote these fifty short talks for boys, issued by Fleming H. Revell in New York in 1921. They grew from his weekly Sunday school lessons in The Sunday School Times. Talks run from building, work, loyalty, and keeping fit to showing off, drifting, friendship, talents, and faith, each in a few pages.

Smith speaks straight to boys in plain, warm terms, with a short text or tale to open each talk. He urges patience, courage, endurance, and faith, and he ties daily habits to larger choices. The book still works as a set of brief, moral pep talks, best read one at a time rather than straight through.
17182-within-the-temple-of-isis:
Belle M. Wagner's 1899 Denver book, dedicated to her husband Henry Wagner, claims a unique place: no other book in print like it. Its publisher's preface says God's word was law in the Temple of Isis, as read by hierophants one with the fountain of being. Isis means mother of all, Osiris father of all, and the temple of two truths, matter and spirit, must be realized within.

Wagner writes in the astro-philosophical style of her press, mixing Egyptian symbols with lessons on purity, sincerity, and hidden wisdom. The book suits readers of Victorian occult and New Thought writing. Modern readers will find a curious, earnest work of esoteric faith from the American West at century's end.
17241-atlantis:
Gerhart Hauptmann's 1912 novel, translated by Adele and Thomas Seltzer, opens aboard the German mail steamer Roland, bound from Bremen to New York on January 23, 1892. Frederick von Kammacher wires from Paris for a cabin in haste, and joins a floating household of officers, stewards, cooks, a doctor, and four hundred steerage souls beside one hundred cabin guests.

The voyage becomes a tale of love, art, and fate on the Atlantic, with the sea as both road and judge. Hauptmann, a Nobel laureate, writes in rich, serious prose about a man fleeing his past. Readers who like ship novels with a literary bent will find a long, brooding voyage worth the slow crossing.
18105-genesis:
H. Beam Piper wrote Genesis as a feature novelette of lost worlds, first run in Future combined with Science Fiction Stories in September 1951. Piper asks whether a proud old race met its end, or its start, on a far planet, and whether gaps in man's past hide such a tale.

Aboard a great ship, a thousand colonists sleep, play, and work while the vessel bears them to Tareesh. Kalvar Dard, the army officer who will lead them, plans landings and guards morale as the disc of the new world grows. The tale is brisk, thoughtful science fiction, a fine sample of Piper's work on lost colonies and new worlds.
18314-types-of-naval-officers-drawn-from:
Captain A. T. Mahan of the United States Navy wrote this study of British naval officers in the age of sail. Mahan, already known for The Influence of Sea Power upon History, opens with the state of naval war at the start of the eighteenth century. He then traces how war at sea changed through that century and after.

Each portrait stands for a type of officer. Hawke shows the spirit, Rodney the form, Howe the tactician, Jervis the disciplinarian and strategist, Saumarez the fleet officer, and Pellew the frigate captain. Readers get both sea history and a study of command: how daring, order, and judgment each shaped battles, fleets, and the men who led them.
1871-the-deputy-of-arcis:
Election season comes to Arcis-sur-Aube, and the whole town — candidates, counts, countesses, and newspaper men — turns out for the bustle. Candidates, counts, and countesses maneuver for votes. A young countess turns to her husband to ask what 'later' means, hearing that later is the end of the world.

The novel follows the election through drawing rooms, newspapers, and back rooms, with Maxime promising to win his cause if his friends hold firm. Balzac writes politics as comedy and as corruption together, and the book remains a sharp picture of how French provincial power was bought, flattered, and lost.
18721-the-victim-a-romance-of-the-real-j:
Thomas Dixon published this historical romance at New York and London in 1914 with Appleton, pictures by J. N. Marchand. Dixon presents Jefferson Davis as a man forced by his people to lead the Southern cause, building a war engine that held off a far larger North for four years. A prologue and chapters on Richmond, the house on Church Hill, the fatal victory, and the aftermath carry the tale.

Dixon claims his scenes rest on authentic records in his hands, with no liberty taken on key facts. Readers should note his strong Southern sympathy shapes the portrait throughout. The novel is a vivid, partisan window on Civil War memory.
18774-the-sun-of-quebec-a-story-of-a-gre:
Joseph A. Altsheler published this novel in 1919 with Appleton, reprinted in 1947, as part of his French and Indian War series. Its heroes are Robert Lennox, a lad of unknown birth, Tayoga the young Onondaga warrior, and David Willet the hunter, facing French officers such as St. Luc and commanders Montcalm, Wolfe, and Braddock. A long cast list sets out friends and foes.

Chapters run from old friends and a chest of drawers through a pursuit of the spy Garay, a voyage out to sea, an island, a pirate's warning, and a sloop of war. Altsheler mixes forest adventure with the great crisis at Quebec. The novel is a rousing boys' history tale.
18956-autobiography-and-letters-of-orvil:
Mary Dewey edited this memoir of her father, Orville Dewey, a noted Unitarian preacher in New York. She built it from papers he began at her urging, plus choice letters from his long life. An opening sketch sets his place among the preachers and thinkers of his day.

Dewey recalls a strict farm childhood, early fears about faith, and slow steps from dread toward doubt, reason, and at last a calmer trust. His letters then show his church work, his friends, and his views on art and public life. Readers meet a man whose pulpit fame faded with time, told here in his own voice.
18989-how-women-love-soul-analysis:
Max Nordau's stories, translated from the German, appeared in English as How Women Love, with the subtitle Soul Analysis. Nordau was already known for Degeneration and The Malady of the Century. The American edition, copyrighted in 1898 and 1901, gathers five stories under one cover.

The contents run from Justice or Revenge, set in a Hungarian village, through Prince and Peasant and The Art of Growing Old, to the title story and A Midsummer Night's Dream. Each tale turns on love, pride, and the gap between feeling and judgment. Readers get late nineteenth-century psychological fiction, direct in style and interested above all in motive and character.
19263-diary-of-the-besieged-resident-in-:
The diary of a besieged resident in Paris reprints letters from the Daily News. They cover the siege of 1870 to 1871. New letters and a preface appear in a second edition of 1871. The writer stays in Paris as Prussian armies close round. He notes consuls who leave their posts, Victor Hugo's appeals, and small acts of patriotism.

A child lays her doll in the arms of the statue of Strasbourg. Crowds in uniform shrug at the post office. News of the Emperor's capture spreads in confusion. Readers get a vivid, day-by-day view of a city under siege, sharp on rumour, courage, and daily strain.
19630-maha-bharata-the-epic-of-ancient-i:
Romesh C. Dutt condensed the Mahabharata, the epic of ancient India, into English verse, published in London in the late eighteen hundreds and dedicated to the Marquis of Ripon. Twelve books carry the tale from a tournament and a bride's choice to the fatal dice, exile, and great war.

Falls of Bhishma, Drona, and Karna mark the war's grim peaks, followed by funeral rites and a horse sacrifice. Dutt's version brought India's vast epic to English readers in readable verse, and it remains a beloved door into the poem. The Savitri passage has Yama tell the faithful wife that the dead come not to life, and bid her ask another boon.
19912-the-insurrection-in-paris:
The Insurrection in Paris recounts the Paris Commune of 1871, written by an eyewitness. The author long resisted writing, he confesses. In his excursions he had seen armed bands of every sort. Thousands of individuals of all social positions filled them. So many nationalities mixed there too. He decided compatriots deserved a sincere recital from a disinterested hand. His account aims at that honesty.

The Commune ruled Paris for two months after France's defeat by Prussia. Its fall in Bloody Week killed thousands in the streets. Foreign witnesses wrote many of the surviving narratives. This one stresses the Commune's mixed, improvised character. It is primary testimony from inside a revolutionary city. Read it against official French accounts.
19930-the-boy-ranchers-among-the-indians:
Willard F. Baker wrote The Boy Ranchers series for young readers. Among the Indians takes the boys trailing the Yaquis. Slim, a tall lanky rider on a pony of like build, ambles into view. He tops a slight rise of the trail as Nort laughs. The boys ride a borderland of ranches and raids. Yaqui country lay across the line in Sonora, Mexico.

Boy rancher books taught riding, tracking, and nerve by story. Baker's boys work cattle between adventures. The Yaqui wars were recent and real when he wrote. His fiction softens that history into pursuit and escape. Series readers followed the same crew through many volumes. This one shows the border adventure at full gallop.
2078-thais:
Anatole France, in Robert B. Douglas's translation, sets a novel in fourth-century Egypt, where the hermit Paphnutius leaves the desert to save Thais, a celebrated courtesan of Alexandria. He hopes to win her soul for heaven. France won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1921, after Thais had made his name across Europe.

The attempt reverses itself: Thais finds faith and peace, while Paphnutius discovers his own desire. France writes with irony and beauty, and the book became famous for its bold treatment of holiness, love, and doubt. The novel's reversal, in which the saint falls and the sinner rises, shocked pious readers of its day.
20816-socialism-as-it-is:
Roosevelt spoke of a social reordering of the United States, notes Socialism As It Is. A piece in La Follette's Weekly warned against reforms that spare root evils. William English Walling opens his survey of the world-wide revolt with such signs.

Walling, a socialist who knew the movement from inside, maps its parties and plans. Strikes, votes, and revolts across many lands fill his account. He writes for readers who want the facts, not slogans from either side. The book froze a moment in 1912 when socialism seemed poised to reshape the whole industrial world.
20911-the-rose-of-old-st-louis:
A captain stands in a boat's prow, eyeing a village on bluffs past muddy swirls. Mary Dillon opens The Rose of Old St. Louis, from 1904, on that wide river view. Politeness, not true need, prompts the narrator's query on their goal.

French St. Louis, river trade, and old families fill Dillon's historical tale. The rose of the title blooms amid rival claims and young love. Dillon knew the city's French past and wove it with care. Her book keeps a vanished St. Louis alive: Creole manners, keelboats, and a frontier port on the great Mississippi's banks.
21494-trapped-by-malays-a-tale-of-bayone:
George Manville Fenn sets Trapped by Malays in the seas where bayonet meets kris, the wavy Malay blade. A young officer hears laden footsteps pass his quarters at night, then a low call like a night bird. The tale opens in tricks, pranks, and barracks high spirits.

Fenn keeps the action near constant from the first chapters on. Disaster follows disaster, and each escape breeds a fresh trap. The cast recalls his own Middy and the Ensign, with new faces and fresh ground. Readers who love suspense at full stretch will find this a lively, breathless yarn.
22003-the-first-four-books-of-xenophon-s:
Xenophon, an Athenian soldier, marched with ten thousand Greek mercenaries hired by Cyrus the Younger. Cyrus meant to seize the Persian throne from his brother Artaxerxes. Xenophon later wrote the Anabasis, the classic account of that march. The version here is J. S. Watson's literal English rendering, printed with notes for students in the Handy Literal Translations series.

The first four books cover the long march inland and the start of the retreat. Cyrus falls in battle, the Greek generals are seized by treachery, and the men must fight their way home. They cross harsh mountains in winter with enemies on every side. Generations of schoolboys learned their Greek from these pages.
22023-the-scottish-reformation-its-epoch:
Alexander F. Mitchell, professor of church history at St Andrews, delivered the Baird Lecture for 1899 on the Scottish Reformation. Ill health dogged the work, and the lectures were published after his death in 1900. D. Hay Fleming edited the volume and added a life of the author. Mitchell treats the Reformation by its epochs, episodes, and leaders, as his title promises.

Chapters take up reformers such as Alexander Alesius and Andrew Melville. Long extracts from original sources fill the appendices. Mitchell writes as a church historian who knew the records at first hand. His lectures remain a solid, detailed account of how Scotland broke with Rome and built a Presbyterian church.
22067-the-story-of-a-cannoneer-under-sto:
Edward A. Moore was eighteen and a junior at Washington College in Lexington, Virginia, when the Civil War came. His Story of a Cannoneer under Stonewall Jackson, published in 1907, tells what followed. In the session of 1860 and 1861, he recalls, the students cared more for the coming storm than for their professors. A few classmates were born secessionists; most were decided Union men at first.

Moore joined the Rockbridge Artillery and served with Jackson in the Army of Northern Virginia. He writes of guns, marches, hunger, and the death of Jackson himself. His memoir is valued for its clear, unboastful soldier's eye. Few artillery accounts from the Confederate side read better.
22084-oration-on-the-life-and-character-:
Henry Winter Davis, a Maryland congressman who backed the Union and emancipation, died young in 1865. Congress honoured him with a memorial day in the House of Representatives. The Secretary of the Treasury and other high officers attended. After prayer, the Declaration of Independence was read aloud, and a band played a dirge.

Speaker Schuyler Colfax then introduced the orator of the day. His address traces Davis's life, his fierce speeches, and his stand against slavery's friends in a border state. Such published orations were the official memory of the Civil War generation. This one shows how the House wished Davis, a sharp and lonely figure, to be remembered.
22814-a-practical-guide-to-self-hypnosis:
Melvin Powers published A Practical Guide to Self-Hypnosis in 1961, and his central claim runs through every chapter. All hypnosis, Powers argues, is really self-hypnosis. A person enters the state only when fully ready, and hidden resistance can block the result even when the person insists he wants it at once.

The chapters turn that idea into practice. Readers get steps for relaxing, focusing, and giving themselves suggestions, plus counsel on why early attempts may fail and why practice matters. Powers writes in plain, direct language for lay readers rather than doctors. The guide remains a period piece of the American self-help shelf, and a clear window into how hypnosis was sold to the public then.
22956-rollo-in-paris:
Jacob Abbott's Rollo reaches London on his way to Paris in Rollo in Paris. Hotels there, the narrator explains, generally dine at six or seven o'clock, each family in its own private parlor. One evening near eight, a waiter clears the cloth from the table where Rollo, his parents, and his cousin Jennie have dined.

Abbott built his famous series on travel handled as education. Rollo asks questions, adults answer them well, and a foreign city becomes a lesson in geography, manners, and money. Paris waits across the Channel, with its monuments and its French. Generations of American children toured Europe first through Rollo's eyes. The calm, reasoning tone remains the series' trademark, as distinctive as any adventure.
24070-the-girls-at-mount-morris:
Amanda M. Douglas published The Girls at Mount Morris in Chicago in 1914, with M. A. Donohue and Company. Douglas, author of the Sherburne series and A Little Girl series, opens with Lilian Boyd entering a small, rather shabby room, where her mother sits sewing muslin with a weary smile.

Lilian puts down five dollars for her mother. Madame Lupton sails on Saturday, she says. What a wonderful trip Paris must be. Mrs. Cairns will finish the rest, since Madame praised everything Lilian's mother did as so neat. Chapters follow a new outlook, food for consideration, and the grace of endeavor, through Zaidee, an escapade, and a supreme moment. A strange confession, whose child am I, and unraveling tangled threads lead to a mother's love and a true home.
24201-the-eye-of-osiris:
R. Austin Freeman wrote this detective story, published by P. F. Collier and Son in New York with copyright in 1911. Its narrator studies under John Thorndyke, lecturer on medical jurisprudence at St. Margaret's Hospital, a teacher of profound learning and endless resources who lights up a dry subject by analyzing cases from the papers. Thorndyke's cases turn on facts chemical, physical, biological, and even historical.

Chapters follow the vanishing man, the eavesdropper, legal complications and a jackal, and the water-cress bed. Later comes John Bellingham's will, a museum idyll, the sphinx of Lincoln's Inn, the coroner's quest, the probate court, and circumstantial evidence. Readers get a classic Thorndyke puzzle, where law, medicine, and Egyptology meet.
2434-new-atlantis:
Francis Bacon's New Atlantis describes an imaginary island, Bensalem, where a society devoted to science governs wisely. The unfinished fable, published after Bacon's death, centers on Salomon's House, an institution for research and invention that anticipates the modern laboratory. Bacon's vision links knowledge to human welfare.

The work is short, stately, and hugely influential on the idea of organized science. Readers of utopias will find a founding text, more program than story. Its calm idealism still appeals. Bacon's Salomon's House inspired the founding of the Royal Society. Bacon wrote it near the end of his life, after his fall from power.
24648-a-theory-of-creation-a-review-of-v:
Published at Boston in 1845, this pamphlet reviews Vestiges of the Natural History of Creation, the anonymous scientific romance from Wiley and Putnam. Its reviewer calls Vestiges among the boldest and cleverest scientific romances ever read, by a bold writer who offers a hypothetical history of creation.

The review follows that history from the earliest period down to the present day, weighing its guesses about stars, earth, life, and man. Written before Darwin, it shows American readers grappling with evolution's first popular form. Readers of science history will find it a sharp, readable window onto the debate Vestiges stirred.
25234-cum-grano-salis:
David Gordon's Cum Grano Salis, illustrated by Emsh, is a science-fiction story about hunger on an alien world. Colonel Fennister of the Space Service surveys the glowing coals of Storage Shed Number One, burned by what his men call a dirty trick of lightning.

Food runs short, and the spacemen face an ugly question: can men eat monkey food, and what comes next when that fails? Doctor Pilar sends the monkeys' rations to the mess hall, while lab animals wait as a secret reserve. Gordon's title warns readers to take survival logic with a grain of salt.
25619-mystic-london-or-phases-of-occult-:
Rev. Charles Maurice Davies, author of Orthodox and Unorthodox London, surveys occult life in the metropolis in this 1875 volume from Tinsley Brothers. A Hamlet epigraph opens the book: there are more things in heaven and earth than are dreamt of in philosophy.

Davies, a clergyman observer, visits mediums, spiritualists, and seekers across London, recording seances, claims, and characters with a reporter's eye. The book treats mystic London as a social world as much as a creed. It shows how Victorians chased wonders, comfort, and meaning beyond orthodox church walls. This volume extends Davies's earlier survey of London religion into seance rooms and occult circles.
26450-the-story-of-paris:
Thomas Okey's Story of Paris, first published in 1906 and reprinted in 1919, with illustrations by Katherine Kimball, traces the city's history for general readers. A Montaigne epigraph opens the book, praising Paris as the glory of France and one of the noblest ornaments of the world, beloved even with its spots, blemishes, and warts. Okey follows the city through kings, wars, and revolutions.

One much-canvassed episode shows Charles IX at a Louvre window, firing a long arquebus across the river at Huguenots who had escaped massacre and rode up to learn what passed. Okey reports the story as debated, not settled. The volume blends chronicle, anecdote, and description, guiding readers through streets and monuments shaped by centuries of Paris life.
26543-clematis:
Bertha and Ernest Cobb published this children's story with G. P. Putnam's Sons in 1917, in a book dedicated to Priscilla Cobb. It opens in early spring on a city street, where a shabby little girl in a faded blue cap sits alone on Chambers Street. A policeman wonders where she belongs, and the lost child soon reaches a children's home.

Chapters follow Clematis through her first night, hard lessons, a secret, two doctors, and a long anxious night of illness. A trip to Tilton and life in the country bring animals, work, and a grandfather's house into the tale. Hunting for Clematis and the true fairy story close a gentle book about a homeless girl finding care.
26599-a-black-adonis:
Albert Ross published this novel at New York in 1896, in his Albatross series. It opens with Shirley Roseleaf, a young writer of about twenty, waiting anxiously for a publisher's letter about his romance manuscript. Rejection sends him into a social world of dinners, dances, and country visits, where Millicent, Daisy, and Archie cross his path.

The novel's sharpest note is struck in its epigraph, where a Black man says he cannot touch the hand of a white woman, though God made all nations of one blood. Chapters titled A Question of Color and Black and White carry that theme through courtship, jealousy, betrayal, and a burglar in the house. Ross uses a light society plot to press a grave question about race and love.
26716-the-crown-of-wild-olive-also-muner:
John Ruskin, M.A., gathered six works into this illustrated library edition, published by the Colonial Press Company at Boston and New York. The volume joins The Crown of Wild Olive, Munera Pulveris, and Pre-Raphaelitism with Aratra Pentelici. It also holds The Ethics of the Dust, Fiction, Fair and Foul, and The Elements of Drawing, with plates and woodcuts throughout.

The Crown of Wild Olive offers three lectures on work, traffic, and war. Munera Pulveris treats definitions, store-keeping, coin-keeping, commerce, government, and mastership. Aratra Pentelici lectures on the division of arts, idolatry, imagination, likeness, and structure, with plates from the porch of San Zenone at Verona to the Arethusa of Syracuse. Ruskin's preface recalls the Wandle's sources and the villages of Beddington and Carshalton.
27305-the-rural-life-problem-of-the-unit:
Sir Horace Plunkett's The Rural Life Problem of the United States, Notes of an Irish Observer, was published by Macmillan in 1910. It grew from five articles in the New York Outlook under the title Conservation and Rural Life. American friends interested in the rural life problem asked Plunkett to republish the series.

America has been, as to many Irishmen, a second home to him, and his notes come in friendly recognition of kindness he cannot hope to repay. Writing as a student of American social and economic problems, he weighs the country's farm life against older English-speaking countries and its abundance of agricultural resources.
27587-a-victor-of-salamis:
William Stearns Davis, author of A Friend of Caesar and God Wills It, published this tale of the days of Xerxes, Leonidas, and Themistocles with Macmillan in 1907. Its epigraph calls Athens the eye of Greece.

Davis argues that the invasion of Greece, with Thermopylae, Salamis, and Plataea, ranks among history's most dramatic events. Had Athens and Sparta succumbed to Oriental superstition and despotism, he says, the Parthenon, the Attic theatre, and Plato's dialogues would have been near impossible. Many scenes took shape on the actual fields of action during a recent visit to Greece. The novel gives a glimpse of the land of the Hellene.
27795-apologia-diffidentis:
W. Compton Leith published Apologia Diffidentis with John Lane at the Bodley Head in 1917, in a third edition, following his Sirenica. The book is an apology for a shy, furtive existence, written in solitude because the diffident, as Leith says, never speak if they can write.

Leith traces his shyness to boyhood, when at twelve he first incurred the obloquy of being shy, and compares shy souls to shore pools open to the sky at the lowest tides. Elegant and confessional, the book turns a private weakness into a literary subject with wit and melancholy.
28017-otherwise-phyllis:
Meredith Nicholson published Otherwise Phyllis with Houghton Mifflin in Boston and New York in 1913, with a frontispiece in color, dedicated to Albert B. Anderson of Montgomery. The contents move from The Kirkwoods Break Camp and The Montgomerys of Montgomery through A Transaction in Apples and The Otherwiseness of Phyllis.

The novel opens with Phil Kirkwood breaking camp, her camera safe on top of the wagon and her suitcase tied to the tailgate, as her father smothers the campfire. Nicholson's Hoosier novel follows Phyllis, her family, and the small-town world of Montgomery, with humor, romance, and local color.
29109-les-parsis:
D. Menant wrote this study of the Parsis, translated in part by Ratanbai Ardeshir Vakil and printed for private circulation in London in 1902. The Parsis, descendants of the ancient Persians, fled to India and settled chiefly in the Bombay region, with smaller groups remaining in Yezd and Kirman in Persia.

Menant traces their exodus, their fellow Zoroastrians left in Persia, and their population, costumes, usages, and festivals. He draws on the Bible, classical historians, national tradition, and inscriptions newly studied by European scholars. Readers get a compact early account of a small community that kept an ancient faith alive in exile.
2927-the-darwinian-hypothesis:
Thomas Henry Huxley's essay The Darwinian Hypothesis defends Darwin's Origin of Species as a work of growing immensity in scientific speculation. Huxley admits a preference for moral themes, quoting the Homeric sage who had seen cities of men and manners. Yet he insists that science lifts us out of ourselves and transfigures mortality. The essay treats Darwin's theory as a hypothesis to be tested, not a creed.

Huxley profiles an earlier naturalist who knew the lower forms of life better than any man of his day. Cuvier not excepted, he saw fine links of affinity joining all living beings. The highest creature grades into the lowest by multitudinous steps. The essay remains a landmark of Darwinian advocacy, learned and combative.
30489-phrenological-development-of-rober:
George Combe studies Robert Burns through phrenology, working from a cast of the poet's skull moulded at Dumfries on 31 March 1834. Engraved and published in Edinburgh in April 1834 and reprinted in January 1859, the pamphlet shows views of the skull and a key to the phrenological organs.

Combe, author of A System of Phrenology and The Constitution of Man, records Burns's birth on 25 January 1759 and death at Dumfries on 21 July 1796. He reads the skull's organs as signs of character, in the now discredited science of his day. The work survives as a curious record of how one age tried to read genius in bone.
31449-across-the-plains-to-california-in:
Lodisa Frizzell's journal records a journey across the plains to California in 1852, from the Little Wabash River in Illinois to the Pacific Springs of Wyoming. Edited from the original manuscript in the New York Public Library by Victor Hugo Paltsits, keeper of manuscripts, it was reprinted in May 1915 from the library's bulletin of April 1915. An illustration from a watercolor by Mrs. Frizzell herself accompanies the narrative.

Day by day, the journal follows an overland party through prairie, river crossings, and encounters on the trail. Its value lies in its immediacy: a woman traveler writing as she went, not recalling the trip years later. Readers of western history will find a firsthand account of emigration at its height, told in plain, daily entries.
31624-a-brief-history-of-element-discove:
Glen W. Watson's Brief History of Element Discovery, Synthesis, and Analysis, dated September 1963, comes from the Lawrence Radiation Laboratory of the University of California. It traces how new elements were found, made, and proved, with a table of the transuranium elements moved to the end of the text. The book's notes explain its signs for subscript and superscript numbers and for Greek letters.

Watson's history covers the chase for elements beyond uranium, where discovery means synthesis in the laboratory and analysis must confirm what was made. It is a compact technical history, written for readers who want the record of the search rather than a popular account.
32436-duel-on-syrtis:
Poul Anderson's tale, printed in Planet Stories in March 1951, follows Riordan, a bold, ruthless big-game hunter famed through the System. From firedrakes of Mercury to ice-crawlers of Pluto, he has slain them all, yet his trophy room lacks one item. Now Riordan swears he will bag forbidden game roaming the red deserts: a Martian.

On Syrtis, night whispers a warning through wind, half-sentient lichens, and dwarfed trees, carried by small creatures under crags and dunes. Kreega, a Martian alone for a hundred miles, feels dread pulsing through his brain: they are hunting again. Anderson pits hunter against hunted on a vast, lonely Mars, where the prey's senses and the night itself become part of the duel.
32612-the-irish-constitution-explained-b:
Darrell Figgis explains the Irish Constitution, printing an introduction, an explanation, a draft text, and the Articles of Agreement for a treaty between Great Britain and Ireland. His first rule is simple: a constitution should hold only what is fundamental and lasting.

Figgis warns against writing temporary, experimental, or doubtful matter into the basic law, since such matter belongs to ordinary lawmaking. He argues that a stable state needs firm foundations, and that change to the basic law should differ in kind from the daily work of a legislature. Figgis writes for citizens, not lawyers alone. His plain style makes a hard subject clear to a general reader.
32698-thoughts-on-the-religious-instruct:
William S. Plumer argues, in this Savannah book of 1848, that enslaved Black people in the American South should receive steady religious teaching. He opens with scripture and then traces missions by the United Brethren, who began work in the Danish West Indies in 1732 and spread to Jamaica, Antigua, Barbados, St. Kitts, and Tobago.

Plumer reports planters won over when teaching seemed to order rather than unsettle their estates, and he cites Georgia plantations where instruction went with neatness and good crops. He also urges ministers to preach to white congregations, so that the whole church would own the work.
32974-the-elements-of-blowpipe-analysis:
Frederick Hutton Getman, a chemistry instructor at Stamford High School, wrote this 1899 manual to teach blowpipe analysis, the laboratory art of testing minerals by heating them in a flame. Early chapters explain the apparatus and reagents. Early chapters lay out a general outline of the method: trials on charcoal alone, trials with sodium carbonate, and trials in a tube. Each step narrows what a sample can be.

The book is practical through and through, giving students a sequence of tests they could carry out with modest gear. In an age before quick instrumental analysis, the blowpipe was a chemist's portable laboratory, and Getman's clear order made it teachable in schools. The manual now reads as a window on how mineral study was done by hand, flame, and careful watching.
33119-battery-e-in-france-149th-field-ar:
Frederic R. Kilner's Battery E in France, published in Chicago in 1919, records the 149th Field Artillery of the Rainbow, or 42nd, Division in the First World War. Kilner dedicates the record to the battery's dead, named with places and dates of death. The author's note admits that a battery of nearly two hundred men, active in diverse places, cannot be fully told in one short book.

What follows is a unit history written close to events, naming men, guns, and ground in France. Kilner writes for the battery's own men and their families, preserving a record that larger histories would lose. For students of the American Expeditionary Forces and of the Rainbow Division, it remains a valuable, human-scale account of artillery war in 1918.
34266-the-graysons-a-story-of-illinois:
The Graysons is a novel of Illinois by Eggleston, author of famed past tales of school and road in the west vale. Pictures by a kin of his house fill its form. It came out at New York, its rights set in law in the late eighteen eighties.

Its word at the front tells how the book grew. He had thought, he says, to close his run of tales of life in the great west vale with a book of the years past. But a sheet chief asked him for a short tale for a great sheet, to be built on a lore tale of a trial of the young Lincoln. The theme grew in his hands, he owns, till the full novel stood there.
34871-the-englishman-from-paris:
Arthur Murphy wrote this farce in 1756; it survived in manuscript and was printed by the Augustan Reprint Society in 1969, with an introduction by Simon Trefman. The play is a sequel to Samuel Foote's The Englishman in Paris.

Trefman's introduction tells a sharp story. Foote, Murphy's friend and mentor, heard the whole plot in confidence one summer, then hurried out his own version first. Murphy's plan had been to bring Foote's boorish young squire home from France as a Frenchified fop at odds with his family. The introduction explains why Murphy stayed quiet about the play. Scholars get a lost farce plus the quarrel that buried it.
35084-london-in-modern-times-or-sketches:
Sketches of London in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries make up this book, printed in New York in 1851 for the Sunday-School Union. Its full title calls the city the English metropolis, and the introduction promises a look back into a past crowded with the picturesque, the romantic, and the religious.

Old buildings, the writer says, turn into poetry when great men were born or died in them. Narrow dirty streets where such men walked become green alleys in the mind. Tales of valour and suffering, of heroism and patience, crowd in alongside warnings from vice and crime. The broad thoroughfare itself is a river of human life, rolling for centuries between its banks, now calm and now stormy.
35125-dumas-paris:
Francis Miltoun wrote this guide to the Paris of Alexandre Dumas. Page printed it at Boston in 1904 with two maps. Miltoun also wrote Dickens London and French cathedral books. A portrait of Alexandre Dumas serves as the frontispiece art.

Contents trace Dumas early life in Paris and his writing career. His contemporaries and the Paris he knew fill the next chapters. Old Paris, the Seine banks, and the Second Empire follow on. The Louvre, Palais Royal, Bastille, and royal parks close the tour. French provinces and foreign lands fill two append chapters at the end of the guide.
35227-a-selection-from-the-poems-of-will:
A Selection from the Poems of William Morris opens with Rossetti circle lore. Franz Hueffer came into that circle, a letter shows. Lucy Rossetti wrote most of that letter. Hueffer was a broad-headed, able German, it says. He spoke and wrote fine English before naturalization. Gabriel Rossetti laughed at his heavy enthusiasms, it adds.

Rossetti coined a rhyme on Huffer's Schopenhauer talk. Morris, called Topsy by his friends, took such sallies too. His shock of black hair earned that name. The text notes an HTML form with the book's pictures. Page scans wait at the Internet Archive as well. Morris the poet, craftsman, and printer stands behind the verse chosen here. A gossipy frame of letters and rhymes sets the poems in the warm, teasing world that made them.
35361-the-wicked-marquis:
The Wicked Marquis is a novel by Phillips Oppenheim, copyrighted in 1919 by Little, Brown and issued at Toronto by McClelland and Stewart, with pictures by Will Grefe. The frontispiece shows luncheon at 94 Grosvenor Square, an exceedingly simple meal. Chapter one brings the Marquis of Mandeleys out of the Law Courts one May morning.

Reginald Philip Graham Thursford, Baron Travers, leaves the gloomy building without haste, yet plainly glad to be gone. Piloted across the Strand by his fawning companion, he unlocks his lips at last with a slow, pointed curse. Tall and slim as a marquis should be, he hides a calamity behind ease of manner. The tale turns on the title he succeeded to and the head-keeper at Mandeleys named in a picture caption.
35383-the-little-missis:
Charlotte Skinner wrote The Little Missis, a tale with six pictures, printed at London. Her chapter list runs to twenty-nine heads, with names such as A Testing Time, Will God Answer, and Love's Hospital. Faith is plainly a thread through the whole.

The story opens with Phebe, a bright young girl, taking tea with Mrs Colston, an old woman who works a mangle. Phebe has two secrets to tell, and the talk turns at once to love. Later chapters bring Bessie, Ralph, and a Deborah who hears a call. Skinner writes warmly of home, church work, and loyal love.
35561-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
Volume Fenton to Finis of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica holds entries in that stretch of the alphabet. The hosted text opens with a long list of small fixes made by the copyists. Those notes name the articles they touch.

Corrections fall in pieces on Ferdinand the Fifth, the poet Robert Fergusson, and fermentation. Fever and fibres also get fixes, down to one wrong letter at a time. The notes show the care taken to copy a vast work of reference true to print. Behind them stands the full run of articles from Fenton through Finis, a slice of a famed edition.
35831-the-outdoor-chums-on-a-houseboat-o:
The Outdoor Chums on a Houseboat, or The Rivals of the Mississippi, is a boys' adventure tale by Captain Quincy Allen. It was copyrighted in 1913 by Grosset and Dunlap. Allen wrote a shelf of Outdoor Chums books, on lake and in forest.

The four chums are college boys of the Rod, Gun and Camera Club: Frank, Will, Bluff, and Jerry. Will has great news and will not tell it till all four are together. The news is a houseboat trip down the great river. Bluff names the boat, and the first night afloat brings peril on the river. The chapters promise a runaway houseboat, an unwelcome passenger, and a bobcat on board. A rival crew races them down the stream. The finish of the voyage leaves the boys rivals no longer.
36266-the-bible-what-it-is:
Charles Bradlaugh, writing as Iconoclast, tests the Bible book by book in pamphlets sold by Holyoake and Co of Fleet Street. A transcriber's note grants that copies found cover just the first nine books of the Old Testament. Bradlaugh may never have finished the full run from Genesis to Revelations, the note adds with care.

Book one opens on Genesis by asking what the name Bible means and whence it came. Bradlaugh traces the word to a Greek term for books, first used in that sense by Chrysostom in the fifth century, he writes. He counts thirty-nine Old Testament books, twenty-seven New Testament books, and fourteen Apocrypha books. Hebrew, in which God taught Adam to speak by Parkhurst's claim, gets a sharp look next.
3688-the-chronicles-of-clovis:
Saki, the pen name of Hector Hugh Munro, writes short stories about Clovis Sangrail, a witty young man who punctures polite society with epigrams and pranks. The volume, introduced by A A Milne and dedicated to a lynx kitten with its reluctantly given consent, gathers tales first printed in newspapers. Milne's introduction notes that some good things we want to share, like a favorite restaurant, and some we guard jealously.

Clovis appears at country houses, London drawing rooms, and seaside hotels, where his talk turns dull weekends into mischief. Saki writes with brevity and bite, favoring surprise endings. The book suits readers who enjoy Edwardian satire and a hero whose manners are perfect and whose morals are gloriously unreliable.
37221-the-biological-problem-of-to-day-p:
Oscar Hertwig wrote a science book on how a new life grows from a seed. The book came out in London in 1896 in a set of science hand books. Chalmers Mitchell made the English form with a word list. Hertwig led a body lore school at the University of Berlin. His ask is plain: is growth pre-formed or made step by step?

Part one sets out Weismann's germ plasm thought in full. Germ cells bear set bits that fix each part, that school holds. Part two builds Hertwig's own view of growth. He weighs cell, food, and place in the new form. Life science fans get a core fight in clear terms.
37253-in-the-land-of-the-great-snow-bear:
Gordon Stables wrote a tale of love and heroism, illustrated by Gordon Browne and published by the Sunday School Union at London. Its first chapter is set at Dunallan Towers on the banks of the winding Nith, once the happiest and gayest of mansions, now gloomy and desolate. There the boy Claude Alwyn grows up unusual, even in infancy.

The narrator argues that individuality is stamped on a child from birth, and that early company moulds but cannot alter it. His matter comes from an old journal handed to him by its writer. Lord Alwyn had married an English baronet's only daughter, to the grumbling of Scottish neighbours who thought a goshawk should not mate with a ringdove. Northern adventure follows the boyhood.
37453-the-barber-of-paris:
The Barber of Paris, a novel by Charles Paul de Kock, was translated into English by Edith Mary Norris. The Brainard Publishing Company issued it at Boston and New York, with copyright from 1903. The tale is told in two volumes of intrigue and comedy.

The chapters promise a great nobleman and a barber, a history of sorcerers, the Chevalier Chaudoreille, a music lesson, an abduction, and a night adventure on the Pont-Neuf. The story opens on an evening in December 1632, when a man walks fast down the Rue Saint-Honoré toward the Rue Bourdonnais. De Kock was a prolific French novelist of Parisian manners, and Norris's translation brought one of his historical romances to English readers at the start of the twentieth century.
37728-south-and-south-central-africa-a-r:
H Frances Davidson wrote South and South Central Africa, a record of fifteen years of missionary labors among primitive peoples. The Brethren Publishing House at Elgin, Illinois printed it for the author in nineteen fifteen. Davidson dedicated it to Dr W O Baker, chairman of the missionary board of the Brethren in Christ Church.

Early chapters trace the start of foreign mission work in eighteen ninety four, Davidson's call, and the sailing in eighteen ninety seven. The party lands at Cape Town, picks Matabeleland, and treks to the Matopo Hills in eighteen ninety eight. Later chapters add new workers in eighteen ninety nine, sickness and deaths in nineteen hundred, a return to America in nineteen four, and new missions at Mapani and Mtshabezi. Church readers get a field record of the first Brethren missions in south central Africa.
37884-folk-tales-of-the-khasis:
Folk-Tales of the Khasis is a gathering of tales from the Khasi people, set down by Mrs. Rafy and printed at London in 1920. The book holds thirty-two tales, with pictures of Khasi peasants, hills, and waterfalls. Many tales ask how a thing came to be: what makes the eclipse, why the peacock wears fine feathers, how the dog came to live with man.

Others tell of gods who came to dwell with mankind, of U Raitong the Khasi Orpheus, and of the leap of Ka Likai. Beast tales stand beside sacred ones, such as the lost book and the blessing of the beggar. The set keeps a hill people's lore in print for far readers.
37915-notes-on-the-book-of-genesis:
Henry Longstreth issued notes on the book of Genesis at Philadelphia in 1863, in a first American edition. The notes run chapter by chapter through the whole first book of the Bible. Groups of chapters share long notes at the end of the set.

A warm preface urges the notes on all who love the plain gospel of grace. It praises their deep tone and their clear pair of claims: man's full ruin in sin, and God's full cure in Christ. Rest for a torn heart, the preface says, comes only when a soul sees that sin was judged once for all on the cross.
37928-gas-burners-old-and-new-a-historic:
Owen Merriman wrote Gas Burners Old and New, a treatise on invention in gas lighting, reprinted in London in 1884. The pieces first ran in the Journal of Gas Lighting. A preface hopes the book will lessen suspicion and prejudice against gas, born of ignorance. Contents run from the first gas-burner to incandescent burners.

Chapters treat the batswing burner, the union-jet or fishtail, and how light is produced from coal gas. Later parts cover Bronner's burners, Bray's burners, Argand burners, and governor burners. Merriman notes that one burner may give twice the light of another for the same gas, at no higher first cost. Knowing that, he argues, is of great value to the consumer.
37937-a-wanderer-in-paris:
Lucas wrote this account of Paris wholly from the outside, as he warns in his preface. It holds only so much of the city as a foreigner with no French friends may observe on holiday visits. Methuen first published it in August 1909, and this tenth edition of February 1913 testifies to its welcome. Sixteen illustrations in color by Walter Dexter and thirty-two reproductions from works of art fill the book.

Lucas had already wandered in London, Florence, and Holland in print, and Paris gets the same genial, sauntering treatment. A note in this edition owns that the theft of the Mona Lisa has turned his pages on the Louvre's chief treasure into the past tense. The book is a holiday companion: streets, pictures, and Parisians, taken at a walker's pace by a cheerful amateur.
37992-the-king-of-pirates-being-an-accou:
The King of Pirates is a pamphlet of 1720 presenting two letters said to be from Captain Avery, the pirate who was fabled to have made himself mock king of Madagascar. The letters, one written from Madagascar and one after his escape, claim to give his own account of his rambles and piracies. The publishers promise that the sham accounts already in print will here be detected and corrected.

The preface argues the case at length. Earlier writers, it says, made Avery's story as monstrous as they pleased, because the world expected monstrous things of him. On the great scandal of his career, the taking of the Great Mogul's daughter, the letters insist she was robbed but otherwise used with decency. The pamphlet is an early exercise in pirate myth-making, selling the correction of a legend as eagerly as the legend itself.
38078-siam-the-land-of-the-white-elephan:
George Bacon put in one book the best tales of Siam by past guests. Frederick Wells Williams gave the book a fresh form in 1893. It sits in a set of books of travel with plates. A great shrine, Wat Chang, fronts the book in a plate. Williams cut what was wrong or old, he says in his note.

Old guests like Pallegoix, Bowring, and Mouhot ground the tale. Siam is named the land of the white elephant in the title. Kings, shrines, trade, and folk ways fill the short book. Williams grants a full true book on Siam was yet to come. Home readers got a fair view of a far land.
38219-a-general-introduction-to-psychoan:
A General Introduction to Psychoanalysis, by Sigmund Freud, was published in New York in nineteen twenty by Horace Liveright. The authorized translation carries a preface by G Stanley Hall, president of Clark University. The book prints Freud's lecture course in three parts.

Part one treats the psychology of errors: slips of speech, misreading, and temporary forgetfulness. Freud argues such small failures are not accidents but evidence. Part two turns to the dream, its censor, its symbolism, and wish fulfilment. Part three builds the general theory of the neuroses, through symptoms, resistance, the libido, and transference. Twenty-eight lectures carry a lay audience from everyday blunders to analytic therapy. The volume introduced psychoanalysis to the English-reading public.
38371-exempting-the-churches-an-argument:
James Morton wrote a plea in 1916 against freeing church property from tax. He calls the practice unjust and against the nation's founding law. Two quotes head the work. One states that no person shall be made to support a place of worship against his consent. The other, from Ingersoll, holds that to free a church from tax is to pay part of the priest's pay.

The plea opens with the long fight of the free spirit against special favour. Kings, kaisers and born rulers, it says, are drags on the wheel of progress. Their day is ending, and rule by birth is now seen as a lie. Church tax freedom stands in the same line of favour, Morton argues.
38709-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The eleventh form of the great fact book fills this long text. The span of this part runs from the word cube to a French name. Notes at the front tell how the plain text form was made of the print. Small marks for roots and Greek script are shown by set signs.

Slips in the print are named and set right in the notes list. A bird's name, a vine clan, and a town of the east show the kind. A long piece on the bent line in sums stands in this span. It speaks of nodes that fade and points that lie in a row. The fix list shows the care the typists took with the old print. The span is one slice of the last great print of the work.
38715-a-singular-metamorphosis:
May Evelyn Skiles wrote A Singular Metamorphosis, a novel published in 1902. Only seven chapters stand in the contents, which is itself a hint of the book's odd shape. The tale is set in an old mansion with a secret at its center.

Miss Fiske has lived several years with the Tracys, brother and sister, in their great house. A mystery hangs over the household: at fixed times of the year, when she comes near certain parts of the mansion, she is turned back. The chapters promise a demand for explanation, the advent of Ralph and a rejected proposal, misunderstandings, and a startling revelation. Two couples take a walk in the last chapter. Readers get a household mystery that turns on what the Tracys hide, and why.
39395-the-expositor-s-bible-the-book-of-:
Marcus Dods wrote a reading of Genesis for a famed series of Bible handbooks, sold in New York by Armstrong. Thirty one chapters follow the book from the creation to the blessings of the tribes. A man who wants the age of the earth, Dods says, must go to new books on the stars, the rocks, and old bones.

No one, he says, dreams of sending such a student to the Bible for facts of that kind. Scripture does not aim to teach the facts of nature. Its aim is to show what bond the world has with God. The chapters then take the fall, Cain and Abel, the flood, and the call of Abraham. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph fill the rest.
39677-a-classified-catalogue-of-works-in:
A Classified Catalogue of Works in General Literature lists Longmans’ books by kind. Longmans, Green, and Company kept shops in London, New York, and Bombay. Their house stood at Thirty Nine Paternoster Row in those years. Each class of books takes its own part of the long roll.

History, politics, and state memoirs lead the proud array. Lives and personal memoirs stand next in the set scheme. The Badminton Library of sport and the Fur and Feather set shine there. Travel, colonies, and high adventure fill their own full part. Verse and drama, fiction and humour, each take a wide span. Cookery, house rule, and fine arts crowd the late pages. The Silver Library and books for children close the trade list. An index of authors, from Abbott to Buckle and past, ends it.
39703-the-first-boke-of-moses-called-gen:
Tyndale's translation of Genesis, 'The First Boke of Moses called Genesis,' is printed here in blackletter form, with wide variations in spelling and punctuation retained. Transcribers note that the King James Version, which took up most of Tyndale's rendering, was consulted where the worn type is hard to read. Abbreviation marks and superscript letters are kept as marks in the text.

Tyndale's address to the reader stands before the book. He recalls asking the learned to amend whatever was amiss in his New Testament, and answers the hypocrites who attack the work. Some say scripture cannot be translated into English, some that lay people may not lawfully have it in their mother tongue. Others claim it would make them all heretics, or make them rise against the king. Tyndale charges that his enemies forbid the book lest temporal rulers see their falsehood if scripture came to light.
39915-gouverneur-morris:
Theodore Roosevelt wrote this life of Gouverneur Morris, first printed under copyright in 1888 for the American Statesmen series. Morris, who helped frame the Constitution, was among the most brilliant of the founders, though not the greatest. Roosevelt complains that his only earlier biographer, Jared Sparks, buried him in dull, endless praise.

Sparks had gathered facts, letters, and diary extracts with great industry, but wrote without life or judgement. Roosevelt sets out to do better: a short, sharp life that weighs the man as well as lauds him. The book is as much a lesson in how lives should be written as it is the story of Morris himself.
40162-the-humour-and-pathos-of-anglo-ind:
Doctor Ticklemore's extracts from his brother's notebook on the humour and pathos of Anglo Indian life were edited by Mayer and printed at London in 1895. The Elephanta and her passengers open the set. If the reader could call back the flight of time some twenty years, the tale begins. Transported on board the homeward bound steamer Elephanta, he would see some twenty persons assembled in the saloon near the piano.

Captain James Ward, the commander of the vessel, stood in the centre of the group. Captain Whistler and life in cantonment at Secunderabad follow. Miss B and her present, the delights of Indian music, and a passage of arms between a colonel and a lady fill the middle. The race stand and the fancy ball, worshipping titled folk, and curious Moplah customs close the shelf. Raj life is drawn with love and a grin.
40293-vie-de-bohe-me-a-patch-of-romantic:
Orlo Williams wrote Vie de Boheme, a patch of romantic Paris, first published in 1913 and printed at Boston. The contents move from the true bohemia through a fringe of history to the sickness of the age. Parisian society and the viveurs follow, then the romantic bohemia and the second cenacle. Schaunard and Company and Murger and his friends close the tale of the set.

Pictures by Gavarni, Lami, and Meryon fill the list, from fashion plates to old Paris streets. A line from Murger heads the first chapter, calling bohemia the stage of artistic life. Williams begins by blaming newspapers for keeping catchwords alive past their hour. Amusements of bohemia and the Paris of bohemia round out the survey.
40306-nooks-corners-of-old-paris:
Nooks and Corners of Old Paris is a guide to the city's vanishing streets by Georges Cain. Cain curated the Carnavalet Museum and the historic collections of Paris. Frederick Lawton translated the book, and E Grant Richards published it in London in 1907. Victorien Sardou supplied a preface. More than a hundred illustrations show the old quarters.

The frontispiece shows the Rue du Chaume in 1866, now the Rue des Archives. The engravings list the Place de la Bastille, the Pont-Neuf about 1850, and the Louvre about 1785. Demolition scenes record streets being cut away in the 1860s. Other plates show the Conciergerie, the Sainte-Chapelle, and the Isle of Saint-Louis. Cain dedicated the work to A G Lenotre in December 1905. The book preserves, street by street, a Paris that Haussmann's boulevards were sweeping away.
40480-the-quest-of-the-four-a-story-of-t:
Joseph A Altsheler wrote The Quest of the Four, a story of the Comanches and Buena Vista, with copyright in 1911. Altsheler also wrote The Last of the Chiefs and The Young Trailers. The tale opens in New Orleans, on a brilliant spring day at the Place d'Armes. Phil Bedford, a tall boy, dreams as he walks across the square.

Phil's blue eyes, fair hair, and white skin mark him as a northerner, from Kentucky or Virginia perhaps. His mind roams the vast Southwest, over mountains, plains, and deserts he has never trod. He is bound on a vital quest into that unknown land. Contents promise a Comanche village, a medicine lodge, and the Pass of Angostura. The tale builds to Buena Vista and a castle of Montevideo.
40492-sylvie-souvenirs-du-valois:
Gérard de Nerval wrote Sylvie, Souvenirs du Valois, translated by Lucie Page, issued at Portland, Maine, by Thomas B Mosher in eighteen ninety six. An Andrew Lang sonnet on Nerval heads the book. A Lang essay, Sylvie et Aurélie, stands in the appendix. Fourteen short chapters fill the tale. Chapter one is A Wasted Night. The Valois country of Nerval youth is the scene.

Of all that were thy prisons, ah untamed, ah light and sacred soul, none holds thee now, Lang sonnet opens. In the tale, a Paris actor love for Aurélie draws the teller back to Loisy and Ermenonville. Memories of Adrienne, a village girl turned nun, and of Sylvie, a peasant sweetheart, weave through the nights. A Voyage to Cythera and The Ball at Loisy fill the middle. Poetry lovers get a jewel of French prose in English.
405-adventures-and-letters-of-richard-ha:
Charles Belmont Davis edits this life of his brother, war reporter and novelist Richard Harding Davis, in twenty chapters plus letters. Born in Philadelphia in 1864, Davis rose from college days to New York papers, then to wars in Cuba, Greece, South Africa, and Europe. Plays, travel pieces, and books filled the years between campaigns.

Letters and memories show a man loved for dash, charm, and nerve under fire. His brother stresses the Philadelphia home that shaped him and the friends who mourned him young. The volume serves as both life and tribute, rich in firsthand detail of a reporter's age.
40538-encyclopaedia-britannica-11th-edit:
The hosted text is one slice of the eleventh edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica, running from Husband to Hydrolysis. That famed edition set out the best learning of its day in long, signed articles. This slice takes in words from Huss and Hyacinth to Hydraulics.

Short notes at the front tell how small numbers, Greek letters, and side heads were handled in the plain text. The slice holds lives, plants, faith terms, and large works of applied science side by side. Hydraulics gets long treatment, with figures on water works such as those at Manchester. Readers can dip in for one topic or browse the range of a great reference shelf. The text keeps the tone and depth that made the eleventh edition a classic.
406-appreciations-of-richard-harding-dav:
Friends and peers pay tribute to war reporter Richard Harding Davis in this memorial volume. Gouverneur Morris, Booth Tarkington, Theodore Roosevelt, Winston Churchill, Irvin Cobb, and others each add a short piece. They recall Davis as a man who stayed boyish at fifty-two, yet faced fire in Cuba with calm nerve.

Anecdotes tell of pirate games, hunts, and wounded men carried in under fire. The Rough Riders, the writers say, made him an honorary member for deeds, not charm alone. Together the pieces form a fond portrait of a reporter who lived his tales as boldly as he wrote them.
41134-the-white-rose-of-memphis:
The White Rose of Memphis is a novel by Falkner, first copyrighted in 1881. Lines from Lovelace stand at its front, on freedom in love and a soul set free. A publisher's preface tells the book's strange fortune in print. For thirty one years, it says, this book has met the favour of the public. Its sale had reached one hundred sixty thousand copies by the time of this preface.

The sale was still growing steadily, the preface boasts, though the plates were worn. This thirty fifth edition is printed from new plates. It is offered in the belief that it will outlive its years of copyright, the publishers add. Few works of fiction, they claim, are credited with such favour or such a spread. Falkner of Mississippi wrote this romance of the river city in his years of local fame.
41526-a-little-girl-in-old-st-louis:
A Little Girl in Old St Louis, by Amanda Douglas, was published at New York by Dodd, Mead in 1903. Douglas had written like tales of old Boston, Detroit, and Washington. Her heroine here is Renée de Longueville, named in the first chapter. Old St Louis itself takes the second chapter as its stage.

A new home, the sowing of a thorn, and a touch of sorrow follow. By the fireside and at the king’s ball, the girl’s world widens. A surprise, prisoners, and a spell in the wilderness raise the stakes. Passing years and gathering thistles mark the later chapters. Douglas wrote history for girls as a story of one child’s life. French old St Louis, on the great river, gives her a rich and little used setting.
41648-millais:
A Lys Baldry wrote a short book on the painter Millais, who lived from 1829 to 1896, for a series of colour art books edited by T Leman Hare. Each book in the set pairs one painter with one writer, and names at the front run from Bellini and Botticelli to Turner and Whistler. Colour plates show the painters key works.
