Plate one, shown at the front, is The Order of Release, held at the Tate Gallery in London. Baldry says Millais counted it among his greatest wins, and praises its earnest, thoughtful truth to life. A wife brings the order that frees her wounded Highlander husband, her face mixing love with triumph over a wavering jailer.
4268-cousin-phillis:
Elizabeth Gaskell published Cousin Phillis in 1863. The story is told by a young clerk who lodges above a pastry-cook's shop in Eltham. He works under the engineer building a branch railway to Hornby. His father, a mechanic with inventive genius, placed him in a post above his own station.

His father devised several improvements in railway machinery. The four parts follow the narrator's growing friendship with his cousin Phillis and her family. Railway work, learning, and courtship disturb a quiet country household. Gaskell's short novel is admired for restraint: small choices, and the arrival of new ideas, change lives without melodrama.
42722-historic-paris:
Jetta Wolff's Historic Paris was published by John Lane at London and New York in 1921, with fifty-nine illustrations. Wolff also wrote The Story of the Churches of Paris, and the dedication is to France, the beautiful, the valorous. Fifty-two short chapters walk the city by quarters: three palaces, old streets, the great markets, the Palais de Justice, the Temple, and the home of Madame de Sevigne. Notre-Dame, the Ile Saint-Louis, the Hotel de Ville, the Place des Vosges, and the Bastille follow.

The route continues through the Luxembourg, the Invalides, the old mansions of the Rive Gauche, Montmartre, the Gobelins, and Pere-Lachaise. A final group treats the boulevards, quays, and bridges. The frontispiece shows the clock tower and pointed towers of the Conciergerie above the flower market. Wolff writes a walker's history, building each quarter's past out of its standing stones.
42835-tommy-tregennis:
Tommy Tregennis is a tale for the young by Phillips, with prints in hue by a named artist in its full print form. A note at the front tells where that bright form can be had, and where page scans rest. The house that put it out was a New York firm of long stand.

Its plate list tells the shape of the tale in glimpses. Ladies talk to a nurse while a child waits by. A boy leads a horse up and down a lane with pride after the meal. A mother croons to her lamb, and two folk creep at a slow pace on rough stones. A mother scans an angry sea at dusk with fear, and a day of grief at a grannys grave closes the hints.
42888-fur-farming-for-profit-with-especi:
Fur Farming for Profit, with Especial Reference to Skunk Raising, is a practical manual from a fur farm company at Spencer, Indiana. Its price was one dollar, printed on the title page beside a picture of a skunk. Advertisements around the text offer top prices for live mink and mink pelts. Ginseng and yellowroot are also bought by the advertisers.

Inside, pens, feeding, breeding, and killing for pelts are the working subjects, with skunks stressed as a cheap and hardy stock for beginners. The mix of instruction and trade ads shows a rural boom sold by mail. Small farmers were urged to turn backyard stock into cash income from the fur trade.
42971-macaulay-s-life-of-samuel-johnson-:
Charles Lane Hanson edited a school form of Macaulay's Life of Samuel Johnson for Ginn and Company. The rights date is 1903, and Hanson taught English in Boston. His long opening part gives Macaulay's life, his peers, and how to study his work. Timelines for both Macaulay and Johnson help set the scene.

The main text gives Macaulay's life of Johnson in full, then part of his essay on Boswell. Notes at the back run from page 77 and gloss hard points. Students gain two famed critics in one small book. The mix shows how Macaulay judged Johnson's talk, books, and fame.
43155-thorpe-regis:
Frances Peard wrote a village novel in an edition dated at Boston in 1874. It opens on the word change, which nowadays suggests growth and progress, yet must here be read backwards. Thorpe Regis was a straggler, left behind by the great march of an ever-increasing population.

Once the great high road to London ran through it, and twice a week the London coach lumbered up to the Red Lion. Horses were changed, cramped passengers stretched their limbs or drank ale in the stuffy little bar, and country boys felt a proud proprietorship in the Defiance and the Highflyer. Those days are gone as the tale begins, and the quiet left behind is its subject.
43329-the-life-of-jefferson-davis:
A biography of Jefferson Davis by Frank H Alfriend. Publishers in Cincinnati, Chicago, Richmond, and other cities issued it in 1868. Alfriend had edited the Southern Literary Messenger. Copyright was entered a year before publication. His preface confesses a painful sense of inadequacy. Earnest conviction, he says, emboldened him more than confidence did.

He claims facts only, drawn from acquaintance and documents. Labour over papers within his reach supports the narrative. He denies any aim of sectional bitterness. Yet he writes openly as a Southern man. Vindicating the South and its late leader is his stated incentive. The book appeared just three years after Appomattox. It stands among the first lives of the Confederate president.
43448-second-annual-report-of-the-kensin:
The Kensington Church of England District Visiting Society issued its second annual report in London on February 3, 1846. Archdeacon Sinclair, the vicar, served as president of the group. Shephard served as treasurer, with three joint secretaries.

The report covers the work of the society in 1845 and was read at the annual meeting at the National School. Members voted to accept the report and print it for subscribers. Lists name the full committee, auditors, and the collector in Hornton Street. The pamphlet is a small window into parish visiting and church charity work in early Victorian London.
43633-the-royal-life-guard-or-the-flight:
Alexander Dumas's The Royal Life Guard, or The Flight of the Royal Family, is a historical romance of the suppression of the French monarchy. Ogilvie issued it at New York in the Sunset Series at twenty-five cents, in Henry Llewellyn Williams's translation from the latest Paris edition. The first chapter opens on the changed France: a limited monarchy, Louis the Sixteenth sworn to the constitution. He was absent from the Te Deum, since he would tell a lie but not commit perjury.

Marie Antoinette, the daughter of Austria, stands as the people's foe, while Mirabeau has been bought by the court with paid debts and a monthly salary. The head of this copy carries Ogilvie's advertisements first, for Cooper's Leather Stocking Tales and a matrimonial advice book, before the title page. Dumas's tale builds toward the royal family's flight, the Varennes episode of the Revolution.
43928-the-british-woodlice-being-a-monog:
The British Woodlice is a study of the land shell beasts of the British Isles, by Webb and Sillem. One of them taught life lore for two shires and ran a sheet on shells. The work first ran in a field club sheet of Essex, in the years just past.

The club let it be struck anew by their kind leave, its note says. Twenty five plates and near sixty cuts in the text show each kind. It came out at London in the first years of the last age. Its first words weigh a hard fact of its field: no group of beasts is so oft met with, it holds, and yet so little known. The book then sets each British kind in its place, with its marks, haunts, and spread.
43966-witchcraft-and-superstitious-recor:
Witchcraft and Superstitious Record in the South Western District of Scotland gathers lore by J Maxwell Wood. Wood edited a Galloway journal for a decade, his title page notes. Drawings by John Copland picture the text. The Dumfries edition is dated nineteen eleven. Its cover lists its fields: witch trials, fairy lore, brownie lore, wraiths, warnings, death customs, and ghost lore.

In his preface Wood says remnants of old world customs still linger in Dumfriesshire and Galloway. They suggest a remoter time when belief ruled daily life, he writes. He gathered the available material on such matters, he says. His aim is to record his gleanings much as they were received. He will not subject them to higher analysis, he adds. Chapters treat traditional witchcraft first, then narratives and trials.
43979-the-real-jefferson-davis:
Landon Knight wrote this life of Jefferson Davis, the real man. Pilgrim Magazine printed it at Battle Creek in 1904. A photo of Davis in 1865 fronts the volume here. A verse on peace flowers over the old battle storm opens it.

Contents run from birth and schooling to army service first. Briarfield life, first politics, and the Mexican War follow in turn. Buena Vista hero, senator, and war secretary mark his rise. Confederate president, Sumter, Shiloh, and Gettysburg fill the war chapters. Davis and Gettysburg and the chief of a heroic people fill two more war chapters.
44140-george-whitefield-a-biography-with:
George Whitefield, a biography with special reference to his labors in America, was compiled by Joseph Belcher. The American Tract Society published it at New York. Belcher had written the life of Carey, the missionary to India. The contents begin with the moral state of Great Britain in the early seventeen hundreds.

Whitefield's birth in Gloucester, his early life, and his entrance at Oxford fill the first chapter. There he joined the Wesleys and other Methodists, passed through illness and mental trials, and found relief. Ordination and his first sermon end the chapter, covering 1714 to 1736. The second chapter treats his success as a preacher in England and his first visit to America. It tells of Savannah and his orphan asylum's origin. Whitefield was the great travelling preacher of the Great Awakening, and Belcher's life served the evangelical readers who cherished his memory.
44645-a-short-view-of-the-immorality-and:
Jeremy Collier, an English clergyman, published this attack on the London stage in 1698. He charges the plays of his day with two faults: loose morals and open contempt for religion. The contents show him proving each charge with scenes and lines taken from named plays, and with long lists of swearing, mockery of clergy, and abuse of Scripture.

Collier also argues from the past, claiming that Greek and Roman plays were cleaner than the English ones of his time. He gives short studies of Plautus, Terence, Seneca, and the Greek stage to make the point. Even Ben Jonson and other playwrights are called as witnesses against the stage. The book stirred a famous fight over what the theatre should be allowed to show.
47078-a-manual-of-clinical-diagnosis:
James Campbell Todd, a pathology professor at Denver, wrote this manual of clinical diagnosis in 1908. Saunders published it at Philadelphia and London with plates throughout. A frontispiece shows a scale of urinary colors, according to Vogel, as a guide for doctors at the bench.

Todd dedicates the pages affectionately to his father, a doctor himself by name on the dedication. Chapter one treats the sputum, starting with physical examination of the sample. Microscopic work, stained and unstained, follows in the contents, then sputa in disease. Blood, urine and other fluids get the same practical treatment for hospital and office diagnosis.
47233-dr-stearns-s-tour-from-london-to-p:
Samuel Stearns, styled an American philosopher on his front plate, rode from London to Paris in the first heat of the French Revolution. Dr Stearns's Tour pours out its whole scope on the title page. France's customs, manners, rule, science, trade, and fields all come in.

The old form of rule and the new stand side by side. Facts on the royal family and the causes of the late upheaval fill the middle. The fall of the Bastille and dread commotions get their share. A minute account of the grand day at the Champ de Mars closes the tour. Then Stearns does a bold thing: he draws a new constitution, with a road to liberty drawn after it.
48406-the-atomic-fingerprint-neutron-act:
Bernard Keisch explains neutron activation analysis, a way of naming the elements in a sample by making it briefly radioactive and reading the rays it gives off. His booklet opens with puzzles the method can solve: whether a treatment for bone loss is working, and why plastic from a plant is discolored. It can also judge whether 50 museum gold coins said to be 1500 years old are genuine, and match paint from a hit-and-run to a suspect's car.

The United States Energy Research and Development Administration published the booklet in 1972 for general readers. Keisch takes the method into a physics laboratory, a hospital, a plastics plant, a museum, and a crime laboratory in turn. Plain language and photographs carry the science, which can find traces far too small for ordinary chemistry to catch.
48531-the-romaunce-of-the-sowdone-of-bab:
The Romaunce of the Sowdone of Babylone is a Middle English Charlemagne romance, edited by Emil Hausknecht. The Early English Text Society published the text at London in 1881. Hausknecht re-edited the poem from the sole surviving copy, once held by a famed collector. Notes and a word list close the volume.

The long opening essay traces the fame of the Ferumbras story across Europe. It weighs the French, Provencal, and English forms of the tale. The poem tells of the Sultan of Babylon and his son Ferumbras, who conquered Rome. Hausknecht studies the dialect, metre, and date of the English poem. He also compares a Hanover manuscript of the French tale. A sketch of the story guides new readers through the plot. The edition served scholars of early English verse and of the Charlemagne cycle.
48637-pioneer-life-in-illinois:
Perryman wrote this plain tale of early days in Illinois, and Kerr's Printing House at Pana made it in 1907. His portrait heads the book. The preface owns the book's faults upfront: to err is human, he says, and no polish is claimed.

What he sought was the true state of the country in early days. He kept the book's tone and tongue as near to those days as good sense allows. Readers must judge its merits for themselves, he adds, and pardon what faults they find. If some thoughts in it fit readers for the battles of life, and for use to others, his trouble is well repaid. A settler's own record of cabin, field, and town as they were.
48996-india-and-tibet-a-history-of-the-r:
India and Tibet is a history by Sir Francis Younghusband, printed at London in 1910 with maps and pictures. Its full title promises the story of dealings between the two lands from the time of Warren Hastings to 1910, with a full account of the mission to Lhasa of 1904. A portrait of the Dalai Lama stands at the front, and Younghusband gives the book to his wife.

The first chapter takes up Hastings's policy and Bogle's mission of 1774. Bhutanese attacks on Bengal led Hastings to seek friendship and trade with Tibet, and Bogle was received by the Tashi Lama. Younghusband writes as a man who had himself served on that far frontier, and the book mixes archive with memory.
49031-a-migration-legend-of-the-creek-in:
A Migration Legend of the Creek Indians, volume one, by Albert S Gatschet of the Bureau of Ethnology, is number four in Brinton's Library of Aboriginal American Literature. D G Brinton published it at Philadelphia in 1884. A linguistic, historic, and ethnographic introduction fills most of the volume. The map meant for it was delayed and promised with the second volume.

Brinton's prefatory note sets the stake. The tribes of the Gulf watershed may link the races of North and South America. Years before, he had found and printed the legend of Chekilli. Gatschet takes that legend as his centre and groups the ethnography of the whole territory round it. This volume gives the general discussion and closes with the Creek version of the legend and its translation. The Hitchiti version and vocabulary wait for volume two.
49414-monsieur-bergeret-in-paris:
Monsieur Bergeret in Paris is a novel by Anatole France, in an English translation by Drillien. John Lane printed it at London and New York in 1922, in a second edition. The volume belongs to the works of Anatole France in English translation, edited by James Lewis May and Bernard Miall. Bergeret is France's gentle professor, and Paris is where his provincial life has brought him.

The first chapter is a small domestic comedy. Monsieur Bergeret sits at table taking his frugal evening meal. His little dog Riquet lies at his feet on a tapestry cushion. Old Angélique brings in a spring chicken and offers to carve it. The old servant's respect for tradition is profound. France builds a whole philosophy of custom out of a chicken.
49762-diagnosis:
Palmer wrote this science fiction tale for Other Worlds, where it ran in March 1953, with plates by McCauley. Its head note gives the mix: two men and one girl, the old triangle, stirred with a wild oscilloscope. What comes out is adventure, terror, and romance.

What time did you get to bed last night is the first line, a tease between workers. Donald Jensen grills Mary on her night out with Brannan. If you got in by three, it would be early, he scoffs. Mary, arch, will not name the hour. Their experiment needs her fresh, he insists. A tired girl and a haywire scope in a lab set a light tale with a dark turn.
50008-the-kacha-ris:
Sidney Endle wrote The Kacharis, a study put out by Macmillan at London in 1911. Endle had long been chaplain at Tezpur and head of the Kachari mission there. The book was made by order of the government of Eastern Bengal and Assam. Anderson wrote the opening note, and Gurdon added notes as head of ethnology for that government. Photos show weaving, dress, fishing, and village life in Kamrup.

Parts treat the traits of the Kachari folk, their past spread, and their home life. Laws, customs, faith, tales, and old beliefs follow in order. A short grammar and word lists close the main text. Two appendices name kindred tribes and give samples of the Bodo tongue. The book is a full record of a people set by the side of Hindu and Muslim neighbours.
50330-the-substance-of-faith-allied-with:
Oliver Lodge wrote a short faith guide in the form of questions and answers. Lodge was head of the University of Birmingham. The book first came out in February 1907 and hit a sixth form by April. Its full aim is to ally faith with science. Lodge wrote it for parents and those who teach the young.

Parts climb from the rise of man to soul and spirit. He deals with right and wrong, sin, and the root of evil. Grace and the life of Christ in man get late parts. His tone is broad and kind to doubt. Readers get a calm bridge twixt lab and church.
50420-history-of-the-beef-cattle-industr:
Frank Webster Farley wrote this history of the beef cattle industry in Illinois as a thesis for the degree of Bachelor of Science in Agriculture. The University of Illinois approved it in May 1915, under the animal husbandry department. His index starts with the land itself, its people, and its cattle.

Chapters cover the cattle feeding industry, the first silo in Illinois, and the Chicago market. Named cattle barons and pioneer drovers include John Alexander, Jacob Strawn, Benjamin Harris, and Tom Candy Ponting. The range industry and Texas cattle, the pure bred trade, cattle plagues, and the feed industry of the United States complete the survey.
50424-the-impending-crisis:
The Impending Crisis, by Basil Bouroff, was published at Chicago in 1900. The Midway Press Committee issued the book. Bouroff was a graduate student at the University of Chicago. His subtitle names the subject: conditions resulting from the concentration of wealth in the United States. The preface is firm: this is not a novel. Facts come from the Eleventh Census and other reports. Bouroff says the book shows the nation's essential situation. Cities pass fast into the hands of a very few owners. Farmers lose their ground, and city people lose their liberty.

All grow dependent on a few multi-millionaires, he argues. The nation becomes one of tenants paying rent on farms and homes. While wealth grows, most people struggle for bare existence. Bouroff piles up compared statistics from rival authorities to fix the true base of the problem.
50797-tagalog-texts-with-grammatical-ana:
Leonard Bloomfield wrote Tagalog Texts with Grammatical Analysis, in 1917. The University of Illinois published it in its studies in language and literature. The graduate school stood behind the series at Urbana that year. The work falls in three parts, the title page lays out. Texts and translation make the first part of the volume.

Grammatical analysis makes the second part, and a glossary the third. Phonetics opens the analysis: distinctive sounds, syllabication, and accent. Syntax follows, with the sentence and its parts of speech weighed. Static and transient words, and personal names, take their sections. Subject and predicate, and the kinds of attributes, fill the middle. Morphology closes the analysis, from composition to word-formation. Formations are listed by their shapes: one active pattern pairs with its abstract. Bloomfield gives a Philippine tongue in a scholar's full anatomy.
51010-the-novel-what-it-is:
The Novel, What It Is is a short essay on fiction by F Marion Crawford, printed in New York by Macmillan in 1893. Crawford had written Mr Isaacs, Dr Claudius, and A Roman Singer. He asks a plain question, what is a novel.

He opens by saying his answer can only be a statement of opinion, made with deference to his brethren. Before going to work, he holds, a writer must know what he means to do. He grants that a man may know his own meaning yet fail to convey it to others. Much dispute, he says, rests on that gap in definitions. Crawford writes as a working novelist of great fame, not as a school man. Writers and readers get a pro view of the craft in brief form.
51169-section-cutting-and-staining-a-pra:
Colman's Section Cutting and Staining, a practical introduction to histological methods for students and practitioners, appears in a second edition, enlarged and largely re-written, from Lewis of Gower Street, London, in 1896. Colman writes as assistant physician, formerly pathologist, to the National Hospital for the Paralysed and Epileptic. He serves also the Hospital for Sick Children in Great Ormond Street.

The preface lays down his rule: describe a few methods in detail, the ones found to work well in practice, rather than sketch many. Chapters cover the apparatus required, hardening, cutting and mounting, and general staining. Special methods follow for the nerve centres, for micro-organisms and blood, and for injecting blood vessels. The first chapter warns beginners that a price list cannot tell them what they truly need, and bids them make their own reagents and buy spirit and distilled water by the gallon.
51410-dr-elsie-inglis:
Frances Balfour wrote this life of Elsie Inglis, with illustrations, from Hodder and Stoughton. A portrait shows the doctor in 1916, near the end of her work and life. Balfour dedicates the book to Serbia and to the Scottish Women's Hospitals that served there.

In your patience stands the dedication's broken motto for the years 1914 to 1917. Inglis, an Edinburgh surgeon, founded hospitals staffed by women when the War Office refused them. Serbia took her units in, and typhus, retreat and prison could not stop her, in Balfour's tribute by a fellow campaigner for women's causes.
51713-metamorphosis:
Charles de Vet wrote Metamorphosis, a science fiction tale printed in Galaxy Magazine in December 1960. Its teaser runs: the man I searched for could be anybody at all; if I did not find him, there would be nobody at all.

Max Calof hunts his old best friend, Howard Zealley, who now wears another name and another face. A 'bug' in Zealley's brain has made him a stranger. Calof, who has not slept in nine years, signs his name big in a cheap hotel register as bait. With total recall, he lets a list of two hundred names drift through his mind, waiting for a hunch.
51821-hogarth-s-works-with-life-and-anec:
Hogarth's Works, first series, pairs the engraver's plates with a life and anecdotal descriptions of his pictures, written by John Ireland and John Nichols. Chatto and Windus issued the volume in London, with all plates reduced in exact facsimile of the originals. William Hogarth and his dog Trump form the frontispiece, and a full-length portrait shows the artist painting the Comic Muse.

The plate list maps his famous series. The Battle of the Pictures and the Analysis of Beauty plates come early. Then A Harlot's Progress unfolds plate by plate: Mary Hackabout with the procuress, the kept mistress quarrelling, the Drury Lane lodging raided by constables, and the heroine beating hemp in Bridewell. The commentary retells each scene's story as it explains the crowded details.
51903-the-life-times-and-scientific-labo:
Henry Dircks, a civil engineer, wrote this life of Edward Somerset, second Marquis of Worcester, printed in London in 1865. A family group fronts the book: the marquis with Margaret, his second wife, and their infant daughter Mary. Somerset was born about 1601 and died on April 3, 1667, the plate notes. To the life is added a reprint of his Century of Inventions of 1663, with Dircks's commentary on it.

Dircks gives the book to the Duke of Beaufort, of the marquis's own line. In the giving, he praises the marquis's high gifts in constructive ingenuity above all his line. No compeer, Dircks holds, can be named for him among the nobility or the famed men of science of Europe in two centuries. Birth, titles, and deeds of war fade, he argues, before the lasting fame that original genius alone confers.
51978-hogarth-s-works-with-life-and-anec:
Hogarth's Works pairs the plates with a life of the artist and anecdotal descriptions of his pictures, by John Ireland and John Nichols. Chatto and Windus of London issued this second series with the plates reduced in exact facsimile. The volume opens with Marriage A La Mode in six plates, from the marriage settlement to the death of the countess. Beer Street and Gin Lane follow, with the Four Stages of Cruelty and Paul before Felix.

The list of plates runs on through the Four Prints of an Election, The March to Finchley, The Invasion, and The Times. Single prints follow, such as The Laughing Audience, The Five Orders of Periwigs, and The Bathos. Ireland and Nichols write the life of Hogarth alongside, and under each print set down its story and its jokes in detail. The facsimiles let a Victorian reader own Hogarth whole.
51983-the-sin-that-was-his:
The Sin That Was His is a north tale by Packard, of the gold camps of the Yukon. It came out at Toronto in the last years of the great war. Its first part is named for its hero, a card sharp with a jest name of his trade.

Of that man, the text says, the camp at the gold lumps knew a good deal, and yet knew a full as much of nil. He had drifted in one day in a chance way. He found the place paid well to his taste, and he stayed. He was a bird of flight, it seems, who might wait for the spring wash of the gold. His garb was not fine, for camp life lends not to fine dress. Yet he was by far the best clad man that side of the great north town.
52181-hogarth-s-works-with-life-and-anec:
Hogarth's Works gathers the artist's writings with a life and anecdotal descriptions of his pictures. The hosted copy is the third series of the set. A humorous non dedication by Hogarth stands near its front. It is dedicated to no prince in Christendom, for fear of seeming arrogant, it begins. Nor to any man of quality, nor to any learned body, nor to one particular friend, it goes on. Therefore it is dedicated to nobody, it concludes.

If nobody may be supposed to be everybody, then the work is dedicated to everybody, it jokes. The manuscripts behind the volume were written by Hogarth himself, a note says. Had he lived a little longer he would have arranged and published them, it adds. On his death they passed to his widow, who kept them sacred.
52422-congress-hotel-home-of-a-thousand-:
Kaufman copyrighted a cookbook for Chicago's Congress Hotel in 1914, subtitled Rare and Piquant Dishes of Historic Interest. The hotel bills itself Home of a Thousand Homes, and its famous Peacock Alley appears among the pictures. Verses from Byron and a French gastronome season the front matter.

An opening essay weighs the epicure's live to eat against the ascetic's eat to live, settling on a golden mean. Kaufman says the dishes gathered here are the most piquant and rare in the lore of cookery, many tied to anecdotes of famous historical figures. They appear not on the regular bill of fare but on a special menu card from the maitre d'hotel. Beluga caviar with blinis leads, credited by tradition to the Russian Winter Palace.
52429-fifteen-institute-lessons-in-langu:
Fifteen Institute Lessons in Language, Arithmetic, and United States History is a teacher's manual printed at Richmond, Indiana, in 1888. Sanders of Cambridge City, Indiana, held the copyright. The lessons were made for teachers' institutes, the training meetings where working teachers sharpened their classroom craft.

General directions on teaching language open the book. The teacher should question pupils on the reading lesson, put its hardest words on the board, and drill rapid pronunciation and spelling. Pupils name parts of speech, phrases, and sentences as advancement permits. Rules for punctuation and capitals are to be drawn out of the reading matter itself, and pupils must write compositions retelling each lesson in their own words.
52706-about-paris:
About Paris is a volume of sketches by Richard Harding Davis, illustrated by Charles Dana Gibson and published by Harper of New York in 1895. Davis dedicates the book to Paul Bourget. The frontispiece is captioned Paris had taken off her mourning.

Five chapters cover the streets of Paris, its show places by night, and Paris in mourning. The Grand Prix and other prizes follow, and Americans in Paris. Gibson's drawings show concierges at front doors, a girl with a long loaf of bread, and café scenes. Captions name the Château Rouge, the Black Cat, the Moulin Rouge, and a café chantant. One drawing marks portraits of Carnot in heavy black, from the city's mourning. Davis begins with a street he knew best, running parallel to the Rue de Rivoli.
53525-a-handbook-of-fish-cookery-how-to-:
A Handbook of Fish Cookery, by Lucy Yates, teaches how to buy, dress, cook, and eat fish. Ward and Lock published it in London in eighteen ninety seven. Yates had written on the profession of cookery from a French point of view. The handbook falls into four parts for the home cook's use.

Part one treats choosing and buying fish in the market with care. Part two covers the cooking of fish in its main methods and rules. Part three gives tested recipes, and part four is all fish sauces. The opening argues that English fish still holds the best of the market. Foreign fish floods in during closed months when home kinds are scarce. Yates blames plain ignorance for the housewife's dislike of cooking fish at home.
53736-the-fighting-retreat-to-paris:
Roger Ingpen wrote an account of the fighting retreat to Paris for a newspaper's series of war books, published at London, New York, and Toronto in 1914. His first chapter assembles the mobilisation and transport of the British Expeditionary Force, the King's message to his troops, and Lord Kitchener's address, before the advance of the Germans begins.

The battle of Mons on August 23rd gets the second chapter, built on Sir John French's despatch, with the West Kents in action, an aeroplane duel, and a Royal Engineer's experience. Charleroi and the fall of Namur follow in the French lines. A chaplain to a field ambulance and a Gordon Highlander carry the retreat's later chapters. Despatches, stitched into narrative within weeks of the events, are the book.
53814-a-searchlight-on-germany-germany-s:
Searchlight on Germany is a wartime pamphlet by William Hornaday. The American Defense Society published it in New York during the war. Hornaday sat on that society's board of trustees at the time. His title promises Germany's blunders, crimes, and punishment in full. Copies sold at three cents each in lots of twenty five or more.

Hornaday warns of a soft magnanimity toward Germany growing in America. Talk of a whitewashed peace with no annexations alarms him in print. A German peace, he holds, means a German triumph and a new war. Allies have given millions of men and billions in wealth, he says. Each American should know Germany truly before peace terms are set.
53876-nathaniel-parker-willis:
Nathaniel Parker Willis is a biography by Henry Beers in the American Men of Letters series. Houghton, Mifflin published it in Boston in 1890. The copyright dates to 1885. Charles Dudley Warner edited the series. An engraving of Willis in 1837 faces the title page.

A preface weighs the biographer's riches. Willis's own writings are largely autobiographical. A passable life could be stitched from them alone. He also lived much in the world's eye. Newspapers and recollections abound with him. Willis's widow and daughters opened his private papers to Beers. Letters and journals run from his school days to his death. The contents move from ancestry to college life at Yale.
53884-a-biblical-and-theological-diction:
Richard Watson compiled this biblical and theological dictionary, here revised by American editors for English readers. Its long title states the plan: to explain the history, manners, and customs of the Jews and the nations around them. Greek type runs through the entries, a Chrysostom quote stands at the front, and the text was set in two columns.

Entries give accounts of the chief places and persons named in sacred scripture. Other entries set out the main doctrines of Christianity in plain order. Notices of Jewish and Christian sects and heresies fill out the work. A reader with a Bible in hand could turn here for the land, the customs, and the beliefs behind the text. Church readers of its day kept it by the family Bible.
53994-stella-maris:
Stella Maris is a novel by William J Locke, pictured by Frank Wiles. The London edition is dated nineteen thirteen. Chapter one opens by explaining the heroine's odd name. Stella Maris, star of the sea, was not her real name, it says. No one would christen a harmless babe so absurdly.

Her mother had her called Stella after a rich old maiden aunt, the tale goes on. The aunt died a year later and left her a comfortable fortune. Her father gave her the family name Blount, which is pronounced Blunt. Walter Herold, a fanciful friend, tacked Maris onto Stella and ran the words together. So the child became Stellamaris to all the world. She was never sure herself how to sign formal papers, the narrator jokes.
53996-where-love-is:
William Locke wrote this novel, first under John Lane in 1903. Grosset and Dunlap later printed it in New York for wide sale. A Solomon proverb on a herb dinner with love heads the book. Chapter one finds Norma Hardacre at dinner with Jimmie Padgate.

Norma calls Ranelagh one of the dullest spots in a dull world. Jimmie, simple and frank, asks why folk go there at all. She laughs and calls guests sheep who follow one leader blindly. Talk turns to Morland King, who took her down to dinner. A proverb of Solomon stands as the book motto.
54077-the-development-of-certain-tendenc:
Kathryn Eleanor Browne wrote a degree thesis on new turns in opera. The text is her typed work for a Bachelor of Music degree. It was made at the School of Music of the University of Illinois. Her own hand fixes stand in the text as she left them. Small typos of the typed draft stand as well, by plan.

She asks where the great stage song form was bound in her day. Old rules of aria and tale bend in the new works she treats. Names and works ground each claim she makes in turn. A word list at the end may aid the new reader. Music past fans get a young mind's map of change. The tone is grave and keen.
5421-the-metropolis:
Upton Sinclair published The Metropolis in 1908 as a novel of wealthy New York society. It opens in a grand hotel corridor, where Montague arrives with a general and gazes around trembling slightly with anticipation. The magnificence of the place is less striking than the quiet power of the people moving through it, and Sinclair uses that arrival to introduce his world.

The novel follows Montague into drawing rooms, hotels, and business circles where fortunes are made and reputations traded. Sinclair, known for exposing American power, turns his eye on high society itself. Readers get a panoramic, critical portrait of New York wealth at the start of the twentieth century.
54233-the-vivisectors-directory-being-a-:
Benjamin Bryan edited The Vivisectors' Directory for the Victoria Street Society in London in 1884, with a preface by Frances Power Cobbe. The book lists licensed vivisectors in the United Kingdom, plus leading physiologists in foreign laboratories. It sold for one shilling and sixpence, or two shillings in cloth.

Cobbe compares the list to pocket maps given to Prussian soldiers in the Franco-German war. Campaigners against animal experiments needed names, licences, and classes of work in one handy form. Parliamentary returns supplied the facts on English licences and certificates. The directory arms debate with names and records, and shows how the anti-vivisection cause organised its case in print.
54365-a-history-of-the-old-english-lette:
Talbot Baines Reed wrote a history of the old English letter foundries, printed at London in 1887. His notes trace the rise and progress of English typography. A true and exact picture of the art of casting and preparing letters for printing fronts the book. It was engraved for the Universal Magazine in 1750, and the inside of Caslon's foundry in that year is shown on a plate within.

In this age of progress, Reed begins, the fine arts are fast becoming trades. The machine is on every side taking the place of the labour of head and hand our fathers called handicraft. Letter founding held out long against the new ways. Reed gathers the scattered records of the old founders into one connected tale. Printers and book lovers get craft history from a man who loved the trade.
54446-the-radio-boys-seek-the-lost-atlan:
The Radio Boys Seek the Lost Atlantis is a boys tale by Gerald Breckenridge. The book stands in a run of radio tales for boys of all ages. Past books took the boys to borders, lost treks, and dark Africa. This book bears a rights line of the year nineteen twenty three.

A cry for help by radio opens the hunt in a desert land. A hid spring, a slave trade tale, and swift ostrich chases fill the road. The lost sea realm of old myth draws the boys and a learned man on. A front print shows a voice heard as if close on the sand waste. Set piece thrills and radio craft share the pull of the tale.
54610-te-tohunga-the-ancient-legends-and:
Te Tohunga presents the ancient legends and traditions of the Maoris, gathered by word of mouth and pictured by Dittmer. It was printed at London and New York in 1907. The book is set as a memorial to Seddon, the late premier of New Zealand, and given to the Countess of Ranfurly, a friend to artists in that land.

The chapters, each with pictures, tell of Tiki, the ancestor of mankind, and of the making of Hawaiki and the stars. Maui wins a long run of tales: the making of New Zealand, his fight with the sun, and his death. James Cowan adds pieces on the children of the mist and the coming of the Maori.
55041-algeria-and-tunis:
Frances E Nesbitt painted and described Algeria and Tunis for A and C Black at London in 1906. A front plate shows the Mosque of Sidi Ben Ziad at Tunis on auction day. Chapters open in El Djezair, the city of Algiers, then move into the countryside.

Plates show old streets, carpet schools, mosques, and garden courts in Algiers. The route runs through the gates of the desert to Biskra, with nomad camps, caravans, and market scenes. Timgad and Constantine get chapters of their own. Tunis, Carthage, Sousse, and El Djem close the tour. Nesbitt joins a painter's eye to a traveller's notes on daily life, dress, and worship.
55398-phyllis:
The Duchess tells a house tale in Phyllis, printed at Chicago, New York, and San Francisco. Belford Clarke made the book. The Duchess had writ Molly Bawn and Airy Fairy Lilian. A Byron tag fronts the tale: ah, love was never without the pang, the agony, the doubt.

Chapter one opens in a shout. Billy, Billy, the narrator calls, eagerly, at the top of her healthy lungs, down the kitchen staircase. There is no reply. Where can that boy be? She shouts again, more lustily, with her neck craned half way down. A sudden movement on the upper landing brings her sister Dora into view. Dora is robed in her best French muslin, its faint blue and white setting off her delicate skin. Hush, she murmurs with hurried emphasis: there is someone in the drawing room. Not Mr Carrington, surely, the narrator breathes.
55494-john-chambers-servant-of-christ-an:
John Chambers: Servant of Christ and Master of Hearts, and His Ministry in Philadelphia, was written by the Rev William Elliot Griffis and printed at Ithaca by Andrus and Church in 1903. Griffis came to the task with a long shelf of his own: books on Japan, Holland, and the first steps of America fill the front list. A portrait of Chambers from about 1873 fronts the life. The double claim of the title sets the theme: a pastor strong in faith and warm in sway over hearts.

His field was Philadelphia, and the book tells that work in full. An earlier short form held one hundred and seventy-two pages with two portraits and an index, sold for a dollar. Church fans get a fond, full life of a city pulpit man of the last century.
55727-the-early-oxford-press-a-bibliogra:
Early Oxford Press is a bibliography of printing and publishing at Oxford from 1468 to 1640. Falconer Madan of Brasenose College wrote the work for the Clarendon Press. It was published at Oxford in 1895, with Henry Frowde in London and Macmillan in New York. Notes, appendixes, and illustrations complete the survey of the early press.

Contents give a plan of the bibliography and a list of its illustrations and tables at the front. The press history is split into the fifteenth century, the early sixteenth century, and the university press from 1585 in turn. A section treats fictitious or lost Oxford books dated between 1459 and 1584 by their claimants. Madan book founded the modern study of Oxford printing, and bibliographers still build on its lists of printers, books, and false imprints.
55864-the-young-wireless-operator-afloat:
Lewis Theiss wrote The Young Wireless Operator Afloat, or How Roy Mercer Won His Spurs in the Merchant Marine. The Wilde Company of Boston and Chicago copyrighted it in 1920. Photographs illustrate the book, a rare thing in boys' fiction of the day. Theiss's other Camp Brady wireless tales are listed at the front.

The dedication gives the book its moral in an image. Few of us know where our arrows come to earth, Theiss writes, but every act sends waves that land somewhere for good or ill. Roy Mercer goes to sea as a young wireless operator in the age when radio was still new. The tale follows his work in the merchant service, where a steady hand at the key could carry a ship through danger. Boys of 1920 got a sea career built on the newest trade afloat.
56727-the-irish-crisis:
The Irish Crisis is an essay by Trevelyan, reprinted from the Edinburgh Review of January 1848 and published in London the same year. Its subject is the great Irish famine of 1847. The author warns that no man can yet fully grasp the nature and bearings of that event.

He offers the piece as a public service, an early attempt to review the famine in the calm temper of a future age. Posterity, he predicts, will trace to that famine the start of a sound revolution in the habits of a long unfortunate nation. Good, he argues, has been drawn out of passing evil before. The essay is thus both a record of the crisis as it stood in early 1848 and a forecast of the change the famine would force on Ireland.
57030-the-pocket-lavater-or-the-science-:
The Pocket Lavater, printed in New York in 1817, offers a pocket form of the science of physiognomy, the reading of character from the face. The text is a translation from a French work that had run through many editions in France. Forty-four copperplate heads show the faces under discussion, and an added inquiry from the Italian writer Porta compares brute and human faces.

The advertisement notes that France had turned with fresh interest to this study. Paris, filled with people from all Europe, gave face readers a wide field. The Briton, Frenchman, German, Russian, Spaniard, Pole, and Turk each had a marked look. Readers then took such types as plain fact. The book is a neat sample of a science now set aside.
57284-manual-of-classical-erotology-de-f:
Forberg wrote a manual of classical erotology, in a literal English version privately printed at Manchester in 1884. Only one hundred copies were made, for Viscount Julian Smithson, the translator, and his friends, and none were for sale. Footnotes cite a Paris collection of five Latin poets on the games of Venus.

The opening chapter, The Metamorphoses of Venus, proposes to review the forms of love that fall into distinct kinds. The author disclaims any unveiling of his own experience, calling himself not so much as a raw recruit at the game. Some copies carried thirty engravings drawn from works on the private life of the Caesars. Scholarship and scandal share the small run.
5731-patty-in-paris:
Patty in Paris follows a young American girl from plans and goodbyes through a sea voyage to Paris and its sights. Chapters move from souvenirs and an aquatic party to the old mamselle, western friends, days at sea, and Paris itself, then on to Versailles, shopping, Chantilly, and making a home. Later chapters add Saint Germain, an expected guest, a motor ride, and a New Year fete.

This gives a bright travel story for girls, mixing sightseeing with friendship, shopping, and small social adventures. Patty's Paris is cheerful and orderly, with museums, gardens, and markets seen through fresh eyes. The book suits young readers who enjoy travel tales, and adults who like a light, old-fashioned picture of Paris before the First World War.
57517-imported-americans-the-story-of-th:
Imported Americans tells how Broughton Brandenburg and his wife studied immigration in disguise, in nineteen o three. Stokes published the book in New York, with sixty six photographs by the author. The pair passed as poor newcomers to learn the system from inside. Twenty two chapters run from a New York tenement to the laws themselves.

They lived first in a Houston Street tenement, then crossed to Naples in steerage. Zones of Italy follow, from Naples and Rome down to the heel and toe. A Sicilian family, the Squadrito of Gualtieri, anchors the middle of the tale. The return voyage, the landing process, and Ellis Island fill the later chapters. Two of the Gualtieri boys struggle in New York in the closing scenes. Laws and their evasion end the inquiry into what to do.
57708-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of Alfred Henry Lewis. Lewis was the author of the Wolfville books, tall tales of a cattle town told by an old cattleman. The index lists his works and then prints the table of contents of each volume.

Wolfville Days, Wolfville, and Wolfville Nights lead the list, followed by The President and The Mormon Menace. Faro Nell and Her Friends, The Sunset Trail, and The Apaches of New York come next. Straight history stands beside the yarns: a story of Andrew Jackson and a story of Paul Jones. Peggy O'Neal and The Black Lion Inn close the shelf. Chapter titles like Cherokee Hall Plays Poker and How the Dumb Man Rode show the flavor. The index is a finder for readers of the whole Lewis shelf.
57714-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled the Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Don Marquis. It gathers the tables of contents of twelve volumes by Marquis. A reader may view the contents of each volume. The title opens the original online file, the notes say. The Cruise of the Jasper B heads the list of works.

That novel's chapters run from a bright blade in a rusty scabbard onward. A schooner, a skipper and a skull, and beauty in distress follow. First blood for Cleggett, mysteries multiplying, and repartee and pistols fill it. Carter, and Other People stands next in the index. Its tales hold Carter, old man Murtrie, McDermott, and Looney the mutt. The Revolt of the Oyster, The Old Soak, and Danny's Own Story stand in the list. The index is a map to Marquis in his many modes.
58048-consolation-in-life-and-death-deri:
J Church preaches comfort for the living and the dying from the life of Christ in a sermon printed in London in 1824. R Weston of Crosby Row in Southwark printed the talk, first given at the Surrey Tabernacle. The date was Sunday evening, the 15th of August, 1824, on the death of Mrs Turner.

Church takes his text from John, chapter fourteen, verse nineteen: because I live, ye shall live also. He opens with Isaiah on the righteous who perish while no man lays it to heart. The loss of a pious wife, mother, and neighbour calls for thought and self-search, he urges. Death is God's knock at the door, and the wise will open, hear the message, and ask why it was sent.
58137-lawn-tennis:
James Dwight wrote a lawn tennis guide printed at Boston and London in 1886. Dwight gives the book to William Renshaw, champion of England, as his friend and pupil. There is at present no work on the game by any known player or judge, he says, and he offers his with great diffidence to fill the gap till something better comes. It is meant for beginners, he adds.

Those who have not seen the best players, nor played against them, are his readers. He had rare chances to study the game against the best men, and most of all against the champion Renshaw and his brother. Court, rackets, strokes, and rules fill part one. The young sport gets its first sound American handbook here.
58228-the-legends-of-the-iroquois:
Legends of the Iroquois collects tales told by the Cornplanter, set down by William W Canfield. Canfield worked from authoritative notes and studies, the title page says. The edition was limited to five hundred copies, printed in October nineteen oh two. A contents list shown in the copy runs from an essay on Indian legends to tales of the natural world.

Among the contents are pieces on the authority of the tales and on the confederation of the Iroquois. The birth of the arbutus and a legend of the river follow. Legends of the corn and the first winter take their turns. A great mosquito, a mirror in the water, and a buzzard earn tales of their own. The book carries the lore of the Iroquois in a form set down from a named teller.
58687-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of the Project Gutenberg works of Joel Chandler Harris. The file lists each Harris book held in the set. Full contents for each volume then follow in turn. Uncle Remus tales lead the roll, as fame would predict.

The Tar Baby tale stands second in the first Remus book. Fox, possum, and terrapin trade tricks through its pages. Plantation songs and wise sayings fill the back parts. Nights with Uncle Remus and Told by Uncle Remus add more beast lore. Mingo, Free Joe, and Gabriel Tolliver show Harris in tale form. A Georgia history and a scout tale join the list. Readers can pick a book by the tales it holds.
59049-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Works of Rabelais is a guide to the five books of Gargantua and Pantagruel in the free web shelf. It was built by Widger as a path through those books. Its lists give each part of all five books, in their true order.

The first book opens with the birth line and old age of the giant. Then come a crazed old verse hoard found in a tomb, and the tale of how the giant was borne eleven months in his mums womb. A feast of tripe, the talk of drinkers, and the giants birth fill the next parts. The guide serves a reader who would jump to one part, or read the whole wild work in its right run.
59052-fata-morgana-a-romance-of-art-stud:
Andre Castaigne wrote and illustrated Fata Morgana, a romance of art student life in Paris, published in New York in 1904. Castaigne dedicated the book to his many friends in America. The story moves in four parts, from the Quat'z-Arts ball to a castle of the Adriatic and a fateful day.

At its center stand Ethel Rowrer of Chicago and Helia, and Phil, who courted Helia in the yard. Early chapters show an initiation into art, the hanging gardens of Paris, and an apartment in the Latin Quarter. Later parts bring a Parisian debut, youthful follies at a country fair, and a final part titled Conscience, with a fight and a rescue by the Fata Morgana herself. Castaigne's own drawings crowd the pages, from the concierge to Helia at the summit of a carnival car. Readers get bohemian Paris drawn from inside.
59373-catalysis:
Catalysis is a science fiction story by Poul Anderson, printed in Worlds of If in February 1956. An epigraph sets its theme: man is a kind of turtle, carrying a shell of warmth and air wherever he goes, and with them his human failings. The scene is Triton, where looking outside means looking into darkness.

At high noon the sun is a sharp spark in a dusky heaven. Its light is about one-ninth of one percent of what Earth gets. Great fields of ice and frozen gases reflect enough to help the eyes, while crags of naked rock stand like blackened teeth. Seventy hours later the moon's other face brings a midnight thick enough to choke on. Inside the lab-dome, Thomas Gilchrist turns from the view with a shudder. He has always hated cold, and the bitterness outside seems to seep in and touch him.
59409-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled an index of Havelock Ellis's works on Project Gutenberg. The Studies in the Psychology of Sex lead the list. Six volumes hold that long work. Essays in War-Time stands in the set. Little Essays of Love and Virtue joins it. The Task of Social Hygiene appears as well.

The Criminal and The New Spirit fill the middle. The World of Dreams stands in the list. Impressions and Comments closes the roll. Full contents prints follow for each book. Volume One holds The Evolution of Modesty. Modesty's meaning gets a long first study there. A finding aid for a bold thinker's shelf, the index lets readers trace how one writer mapped sex, crime, and dreams across forty years.
59975-the-impostor-a-tale-of-old-annapol:
John Reed Scott's The Impostor, a tale of old Annapolis, was published at Philadelphia and London by Lippincott, with illustrations in color by Clarence Underwood. Advertisements for Scott's earlier successes fill the first leaves: The Woman in Question, The Colonel of the Red Huzzars, and The Princess Dehra among them. The title page comes after, and a frontispiece caption gives a taste of the talk.

In that caption Miss Marbury asks after a man of the tale: Miss Stirling, is Sir Edward dangerous, as well as fascinating, or simply fascinating? The question is the book in miniature: a polished world where charm and danger wear the same face. Scott's name on the page is tied to dashing love-stories with a secret at the root.
60012-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
David Widger compiled this index of the Project Gutenberg works of George Ferris on music. Ferris wrote lives of great composers and performers, with the chief set dated 1891. The index gives the tables of contents of each volume in full. One book treats the great German composers, from Bach and Handel to Wagner. An other treats Italian and French masters, from Palestrina to Berlioz.

A third book mixes all three lands and adds a table of dates at the end. Sharp wrote the preface to that mixed volume, as wife of William Sharp. More books treat great violinists and pianists, and great singers in two sets. Names run from Viotti and Paganini to Ole Bull and the Schumanns. The index lets readers find each life fast, across five books of music lore.
60077-the-millennium-and-other-poems-to-:
The Millennium and Other Poems is a book of verse by Pratt, a man of the word of a new faith. It came out at New York in the year past forty of the age. A tract on the new birth and the last end of stuff is bound past the verse. The front note tells where the verse was born, in spots as wide as his life.

Some verse came past the great falls of the north. Some came from a lone jail in a west state, where he lay past eight months in a time of hate. Some came from the white hills of the east and some from the bloom plains of the west. That tract in jail was writ to cheer his self and his friends when death stared him in the face, he says.
60273-leave-it-to-doris:
Leave It to Doris is a tale of a church house home by Ethel Hueston. Her past tales of church house life are named on the title leaf. The book's rights were held in nineteen nineteen. It is sworn to the kin of the hand. With them, she says, she learned the trick of glad life in the tight walls of a church house. Plates by a named hand stand in the book.

The first part bears the name of the chief of the house. The Reverend Artman walks his small room with a grave step. His eyes are dim with care. The lines at his kind lips are set hard. Now and then he looks to the bay pane where Doris sits. She is calm and bright at her work.
60559-the-chaldean-account-of-genesis:
George Smith wrote The Chaldean Account of Genesis from cuneiform tablets. A H Sayce revised this new edition in full. Charles Scribner's Sons issued it at New York. Smith served the British Museum's Oriental rooms. His History of Assurbanipal stands among his works. Izdubar fights a lion in the front plate.

Creation and the deluge fill the book's promise. The Tower of Babel and Sodom's fall join it. Patriarch times and Nimrod complete the list. Babylonian fables and god legends fill the rest. Five years had passed since the first form, Sayce says. Smith set out on his last, ill-fated trip then. The book woke extreme interest at once, he adds. Genesis no longer stood alone after it. Parallel accounts had come to light in clay. A museum man's tablet tales shook Victorian faith and founded Assyriology for common readers in one stroke.
60960-in-an-unknown-prison-land-an-accou:
George Griffith wrote this book of a land of men in chains, printed at London in 1901. Its full head gives the theme: a tale of the men sent out and the free men who plant in New Caledonia, with notes out and home. It is sent forth to the Earl of Dunmore, whose kind ways made the stay in that land far more sweet than it might have been. A face plate and a count of cuts go with the text.

The list of parts splits the book in two. The first part is a streak through the States: dues and coins, towns and forms, and the queen of the state of gold. A sea break parts it from the land of chains. The next part opens with a first note on the men in chains and the planters.
61090-call-him-nemesis:
Donald Westlake pits a lone scourge against crime in Call Him Nemesis, from the September 1961 issue of Worlds of If. The head blurb warns criminals: the Scorpion is on your trail. Hoodlums fear his fury, it says, and so do the cops.

The tale opens in a bank at a bad moment. A man with a handkerchief mask calls out that this is a holdup. Twelve people stand in the room. A manager refuses a check to a stranger, a young garage hand named Rod Strom. Two girls work the teller cages, and the guard dozes by the door in his brown uniform. A mother banks her husband's pay check with her small son at her side. Three robbers, dressed like triplets, hold the room.
6127-the-great-stone-of-sardis:
Frank R. Stockton opens The Great Stone of Sardis at noon on an early summer day, as a westward Atlantic liner nears New York. The old lighthouse on Montauk Point has been sighted, and passengers stir with knowledge that in a few hours they will be ashore.

Chapters promise the Sardis works, Margaret Raleigh, the mission of Samuel Block, under water, voices from polar seas, and good news from Sardis. The devil on the Dipsey, an artesian ray, Lake Shiver, a region of nothingness, and an automatic shell follow. Stockton mixes invention, polar quest, and romance around a wondrous stone.
61614-the-apostolic-tradition-of-hippoly:
Burton Scott Easton's translation of The Apostolic Tradition of Hippolytus was first published by the Cambridge University Press in 1934. Archon Books reprinted it in 1962, with Easton's introduction and notes. The book was planned with his colleague Frank Gavin, whose advice the preface credits throughout.

The introduction treats the early Church Orders. These were manuals of discipline and liturgy that claimed the authority of the whole apostolate. A second part treats the life and works of Hippolytus himself. The translation follows, with notes, a list of the important books from Hauler and Lagarde to Connolly, and indexes. The volume makes the third-century Roman church order usable for students of early worship.
61907-genesis:
Winterbotham wrote a space tale for Planet Stories in the summer of 1941. From the lifeless clay of Venus, his scientist Renzu dreams of moulding a mighty race, with himself as god. The tale opens in the stillness of space, aboard the atom driven rocket called The Traveler.

Captain Vic Arlen commands. A faint cry sounds from the cabin of Harry Renzu, who has hired the ship for his second trip to Venus. Inside, his Venusian slave Gheal crouches on the floor, one long arm raised against a falling cane. Arlen seizes Renzu's arm and takes the cane. This may be Renzu's expedition, he says, but in space the captain rules.
61942-south-to-propontis:
Henry Ackermann wrote this science fiction story for Planet Stories in the fall of 1941. To the south lay Propontis, capital of Mars, the blurb at the front explains. Between it and a homesick Earth youth stretched a burning desert, lair of the deadly Avis Gladiator.

Don Moffat faces death in the first scene, by an uncle's hand in a hut. A sixteen-year-old suspicion stands confirmed too late in his mind as the tale opens. The old electronic gun in his uncle's grimy paw stays steady despite raw liquor, while beyond the door a tiny sun beats on the sterile wastes of Mars.
62186-space-oasis:
Raymond Z Gallun wrote the tale Space Oasis. Planet Stories ran it in fall 1942. Space-weary rocketmen dream of an asteroid Earth, the blurb says. Power-mad Norman Haynes has other plans for it. His control lines spread a doom-net, it warns. Chet, the teller, hauls ore from the meteor swarms.

Nick Mavrocordatus scans a board at the Haynes office. Casualty lists must be posted by Space Code law. Joe Tiffany stands dead by armor defect there. Two men stand missing near Pallas on that list. Space blindness fills a long, grim column. Mental cases fill a longer one below. Ted Bradley's name catches Chet's eye cold. Hard space work with a company town's iron grip gives pulp science fiction a worker's edge here.
63313-neurosyphilis:
E E Southard and H C Solomon wrote a medical monograph on neurosyphilis, presenting modern diagnosis and treatment in one hundred thirty seven case histories. Southard held the Bullard chair of neuropathology at Harvard Medical School. Solomon taught neuropathology and psychiatry there. The book is monograph number two of the Psychopathic Hospital in Boston.

Portraits of Metchnikoff, Wassermann, Ehrlich, Schaudinn, and Noguchi face the title page. James Jackson Putnam supplies an introduction. The volume belongs to a case history series that included volumes on medicine, pediatrics, and surgery. Case based teaching let doctors compare presentations and outcomes. The work records practice just after the Wassermann test and Salvarsan changed the field.
63570-twenty-centuries-of-paris:
Twenty Centuries of Paris is a history of Paris by Mabell S C Smith, printed at New York in 1913. A panorama of Paris fronts the book, with the arms of the city. The chapters march by ages: earliest Paris, Merovingian Paris, Carlovingian Paris, and Paris of the early Capetians. Philip Augustus, Saint Louis, and Philip the Fair follow.

Paris of the Hundred Years' War, the Renaissance, and the Reformation come in turn. Henry the Fourth, Richelieu, and the Grand Monarque carry the story to the Revolution. Paris of Napoleon, of the lesser revolutions, and of Louis Napoleon lead to Paris of today. An appendix and index close the book. Maps show Lutetia under the Romans and France in the time of Hugh Capet. Smith begins from the prehistoric inhabitants of France, whose tools and weapons tell their story.
64572-new-york-the-nation-s-metropolis:
New York, the Nation's Metropolis, was published in 1921. Brentano's issued the picture book at New York. Peter Marcus made the volume. Hewlett, president of the Architectural League, adds an appreciation. Twenty five views make the contents. Times Square and lower Broadway open the list. Exchange Place, Wall Street, and City Hall follow. Brooklyn Bridge is seen from several sides. The Tombs Prison and the Municipal Building stand among them. Queensboro and Hell Gate bridges carry the eye outward. Grant's Tomb and Grand Central Station close the set. An opening essay names the city's character at once.

New York is the city of violent contrasts, Marcus writes. Towers and shanties, palaces and gas tanks crowd one picture. Beauty and squalor, he says, stand in no other city in such relief.
64720-lettres-d-un-innocent-the-letters-:
The Letters of Captain Dreyfus to His Wife gathers the prison letters of Alfred Dreyfus in English. Moreau translated the French volume of eighteen ninety nine for Harper and Brothers. Portraits of Dreyfus and his family face the text in the edition. An introduction by Walter Littlefield sets out the case against the captain.

The letters fall into four groups by the prisons that held their writer. They begin at the Cherche Midi prison and continue at La Santé in Paris. Then come Saint Martin de Ré and the Isles of Salut across the sea. Later letters to his family and one to his counsel form an appendix. Littlefield shows how the charge stressed Dreyfus's supposed bad character as proof. The Paris press had run a long campaign branding him gambler and traitor.
65426-industrial-minerals-and-metals-of-:
Industrial Minerals and Metals of Illinois is a survey by Lamar of the Illinois State Geological Survey, issued at Urbana in 1965 as number eight of its Educational Series. John Frye was chief of the survey. The book opens with the everyday products made from Illinois rocks and minerals, whose sources consumers rarely recognize. The user of a glass bottle, Lamar writes, seldom knows it may have been made from Illinois silica sand.

The driver on an Illinois concrete highway is likewise unaware that its cement, sand, and gravel probably came from Illinois pits or quarries. The figures set the scale: of more than 600 million dollars of Illinois mineral production in 1963, almost 200 million was from industrial minerals. A definition preserved in the copy fixes the term. Industrial minerals are nonmetallic minerals that are not fuels.
65480-a-sketch-of-charles-t-walker-d-d-p:
Silas Xavier Floyd wrote A Sketch of Charles T Walker, pastor of Tabernacle Baptist Church at Augusta, Georgia. The Sentinel Publishing Company issued it at Augusta in 1892. Floyd edited the Weekly Sentinel. Walker was born on January 11, 1858, at Hephzibah, the youngest of eleven children. His father was buried the day before his birth. His mother died in 1866, leaving him an orphan at eight.

In June 1873, hoeing cotton, young Walker resolved to seek the Lord. He left the field for the woods and stayed three days without food, drink, or company. He came out converted, and his uncle, the Reverend Nathan Walker, baptized him that July. In 1874 he entered the Augusta Institute, the theological school that later moved to Atlanta. His ability in school drew notice at once.
65704-guide-to-the-geologic-map-of-illin:
A guide to the stone map of Illinois was printed by the state at Urbana in 1961. It forms number seven of a teaching set from the state survey of rocks. John Frye then led that survey. The guide opens with the ice age shaping of the state.

The face of Illinois is young, it says, a mere span since the last ice left. Great ice sheets, at times a mile high, ground rock from the north and pushed south. When they melted, they dropped their load as drift over most of the state. Ridges of that drift form the mounds on the flat prairies of today. Only the north west corner and the far south kept their old shape.
65739-the-bloudy-tenent-of-persecution-f: The Bloudy Tenent of Persecution appears here in a Hanserd Knollys Society reprint. The society was formed to publish early English Baptist writers, and its officers and council list fill the front pages. Its opening statement regrets that early Baptist writings are little known. It claims Baptists first asserted in this land every man's right to worship God as conscience dictates, resting the claim on argument and scripture alone. No author is named in the pages shown, and the tract's own text lies beyond them.
65776-field-book-pennsylvanian-plant-fos:
Charles Collinson and Romayne Skartvedt wrote the Field Book of Pennsylvanian Plant Fossils of Illinois for the Illinois State Geological Survey, first issued in 1960 and reprinted in 1966. The book belongs to the survey's Educational Series and was prepared because amateur collectors kept writing in with questions. Marie Litterer drew the illustrations.

The authors state their aim at the start: to guide beginners in collecting plant fossils and sorting them in a general way. The book pictures the fossils most often found in Illinois and ties each one to the living plant it once belonged to. A time chart keys the great coal-age plants, from Lepidodendron and Sigillaria to the seed fern Medullosa and the ancient conifer Lebachia. A list of further publications points readers to finer identification. Readers get a pocket guide to the buried forests of the Pennsylvanian age in Illinois.
6596-official-report-of-the-exploration-:
Newton Chittenden reports, in 1884, on his survey of the Queen Charlotte Islands for the government of British Columbia. His letter to the chief commissioner opens the volume. Then he sets out the isles' place, size, and shape. They number more than 150, run 156 miles long, and lie between fifty-one and fifty-five degrees north in the Pacific.

The report goes on to land, water, woods, and the life found there, in the plain style of a public servant. It was written to guide settlement and rule, not to charm a traveler. For readers of Pacific history, this official report gives a first-hand, measured view of a remote archipelago at the edge of Canada.
66041-the-theory-of-psychoanalysis:
Dr C G Jung of Zurich wrote The Theory of Psychoanalysis, issued in New York by the Journal of Nervous and Mental Disease Publishing Company in nineteen fifteen. It is number nineteen in the Nervous and Mental Disease Monograph Series. Drs Smith Ely Jelliffe and William A White edited the series. Outlines of Psychiatry by Dr William A White stands first.

Studies in Paranoia and The Psychology of Dementia Praecox follow in the list. Selected Papers on Hysteria by Professor Sigmund Freud stands fifth. Three Contributions to Sexual Theory by Freud also appears. Dreams and Myths by Dr Karl Abraham and History of Prison Psychoses appear too. The Myth of the Birth of the Hero by Dr Otto Rank closes the visible list. Psychology readers get Jung own statement of his break with Freud theory.
66068-illustrations-of-the-birds-of-cali:
Illustrations of the Birds of California, Texas, Oregon, British and Russian America is a work of bird lore by John Cassin. He was a man of more bands of lore than one, named past his name. The work was made through the years past eighteen fifty three. It was put out at a great east town in eighteen fifty six. Its first plate shows a jay of the south land in hue.

Its bill tells its aim in full. It would hold the marks and forms of all the birds of the north land not gave by past hands of this land. Past that it holds a short view of the bird lore of the whole land. The first words set out the age of its make.
66308-guide-to-rocks-and-minerals-of-ill:
The Illinois State Geological Survey issued the Guide to Rocks and Minerals of Illinois as number five of its Educational Series. The booklet was first printed in 1959 and again in 1960, at Urbana. It grew from the Survey's sets of typical Illinois rocks and minerals, prepared for schools and other educational groups.

The guide opens by granting the puzzle. Illinois, the Prairie State, seems an unlikely place to collect specimens. Yet its prairies rest on ancient rocks, worn down by weather, water, wind, plants, and animals over millions of years. Glaciers strewn boulders and gravel across the state. Every county, the Survey says, holds rocks or minerals in use or of future value. The book teaches beginners what to look for, where outcrops and river valleys expose the stone, and how the state's industry rests on its geology.
66636-the-story-of-andre-corne-lis:
The Story of Andre Cornelis, by Paul Bourget, adapted by Monkshood, was published in London in 1909. Nineteen chapters are listed without titles. The tale is told by Andre himself, and it opens far back, in childhood, with confession at his school chapel.

He recalls being taken to the chapel in tens, at five in the afternoon. The room was cold and empty, with whitewashed walls, numbered benches, a harmonium, a Holy Family, and a blue ceiling dotted with stars. His heart beat hard as he waited to kneel by the priest. Dread at the sliding panel gave way to relief, liberty, pardon, and a sense that wrong doing was wiped away. Readers get a French novel of conscience, guilt, and memory, told from inside one man mind.
66660-polio-infantile-paralysis:
Polio, or Infantile Paralysis, is a health pamphlet in a Prudential Health Series. When polio strikes some child in a community, it says, all parents naturally become concerned for their own children. It is well, it adds, to keep the scale of the disease in mind.

Even during an epidemic, cases are very small beside the total population. About forty five thousand cases were reported for the United States and Canada in 1949, and that was a bad year. About half of those paralyzed recovered completely, it says. Another large group had very slight after effects, and very few cases ended fatally. Yet polio cannot safely be ignored. It is the most frequent cause of deformity in children. The pamphlet explains it as a contagious disease in which a virus attacks the gray matter of the spinal cord. Readers get plain parent guidance from the worst polio years.
66693-bi-sexual-love-the-homosexual-neur:
Wilhelm Stekel, a Viennese doctor of the mind, stands behind this clinical study of love between men. Its full title joins two names for its theme: Bi-Sexual Love and The Homosexual Neurosis. Long praise from the learned press heads this English issue.

Jung, in a Swiss journal, calls Stekel's work the first full use of Freud's method in the clinic. Other voices name it a standard work and a mile stone of the field. Case tales fill the book, and one voice says they will grip even the wary. Teachers, clergy, and students of crime are named as readers with much to gain, next to doctors of the mind.
6677-seventy-five-receipts-for-pastry-ca:
Miss Leslie of Philadelphia offers seventy-five original receipts for pastry, cakes, and sweetmeats, first printed in 1832. Her preface promises a style so plain and minute that servants and readers of modest skill can follow it with ease. Each receipt lists its ingredients and amounts at the head, to ease the shopping and the work.

Leslie notes the faults of English and French cookery books, which often leave a cook guessing at key steps. Her own receipts had been tried by herself and many friends, with uniform success. Seventy-Five Receipts is a charming, practical window on early American baking, still usable in a modern kitchen.
67204-the-memoirs-of-a-failure-with-an-a:
The Memoirs of a Failure presents the life and manuscript of William Wirt Dunlevy, framed and edited by Kittredge in a volume published at Toronto in 1908. Kittredge knew Dunlevy slightly and prints extracts from his bewildering manuscript, most of the book being the memoir itself. Dunlevy appears first as a student at the University of Virginia.

He was older than the other undergraduates and held himself aloof, and Kittredge's classmates watched him from the athletic field. He would stand at the foot of the Rotunda steps gazing at the porticos, or pace the colonnades with his hands crossed behind him, looking toward the Blue Ridge. Kittredge admits the man's character and fate may stay inscrutable, and offers only interpretive biography: the finest thing, he says, is the man behind the manuscript. The frame turns an unknown failure's papers into a small mystery of personality.
67479-the-day-of-resis:
Lillian Frances Mentor wrote a tale of Africa held under an 1897 right, with art by Harry Parkhurst. A strange paper found by a hunt party on the road to Zanzibar starts the long trek. A tall Abyssinian guide named Sedai tells of the odd script on a march to the coast.

Parts to come plunge into caves, a city named On with its own harsh law, and a royal hunt. Gold mines, ice caves, sea beasts in fight, and fields of bright stones crowd the wild roll. Storm, quake, traps of death, and live burial test the band in near fifty chapters of thrills.
67557-the-homosexual-neurosis:
Wilhelm Stekel, a breakaway pupil of Freud, set out his case studies of this theme in a clinical book. The head pages here are all press praise, gathered from the German journals of his day. Jung, in his early years, gives the book its highest word.

We have lacked thus far, Jung wrote, a systematic clinical application of Freudian analysis; Stekel's work fills this need. A standard work and a milestone, says another. A treasury of information for the physician, and much for the teacher, the minister, and the student of crime, says a third. Even the doubters, says Eulenburg, will read these case histories with great interest. Stekel's vivid, hasty style fills the pages.
67856-eris:
Eris is a novel by Robert Chambers, published in New York by Doran in 1922. It is dedicated to his friend Harry Payne Burton. The first chapter opens at Whitewater Farms on a spring morning in 1900. A baby is born at nine in the morning, April the nineteenth. Two pure-breed calves are dropped the same day at near the same hour. Odell hears the news toward noon from his foreman. For twenty years his marriage has been childless.

He had waited in vain for sons to work the farm. Now, after twenty hard years of discord, Fanny has given him a girl. Odell scrapes his boots at the manure pit and broods. A bad winter, an April drouth, and bull calves with no market fill his mind. Word comes that Fanny is bad, and a second doctor has been sent for. The title names the goddess of strife.
67921-poseidon-s-paradise-the-romance-of:
