Poseidon Paradise, subtitled The Romance of Atlantis, by Elizabeth Birkmaier, was published at San Francisco in 1892. A front map is adapted from Ignatius Donnelly map of Atlantis. Three names in the tale, Cleit, Chimo, and Luith, are noted as made up.

Chapter one is a declaration of war, thousands of years before the Christian era. Queen Atlana follows, then Atlantis against Pelasgia, Pelasgian captives, and a kidnapping. A temple, Poseidon festival day, and a silent priest fill the middle. Later come an earthquake, altar fires going out, and the sinking of the island. Pyrrha, the beginning of peace, and happy pairs close the tale. Readers get a romance of the lost island, built on war, priests, and doom.
68315-on-chloroform-and-other-an-sthetic:
On Chloroform and Other Anaesthetics is a medical work by John Snow, published in London in 1858. Benjamin Richardson edited it and wrote a memoir of the author. The preface calls the book the legacy to science of Dr Snow. Its completion was his last act. Richardson's share was the index and the memoir, a painful duty laid on him by a promise to a friend. Snow had died with the work just done.

A historical introduction opens the book. General remarks on inhalation follow. Chloroform then takes the great bulk of the text. Its history, making, and properties are set out in order. The degrees of narcotism are laid down with care. How age, drink, and disease change the drug's action is weighed in turn. The book is the root text of the science of anaesthesia.
68430-isola-or-the-disinherited-a-revolt:
Isola; or, The Disinherited is a verse drama by Lady Florence Dixie, subtitled A Revolt for Woman and All the Disinherited. The Leadenhall Press published it in London, with Scribner's Sons in New York. George Jacob Holyoake supplied remarks on the play, and Dixie dedicated the book to him, in admiration of his long and courageous career.

Quotations on the title pages show the hero, young Fortunatus, a youth with a price on his head, leading a rising as an unknown champion. Dixie explains that the drama was written many years before its printing. It first appeared in the magazine Young Oxford in September 1902 and ran in serial form for six months. An opening poem answers the sneerers in advance: heed not the human sneer, for the world lives on long after those who jeer are dead and gone. Thought, the verse insists, cannot die.
68558-robot-nemesis:
Robot Nemesis is a science fiction story by Edward Elmer Smith, first printed in Thrilling Wonder Stories in June 1939. Its first chapter, The Ten Thinkers, opens in the far future. The War of the Planets is taken to have ended on 18 Sol, 3012, with the Battle of Sector Ten.

In that fight the Grand Fleet of the Inner Planets met the fleet of the Outer Planets in a desperate bid for the mastery of space. Neither side won. Both fleets were so shattered that the survivors despaired of fighting on, and the crippled ships limped home. Since then neither side dares attack, for each waits on a super-weapon. Yet the secret services are so efficient that no such weapon can be perfected in secret. Behind the known stalemate, the tale promises, lies the untold story of the conflict between humanity and the robots.
68617-travels-in-western-africa-in-1845-:
John Duncan's Travels in Western Africa, in 1845 and 1846, was published in London by Richard Bentley in 1847, in two volumes, this being the first. Duncan, late of the First Life Guards and one of the late Niger expedition, journeys from Whydah through the kingdom of Dahomey to Adofoodia in the interior.

His preface gives his career. Born in 1805 on the farm of Culdoch near Kirkcudbright, he enlisted in 1822 in the First Regiment of Life Guards and served sixteen years. Discharged early in 1839, he became master-at-arms in the Niger expedition, where fever at Fernando Po turned to gangrene in a wounded leg and nearly finished him.
68664-the-heart-of-the-railroad-problem-:
Frank Parsons wrote this history of railway discrimination for Little, Brown at Boston in 1906. The common law, he begins, requires common carriers to be impartial: no undue preferences, no unequal or extravagant charges, no refusals to carry. The book's 35 chapters measure American practice against that rule. Passes and politics come first, then passenger rebates, the deadhead car, and ticket scalping. Freight discrimination gets the longest treatment.

Parsons marches through the record of reform: the Granger laws, the Hepburn investigation, the Senate inquiry of 1885, and the Interstate Commerce Act. The Elkins Act, the Wisconsin revelations, and the Colorado fuel rebates bring the story current. Private-car abuses and the long-haul anomaly fill late chapters. His remedies end the book: drastic cures for rebating, rates fixed by public authority, and hints from other countries. Parsons taught at Boston University and wrote as a Progressive, for readers who meant to act.
6883-the-life-of-venerable-sister-margar:
This life tells of Sister Margaret Bourgeois, foundress of the Sisters of the Congregation of Notre Dame, established at Montreal in Canada in 1659. Translated from the French by a religious of Cedar Rapids, Iowa, it rests on a French edition of 1818. That edition so charmed its translator that she took up the task for English readers, though the work was often laid aside for years.

The translator hopes readers will gain as much good from the life as she did, and she sets it against an age of mixed and corrupt books. Margaret's work in a young colony, her care for girls and for the poor, and her steady faith form the heart of the book. It offers her as a model of service in hard times.
69179-travels-in-western-africa-in-1845-:
John Duncan, a former Life Guards soldier who had served on the Niger expedition, wrote this second volume of his travels in western Africa, printed in London in 1847. The journey runs from Whydah, through the kingdom of Dahomey, to Adofoodia in the interior, during the years 1845 and 1846.

Chapter headings list what Duncan met on the road: mountain towns, markets, river ferries, and talks with local chiefs called caboceers. He notes farms, cloth making on native looms, herds of cattle, and a hyena trap. War shadows the route, with ruins, skeletons of the slain, and a front plate showing a mode of execution at Dahomey. Duncan records soil, plants, birds, and the look of the people as he goes.
69227-sir-john-everett-millais:
Baldry wrote Sir John Everett Millais for Bell's Miniature Series of Painters, printed in London in 1908. The book first came out in December 1902. Contents give the life of the artist, the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood, later years, and the last years. The art of Millais, a note on the plates, and a list of his chief works in public galleries follow. A Yeoman of the Guard fronts the volume.

The plate list names Christ in the House of His Parents, The Vale of Rest, and Ophelia. Autumn Leaves and The North-West Passage stand among them. The life opens with the birth of John Everett Millais on June 8, 1829, at Southampton. His father was a Jersey man, of a family settled in that island from before the Norman conquest. At Dinan in Brittany the child began to draw the scenery and the people.
69262-history-for-ready-reference-volume:
History for Ready Reference, volume four, is one part of a large work that sets the past out by subject for quick lookup. This volume runs in letter order through to Tunis. Its entries give main heads at the margin, with sub heads set in below, so a reader can find a point fast.

Cross notes point to other entries in the work, while cited books are listed for deeper reading. Long entries are kept whole, with blocks of text placed near the heads they match. The volume serves students and writers who need a date, a place, or a short account of a past event without reading a full history.
69840-the-piccinino-volume-2-of-2-the-la:
George Sand wrote The Piccinino, here in the second volume of a translation printed at Philadelphia for subscribers only. The edition calls itself the Masterpieces of George Sand, now for the first time completely translated into English. Burnham Ives made the version, and twelve photogravures after paintings by Oreste Cortazzo illustrate it.

This volume takes the tale from chapter thirty-six to its conclusion. Family portraits, a chapter named Bianca, a coup de main, and an idyll lead into deception and jealousy. Revelations, a vulture, a marquis, and a nocturnal journey crowd the close, ending in catastrophe. Bound after it stands a second work, The Last of the Aldinis, with an introduction. A frontispiece shows Signora Aldini with her gondolier on the marble steps. Sand filled the volume with Italian passion.
70133-the-suppression-of-tuberculosis:
Professor von Behring of the University of Marburg argues for The Suppression of Tuberculosis in an authorised translation by Charles Bolduan. Wiley published the New York book in 1904, with Chapman and Hall in London, priced at one dollar in cloth. The main piece began as a lecture at Cassel on September 25, 1903.

Bolduan's preface says the disease can be beaten only when physicians, dairy men, cattle men, health officers, and engineers all grasp its origin. Selections gather Behring's writings on how consumption arises in man and animals. Added pieces cover hygiene of cow stables and the making of milk for infant feeding, with special reference to tuberculosis. An appendix answers critics of the Cassel lecture.
70316-thamyris:
R C Trevelyan wrote Thamyris, or Is There a Future for Poetry, for the To-day and To-morrow series. The series list at the front names its siblings: Haldane's Daedalus on science and the future, Russell's Icarus answering it, and Haldane again in Callinicus, a defence of chemical warfare.

Fournier d'Albe's Quo Vadimus, Dora Russell's Hypatia on woman and knowledge, Rebecca West on the future of sex, and Vernon Lee's Proteus on the future of intelligence keep the company. Trevelyan took the blinded Thracian singer of legend as his mask to ask whether verse itself would survive the machine age. Readers get a 1920s futures pamphlet in classical dress.
70461-an-egyptian-oasis:
An Egyptian Oasis is H J Llewellyn Beadnell's account of the Oasis of Kharga in the Libyan Desert, published by John Murray of London in 1909 with maps and illustrations. Beadnell had served on the Geological Survey of Egypt, and he wrote with special reference to the oasis's history, physical geography, and water supply. He dedicated the book to a fellow geologist, Thomas Barron, who lost his life in the Sudan in 1906.

The chapters cover the roads in, the northern and southern villages, and rule under Persians and Romans. Then the science takes over: extinct lakes, underground water, flowing wells, and the origin of the artesian waters. Ancient underground aqueducts, boring methods old and new, and man's contest with wind-borne sand complete the survey.
7075-the-idol-of-paris:
Sarah Bernhardt's Idol of Paris, in its 1921 English edition, runs in four parts from Paris through Brussels and the country to the chateau. Part one opens in the dining room of a fine house on the Boulevard Raspail, where the Darbois family gathers round a table. A white oilcloth bordered with gold medallioned portraits of French kings serves as the family table cover at meals.

Thirty chapters carry the Darbois story across cities and country houses, through youth, love, and ambition in the world Bernhardt knew as an actress. The novel bears the great tragedienne's name and flair, with Parisian society as its stage. It is a family saga told by a woman who lived at the center of French theater.
70861-the-doings-of-doris:
Agnes Giberne published The Doings of Doris with the Religious Tract Society, and the contents promise a wholesome heroine with a will of her own. Doris arrives at Clover Cottage, and by chapter three Doris rebels.

The chapters proceed through the Morrises, a secret agreement, Doris letting herself go, a cycle ride, and a surprise visit. Then the scene shifts to the mountains: the cry from the chalet, a rotten piece of rock, only a girl, and a superb rescue. Two hearts draw nearer before the squire's advice closes the tale. Giberne wrote science for children as ably as fiction; here she builds a girls' adventure in which courage, not obedience alone, earns the ending.
71222-the-crisis:
W E Burghardt Du Bois edited the first number of The Crisis in November 1910. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People issued the monthly in New York. The price ran one dollar a year, ten cents a copy. Oswald Garrison Villard and Kelly Miller stood among the co-editors.

Contents run from Along the Color Line to a note on the N A A C P itself. Athens and Brownsville, by Moorfield Storey, treats race wrongs in plain terms. Ads offer art and music training at the Touissant Conservatory in Harlem. Readers gain the birth issue of a landmark voice for civil rights.
71286-oliver-ellis:
James Grant, late of the 62nd Regiment, wrote this tale of the Fusiliers. Routledge printed a new edition of Oliver Ellis in London in 1865. Grant had written The Romance of War and Second to None by then.

His preface owns that many men in the tale bore the parts he gives them. They served in Sir Charles Grey's army in the Antilles, in the West Indies war. A duel like the one on the Adder frigate took place on a real ship in a South American port in 1821. A wreck in the Isle of Tortoises came from a strange ship found in a cave at Baccalieu. Fact and tale mix in Grant's brisk soldier style.
71650-the-crisis:
The Crisis, a record of the darker races, was the monthly magazine of the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People. This copy is volume one, number three, dated January 1911, sold at ten cents a copy or a dollar a year from 20 Vesey Street, New York. Du Bois edited it, with a team of co-workers named on the contents page.

The issue opens with Along the Color Line, a news survey, and pages of opinion and editorial comment. Jane Addams writes on social control. A poem, The Teacher, comes from Leslie Pinckney Hill. Another piece studies the employment of colored women in Chicago. A cartoon by John Henry Adams fills a page. Readers of the new civil rights movement got facts, argument, and art in one thin number.
72010-echo-de-paris:
Echo de Paris, by Laurence Housman, author of Angels and Ministers and Prunella, was published in New York in 1924 by Appleton. Housman calls the piece a study from life. The echo, he warns, comes from as far back as the year 1899. It is late September, and three Englishmen sit at a small table by the entrance of a cafe near the Place de l'Opera.

The cafe calls itself the Vieille Rose, and by gaslight it may live up to the name. In the noonday glare its upholstery is plainly magenta. The men wait for a fourth, and the talk turns anxious: is he generally so late? Generally never as early, comes the answer. The play runs as dialogue, wry and light, on Englishmen abroad and the friend who keeps them waiting.
72351-travels-in-the-footsteps-of-bruce-:
Travels in the Footsteps of Bruce in Algeria and Tunis follows the North African road of James Bruce, the famed explorer of the Nile's source. Playfair, British consul general in Algeria, wrote it, and Kegan Paul published it at London in 1877. Its plates copy Bruce's own drawings, starting with the Tomb of the Christian, the tomb of Juba the Second.

Playfair dedicates the book to Lady Thurlow, Bruce's heiress. She had opened to him the priceless drawings long shut in the muniment room at Kinnaird. All the world, he writes, are co heirs with her in Bruce's fame. The chapters trace Bruce's route to Lambessa, the Medrassen tomb, and the Aures mountains. Ruins at Announa, hot springs, and cave dwellings fill the road. The book joins a consul's own journeys to an older traveller's art, rescuing drawings the public had never seen.
72471-the-fayu-m-and-lake-m-ris:
Fayum and Lake Moeris is an irrigation study by Major Brown of the Royal Engineers, published in 1892. Edward Stanford issued the book in London from Cockspur Street, Charing Cross. Brown was inspector general of irrigation in Upper Egypt in his office. Scott Moncrieff, the chief of the Egyptian irrigation service, wrote a prefatory note for the volume.

A frontispiece shows the old Lahun regulator where the Bahr Yusuf turns west into the Fayum. The prefatory note tells how a small band of English engineers, most of them trained in India, had wrought a revolution in Egyptian irrigation in nine years. The Fayum, a desert basin watered since the pharaohs, and its great lake are the subject here. Brown writes as an engineer among ruins: levels, regulators, and the oldest artificial lake in the world, measured for a modern service.
72601-a-rough-sketch-of-modern-paris:
Lemaistre wrote these letters on modern Paris life in 1801, 1802. Johnson printed the second edition in London in 1803. Letters treat society, manners, public curiosities, and amusements there. A Voltaire motto on Paris glory fronts the sketch book.

War still raged when Lemaistre sought leave to visit France in 1801. A legacy claim at Paris drew him, his preface explains. Passport delays held him till peace preliminaries signed that October. He kept a journal as one of the first English arrivals. Three days after peace, the long awaited passport reached his hands at last there.
7265-the-history-of-pendennis:
William Makepeace Thackeray's History of Pendennis follows Pen through fortunes and misfortunes, friends, and his greatest enemy, opening with first love interrupting breakfast. A pedigree, a very young man, Mrs Haller at home, love and war, and the major's campaign carry the early chapters. Meanwhile Laura waits at the door and Pen learns the ways of London and the press.

Thackeray's narrator watches youth with fond irony, letting vanity, affection, and ambition tangle in one young life. A shooting match, a crisis, and Miss Fotheringay's stage world widen the tale from home to society. Pendennis remains a classic novel of growing up, told with humour and a moral eye.
73178-crisis:
Crisis, a story by Cecil Corwin, appeared in Science Fiction Quarterly for spring 1942. Its headnote sets the stakes: Earth's Diplomacy Bureau is staffed by hopeless incompetents, the Venusians are rattling the sabre, and senseless war looms. A little screwball conduct, it adds, can be forgiven if it works.

The mess begins with a haircut. The Martian Karfiness, trimming her chelae one morning, cut herself badly, and fashion that year wore the tentacles about a Martian lady's neck short. Snappish from the slip, she told the Venusian envoy that his fish faced people would be blown out of space if they touched one free electron. Venus severed relations with Earth at once. The tale then moves to the Bureau of Protocol in Alaska, where code clerk Weems and his assistant Helen Carewe open the diplomatic mail.
73366-baharia-oasis:
John Ball and Hugh Beadnell wrote Baharia Oasis, a survey report on its land forms and rocks, printed at Cairo in 1903 for the Survey Department of Egypt. Maps close the book, one in geological colour, plus sections that cut through scarps and folds. Plates list towns and chief water sources.

Baharia, the Little Oasis, lies in the Libyan Desert some 180 kilometres west of the Nile Valley, a four to five day camel march. Ringed on all sides by scarps, it holds a vast field of lone hills in its hollow, unlike the open oases to the south. Chapters treat survey methods, roads to the Nile and to sister oases, water, folk, rocks, and old remains. Exact, dry, and rich in maps, it fixed a remote desert basin on the record.
7369-jim-davis:
John Masefield tells this adventure in the voice of its hero, Jim Davis, a boy born in 1800 in Newnham-on-Severn, Gloucestershire. Orphaned young, Jim is taken from his home by an uncle. He begins to see the wider world: his first coach ride, a night at a coaching inn in Bristol, and the docks where sailors load West Indiamen. The tale is set in the last years of the sailing age.

From those early scenes, Jim's life widens from home and riverbank to the coast and the sea. Masefield, himself a former sailor, fills the story with coaches, inns, ships, and working seamen, all seen through a boy's sharp eyes. It reads as a boys' adventure with a strong sense of place, grounded in the Gloucestershire countryside and the ports beyond it.
73727-metropolis:
Thea von Harbou's Metropolis, in the Ace Books edition following the first English text of 1927, imagines the world of 2026. A city has grown to gargantuan size, and humanity fights to keep its soul against machinery, robots, and complexity. Harbou's own foreword refuses every label: the book is not of today or the future, tells of no place, and serves no cause, party, or class. Its moral stands on one line: the mediator between brain and muscle must be the Heart.

The novel opens with Freder at the great organ, playing until the notes dissolve the room into a sea and the stars dance above the waves. Freder is the master's son in the city of towers, and the vision sets the book's fevered, symbolic key. Metropolis inspired the famous film, which the blurb calls possibly the best science-fiction film ever made.
74127-from-the-indus-to-the-tigris:
Henry Walter Bellew wrote From the Indus to the Tigris, for Trubner in 1874. Bellew was a surgeon of the Bengal staff corps in India. His journey ran through Balochistan, Afghanistan, Khorassan, and Iran in 1872. A grammar and vocabulary of the Brahoe language stand in the book. Records of weather and altitudes on the march fill its appendix.

His preface opens on the steady progress of Russian conquest in Turkistan. Her frontiers advance toward India year by year, he writes. Central Asia thus rises in importance to European politicians, he holds. Travellers report barbarism, bigotry, anarchy, and weak governments there. A common religion holds those states together as their polity decays, he adds. Russia's operations against Khiva open the country as he writes. Bellew gives the march from river to river with a soldier-surgeon's eye.
74631-paris: Paris is a short book in the Today and Tomorrow series of future looking essays, dated 1925 in the record. Companion titles in the series include Daedalus on science and the future, and Icarus by Bertrand Russell. In such company, a Paris volume treats the city of the future. It belongs to a fashion of the twenties, when small books guessed the world ahead.
75074-elementary-cryptanalysis:
Elementary Cryptanalysis is a textbook on solving ciphers by Helen Fouche Gaines. The American Photographic Publishing Company first published it in 1939. A first chapter of general information defines the study's scope. It treats the analysis and solution of cipher, not code. Code is a special form demanding more than elementary knowledge, she says. Invisible inks belong to chemistry rather than to cryptanalysis. Cipher machines are also outside the present scope, she rules. The term cipher implies a method or system of secret writing.

Any plaintext, of any length and language, can be transformed by it. Encipherment makes a cryptogram from such a plaintext. Decipherment is the opposite process with knowledge of the key. Decrypting means solving cryptograms without previous knowledge of keys. Gaines teaches that solving art step by step in this manual. Her book became a standard for amateur codebreakers.
75270-the-return-of-alcestis:
Laurence Housman wrote The Return of Alcestis, a play in one act, issued by Samuel French in New York and London with copyright in nineteen sixteen. A caution warns that the play is subject to royalty and must not be staged without consent. The scene is a chamber in the house of Admetus, King of Pherae. A bridal couch and a domestic altar furnish the stage. Hymen, bearing a torch, speaks first.

Alcestis, her nurse, her daughter, and attendants stand in the cast, with choruses of women and of men. Admetus, his father Pheres, and his son Eumelos complete the list. House of Admetus, whom the gods befriend, peace be within your gates, Hymen opens. Admetus, helped by the hand of Heracles, has won back from the tomb his wife, who blameless died, he sings. Actors and readers get a grave, lyrical Greek revival play in verse.
75300-manners-for-the-metropolis:
Manners for the Metropolis is a wit key to high life by Francis Crowninshield. Its full name calls it a door key to the wild life of the Four Hundred. An Appleton house of New York brought it out in October of nineteen eight. Louis Fancher drew the dress cuts that line the short parts. Parts treat house stays, talk, meals, dance, and cards in sharp turns.

A land house has cast out hearth life and romp kids, the first part jests. The best part of a house stay is the hour you leave, it adds. Bath floods, late lunch dread, and hot water wars fill its guest rules. Bread and jam thanks notes, left caps, and lost golf clubs close a part. Newport and broad rules end the key with more sly digs.
7566-quotes-and-images-from-memoirs-of-m:
Marguerite de Valois, Queen of Navarre, wrote memoirs from the center of France's wars of religion, and this companion volume gathers short passages and pictures from them. She watched courts, factions, and faith divide a kingdom, and she wrote as a witness, not a bystander. Each passage can be traced to its full scene. That link keeps her sharp remarks tied to the events behind them.

Read together, the passages sketch a queen who saw clearly how fortune, envy, and flattery worked on people. Faith, action, honor, and the gap between rumor and fact recur across them. Her self-knowledge stands out most: she judges her own motives as firmly as she judges others. It is a queen's wisdom in fragments, vivid because it comes from inside the storm.
75810-introductory-lectures-on-psycho-an:
Freud gave twenty-eight lectures at the University of Vienna, and Joan Riviere turned the talks into English. The authorized translation first came out in Great Britain in 1922. Ernest Jones, president of the International Psycho-Analytical Association, wrote the preface. A frontispiece shows Schwind's picture of the prisoner's dream, a picture taken up later in the talks.

The first four talks deal with the psychology of errors. They cover slips of the tongue and pen, misreading, mishearing, and forgetting things for a short time. Next come eleven talks on dreams. The last part sets out the broad theory of the neuroses, and it ends with transference and the analytic therapy.
76432-history-and-criticism-of-the-labor:
A Columbia University study in history, economics, and public law, on the history and criticism of the labor theory of value in English political economy. The volume sits inside the faculty's series, with a full scheme of instruction printed up front.

The framing shows the graduate world the work came from: Nicholas Murray Butler as president, and professors including Seligman in political economy and Charles Beard lecturing in history. Fellowships of 650 dollars and scholarships of 150 are listed among the faculty's facts. The library held about 370,000 volumes. Students get a scholarly monograph on how English economists built, and then questioned, the doctrine that labor makes value.
76646-the-songs-of-bilitis:
The Songs of Bilitis, by Pierre Louys, is a set of prose poems said to be translated from the Greek. The hosted copy is a private printing of 1919, in a new English rendering. Only nine hundred and seventy five copies were printed, after which the type was melted down. The book is dedicated to the young girls of the society of the future.

A life of Bilitis opens it. She was born at the start of the sixth century before our era in a mountain village of Pamphylia. Her mother was Phoenician and her father a Greek she never knew. The land of her birth is stony and sad, shadowed by deep forests under the mass of Tauros. Louys invented Bilitis and her songs, yet presented them as a lost Greek poetess's work. The hoax fooled scholars at first. The songs remain famed for their beauty and frankness.
76873-wrecked-among-cannibals-in-the-fij:
William Endicott, third mate of the ship Glide of Salem, told this tale of shipwreck in the South Seas. The Marine Research Society of Salem printed it in 1923. Lawrence Waters Jenkins, of the Peabody Museum, added notes.

Endicott's account tells of wreck and adventure among the Fiji Islands, where his crew fell among cannibals. A second piece describes a cannibal feast at the islands. Word lists for Fiji and for Wallis Island follow, plus the names of the Glide's officers and crew. Pictures show Fiji houses, war clubs, canoes, and the ships of the Salem trade.
77363-a-critical-and-exegetical-commenta:
The Genesis volume of the International Critical Commentary on the Holy Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments. It stands under the editorship of Driver of Oxford, Plummer of Durham, and Briggs of Union Theological Seminary, New York.

The editors' preface draws the field. Many works on the Bible by British and American divines serve popular ends, or the pulpit: the Cambridge Bible for Schools, the Speaker's Commentary, and the Expositor's Bible among them. They have their place, the preface grants. But they do not enter the field of critical study of the Bible. That field belongs to such series as the German handbooks and De Wette's work. The International series was made to hold it in English. Notes at the front record standardized punctuation. Shortened forms are spelled out in full for easier reading.
78285-new-orleans-as-it-is:
New Orleans As It Is is a stark account of life in that city, written by a resident. Its title names its themes: the manners and customs of the place, its morals, its fashionable life, the breaking of the Sabbath, vice, and the slave markets and slavery. It came out at Utica, New York, in 1849 from the press of De Witt C. Grove. A motto holds that truth is stranger than fiction.

The preface says no excuse is needed for the plain speech of the pages. The aim from the start, the writer holds, was to draw a true picture of the crowd of men and women who mingle in the great city. A quote on the title page calls the place a heap of houses and a gulf of evils.
78435-murder-in-paris:
Alice Campbell wrote Murder in Paris, printed in New York, copyright 1930. A note at the front says no living person is meant in the tale. Contents run to forty-two chapters. The first opens on shipboard. Catherine did not at first know what to make of Geoffrey Macadam.

Was his stiffness mere British reserve, she wonders, or was he hiding his vexation at a stranger thrust upon him? If the latter, she longed to tell him how hotly she shared his feeling. For eight days across the Atlantic she had been fleeing the officious care of the lady now making the introduction. That lady, Mrs Hugh Tyler Pope, was no more to be denied than the forces of nature. Then she caught a curious, almost startled look on his face. That look, the tale says, is the starting point of the story.
78482-the-discovery-of-damaris:
Amy Le Feuvre's novel, issued in London from Bouverie Street, opens on a lonely girl in a big upper room of a very old house in a quiet London square. Damaris works at tapestry among Persian carpet, coffee-coloured paper, old china bowls, and a jar of yellow daffodils. One observer calls her a soul built to suffer, too tenderly shod for life's rough stones.

Another who knows her better says she is not awake, and that slumbering fires, once roused, will startle all by their fierceness. The chapters promise an engagement, freedom at last, a country lodging, and a sudden departure. A runaway is tracked, a family meeting held, and a squire's accident and a last ride lead toward the right home appearing.
7862-the-sword-of-antietam-a-story-of-th:
Joseph A. Altsheler's The Sword of Antietam tells a complete Civil War story, yet links to a chain begun in The Guns of Bull Run and carried through Shiloh and Stonewall. Young northerner Dick Mason and his friends stand at the forefront, facing his southern cousin Harry Kenton across the lines.

Principal figures include Colonel George Kenton, Mrs. Mason, her devoted servant Juliana, Colonel Winchester, and Colonel Talbot of the Invincibles. Later volumes will reach Gettysburg, Chickamauga, and Appomattox. Here, Antietam's bloody day tests kinship, courage, and a nation's crisis.
78623-craft-guilds-of-the-thirteenth-cen:
Millett wrote a short history study of the craft gilds of Paris in the thirteenth century. It came out in 1915 as a bulletin from the history and political science staff at Queen's University in Kingston, Canada. The study asks how Paris trades were run, who held power in them, and how rules bound each trade.

A Paris gild, as the study defines it, joined masters, valets, and apprentices who had the right to work at one trade. Members swore to obey the trade rules and to respect the Jurés who watched over the work. The gild guarded the rights of labor against feudal lords and foreign trade rivals. Readers get a clear picture of how work, rank, and town power fit together in the later Middle Ages.
78828-queen-of-the-jesters-and-her-stran:
Max Pemberton wrote Queen of the Jesters and Her Strange Adventures in Old Paris, issued at New York in 1897 by Dodd, Mead and Company. Pemberton had writ Christine of the Hills and A Puritan's Wife. A front print shows a beast spring with a low warning roar. An author's note sets out the source of the tales.

The tales draw on the life of Corinne de Montesson in the Paris of Louis the Fifteenth. She scorned the salons and the galleries of Versailles, Pemberton says. She set up in an old house in Rue St Paul with a band of wits and adventurers. Her aim was to know the dens of the town. She saved rogues from the gallows and was thought a witch or a saint by the poor. The King heard her tales with greed.
79481-final-report-of-the-pennsylvania-c:
The Pennsylvania Chestnut Tree Blight Commission issued its final report at Harrisburg in 1914, covering January 1 to December 15, 1913. Winthrop Sargent of Bryn Mawr chaired the commission, with Harold Peirce of Haverford as secretary. Samuel T Bodine and George F Craig sat among its members. The commission kept offices at 1421 Chestnut Street in Philadelphia.

The blight was then destroying the American chestnut across the eastern forests. Pennsylvania funded the commission to fight it with cutting, quarantine, and research. Its final report closed a losing campaign. The chestnut, once a quarter of the hardwood forest, was doomed as a timber tree. The report is a primary record of that disaster.
8228-the-world-english-bible-web-genesis:
Genesis, in the World English Bible, opens the Bible in clear modern English, lightly reformatted from ebible. org by Martin Ward. In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth, and the narrative moves through six days of creation, the garden of Eden. The fall, Cain and Abel, the flood, the tower of Babel, and the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph. The translation notes a Hebrew marker after God in the first verse, the letters Aleph and Tav.

The World English Bible aims to give a modern, public-domain rendering that anyone can read and share. Its plain style makes Genesis accessible to new readers, while its notes keep some Hebrew detail visible. As the Bible's first book, Genesis sets out origins, covenant, and family saga, and this version tells that story in today's language.
8303-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-03-levi:
Leviticus is the third book of the Douay-Rheims Bible, in Bishop Challoner's revision of the older English Catholic text from the Latin Vulgate. It records the laws given to Israel through Moses for worship and daily life. These cover how sacrifices were offered, how priests were set apart, which foods were clean, and how the Day of Atonement cleansed the people once a year.

Modern readers often find Leviticus slow going, but its rules show how an ancient people understood holiness: as something that touched food, skin, homes, and fields, not only the sanctuary. The book also holds the command to love one's neighbor, later quoted by Jesus. In Challoner's phrasing, the old laws keep their formal, churchly sound.
8343-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-43-zach:
Zacharias preached to Jews back in a ruined Jerusalem, urging them to finish the temple, and his book is a string of night visions. Horsemen ride the earth, a measuring line spans the city, a golden lampstand shines between two olive trees, and a flying scroll curses thieves. Each vision nudges tired builders back to work and promises that God has not left the city.

Later chapters grow darker and stranger, with a shepherd struck down, a king riding a donkey, and nations gathering against Jerusalem. Christians read the donkey-riding king as Jesus entering the city. The Douay-Rheims name Zacharias stands for Zechariah, in Challoner's Vulgate-based text, and the book's pictures have fed art and preaching for centuries.
8355-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-55-gala:
Galatians is Paul's shortest, sharpest letter, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's older English. Teachers had told Gentile converts they must keep Jewish law to belong, and Paul answers with heat: if law saves, Christ died for nothing. Freedom comes by faith, he argues, and the proof is the Spirit's fruit, love, joy, and peace, against the works of the flesh.

The letter also records Paul's public clash with Peter over eating with Gentiles, a frank glimpse of the early church's growing pains. Reformers later made Galatians their charter of grace alone. Short enough to read in one sitting, it still sets the terms for every argument about law, freedom, and belonging.
8356-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-56-ephe:
Ephesians speaks to a port city's church about belonging, and the Douay-Rheims text gives it in Challoner's Vulgate-based English. Believers are described as chosen and forgiven, joined into one body where Jews and Gentiles are no longer strangers. The letter's opening blessing piles grace upon grace, as if praise could barely hold the news.

Practical counsel follows: speak truth, put off old habits, forgive quickly, and let households run on love and respect. The armor of God passage, belt, breastplate, shield, and sword, has echoed through preaching ever since. Short and soaring, Ephesians remains the New Testament's fullest picture of the church as one people.
8361-the-bible-douay-rheims-book-61-1-ti:
Timothy, Paul's young helper in Ephesus, receives this letter of practical counsel, in the Douay-Rheims text as in other Bibles. It tells him to silence false teachers, to appoint overseers and deacons of steady character, and to order prayer and worship. Rules for widows, elders, and slaves fill the middle, and the letter warns, in a line known to all, that love of money is the root of all evils.

Challoner's Vulgate-based English gives the church-order advice its older Catholic phrasing. Because it speaks to how congregations should be run, 1 Timothy became a handbook for clergy across centuries. Its tone is that of a mentor writing to a trusted deputy under strain, urging him to hold fast and set an example.
899-wonderful-balloon-ascents-or-the-con:
F. Marion wrote this history of balloons and balloon voyages, opening with Vincent Lunardi of Lucca, the first aerial traveller in Britain, who rose on 15 September 1784. The book follows the pioneers who dared the skies in silk and gas, from early French ascents to voyages across seas and mountains.

Marion tells of triumphs, wrecks, and the slow conquest of the air, with the wonder of crowds below. His history, first issued in 1870, captures the age when flight was a marvel, not a routine. The book delights readers who love the heroic early days of aeronautics, before the aeroplane stole the show.
9307-life-its-true-genesis:
R. W. Wright wrote this work on the true genesis, or origin, of life, in a second edition of 1884. He opens with Hebrew and Greek texts on seed after its kind, and his own plain translation: each living thing bears its general principle of life within itself. Chapters then treat forests, seeds, migration, and species.

Wright weighs theories of life, refutes materialist accounts, and considers Darwin from a vitalist standpoint, favoring a living principle over mere mechanism. The book is earnest Victorian natural theology. It interests historians of science as a serious, if dated, challenge to Darwin's age.
9745-the-rock-of-chickamauga-a-story-of-:
Joseph A. Altsheler wrote The Rock of Chickamauga, a Civil War novel of the western crisis. Harry Kenton fights for the South, his cousin Dick Mason for the North, with colonels, spies, and cavalry leaders around them. The book belongs to Altsheler's eight-volume Civil War series, from Bull Run to Appomattox. Battles named include Port Republic, Fredericksburg, and Missionary Ridge.

Chickamauga's rock stands at the tale's heart, as cousins meet war's hard choices. Altsheler writes with brisk, boy-friendly pace and care for battle detail. A reader gets a rousing volume of a classic war series, rich in marches, charges, and divided kin.
9833-pee-wee-harris:
Percy Keese Fitzhugh, author of the Tom Slade and Roy Blakeley books, wrote this scout story about Pee-Wee Harris, a small, loud, hungry boy with big ideas. Pee-Wee decides to help a restaurant called Pepsy's by running its advertising department, with his fellow scouts in tow.

Chapters follow the battle of the banana, a tragic predicament, an invitation, and Pepsy's secret, as plans grow grander and funnier. Fitzhugh keeps the humor broad and the scouting spirit earnest. Young readers get slapstick, friendship, and a hero whose confidence always outruns his size.
a-day-s-tour-a-journey-through-france-an: Percy Fitzgerald records a day's tour through France and Belgium in this short travel book. The route runs by Calais, Tournay, Douai, Arras, Lille, Ypres, and St. Omer, with sketches along the way. Fitzgerald offers the trifle as a lesson in seeing much during a short journey. The book suits readers who enjoy brief, observant travel writing.
a-distinguished-provincial-at-paris:
Honoré de Balzac follows Lucien de Rubempré from Angoulême to Paris in Ellen Marriage's translation, the middle part of the Lost Illusions trilogy, as the preparer's note explains. Lucien arrives with a great lady, poems, and hopes of fame. Paris greets him with cold rooms, closed doors, and the price of everything.

Lucien falls in with poor young scholars, then with journalists who teach him to sell his pen and his praise. The theatre, the press, debt, and a love affair with an actress consume his money and his honor. Balzac shows the machinery of literary Paris grinding a gifted young man down, gear by gear.
ade-le-dubois: Mary Langdon Bradbury Savage tells the story of Adèle Dubois, set in the lovely Miramichi valley of New Brunswick and published at Boston in 1865. The first chapter opens at the Dubois House, where Norton settles into a curiously carved old-fashioned armchair before a blazing hearth. He marvels at finding such comfort in a wild region. The house is agreeable and tidy but unlike home, he thinks, an Elim in the desert, with goodly palm trees and abundant water.
adventures-and-letters-of-richard-hardin:
Charles Belmont Davis edited this life of his brother, as the title page states. The brother is Richard Harding Davis, the journalist and story writer. The contents run in twenty chapters. They start with the early days in Philadelphia. They pass through college and first newspaper work. They close with the travels that made Davis the most famous American reporter of his age.

Later chapters follow him as a war correspondent. He covered Cuba and Greece. He covered the Spanish-American War and the Boer War. He reported two coronations and the Russo-Japanese War. The end comes with Vera Cruz, the Great War, and his last days. Family letters and the editor's own memories carry the tale between campaigns. The book is both a biography and a record of a reporter's life before radio and wire photos.
anabasis:
Xenophon's Anabasis, in H. G. Dakyns's translation, tells how ten thousand Greek soldiers marched into Persia and fought their way home. The prefatory note gives Xenophon's life in brief: an Athenian, a pupil of Socrates, who marched with the army and helped lead its return between 401 and 399 B.C. The Greeks had hired themselves to Cyrus, who meant to take the throne from his brother.

Cyrus died in battle, the Greek generals were seized, and the army stood stranded deep in a hostile empire. Across seven books Xenophon records marches, snow, hunger, elections of new leaders, and battles on the long road to the sea. Their shout on first seeing the water became famous.
angelic-wisdom-concerning-the-divine-lov: Emanuel Swedenborg writes on angelic wisdom concerning the divine love and the divine wisdom, opening with the claim that love is the life of man. The work sets out his doctrine of God as love and wisdom united, and of humanity made in that image. Its translator's note introduces a central text of Swedenborgian thought.
apocolocyntosis: Lucius Annaeus Seneca writes the Apocolocyntosis, a satire on the deification of Claudius, here with an English translation by W. H. D. Rouse. The short work mocks the dead emperor's ascent to heaven with savage wit. Seneca's jeu d'esprit remains a sharp example of Roman political satire. The joke is short, and it cuts deep.
appreciations-of-richard-harding-davis:
Appreciations of Richard Harding Davis gathers memorial essays on the journalist by a dozen of his contemporaries, listed at the front. The writers include Gouverneur Morris, Booth Tarkington, Charles Dana Gibson, Theodore Roosevelt, Irvin S. Cobb, and John Fox, Jr. Each knew Davis as a friend, colleague, or fellow traveler, and each writes in a personal voice rather than a critical one.

Morris opens by remembering games of pirates and imaginary elephant hunts with a man of fifty-two who never grew old. Others recall Davis under fire in Cuba, hunting wounded men in front of the trenches, and the Rough Riders making him an honorary member. Together the pieces form a portrait of the era's model reporter, drawn entirely by the men who shared his world.
atlantis:
Gerhart Hauptmann's novel came out in English in 1912, translated by Adele and Thomas Seltzer for B. W. Huebsch of New York. Hauptmann, Germany's leading dramatist, opens aboard the fast mail steamer Roland, sailing from Bremen to New York in January 1892. Her plain English-built saloons, officers, engineers, and stewards are catalogued before the voyage turns to disaster.

Survivors carry the wreck's mark through the later action. The artist Fleischmann retells his rescue endlessly, polishing the tale until his own vanity replaces the facts: dragged out howling, by companions he forgets to credit. Ingigerd, the dancer, draws the hero's troubled fascination. Hauptmann uses the sunken ship as his title's engine: a modern world drowned mid-crossing, its passengers washed up changed.
aunt-phillis-s-cabin-or-southern-life-as:
Mary H. Eastman published this plantation novel at Philadelphia in 1852, answering Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin. Her preface argues that slavery needs no defence from history or philosophy, since the Bible itself records its origin and the laws God gave for his own institution. The title promises southern life as it is, from the slaveholders' side.

Aunt Phillis, an enslaved woman, anchors the cabin scenes, correcting frightened neighbours who swear they saw Aunt Peggy's red eyes glaring at a window. Dialect comedy, plantation households, and set arguments present slavery as a scriptural, household order. Historians read the book as a leading anti-Tom novel: fiction built to rebut abolition, valuable now chiefly as evidence of the pro-slavery case in its own words.
autobiography-and-letters-of-orville-dew:
Orville Dewey, a leading American Unitarian minister, left these memoirs and letters, edited by his daughter Mary Dewey. She explains that her father began writing his memories some twenty-five years before the book, at her urging. He had once been a foremost figure, yet lived so long withdrawn that his death passed almost unnoticed beyond his friends, like an aged tree falling in vast forests.

An autobiography of about a hundred pages leads, then letters fill the rest. Writing from Sheffield in 1847, Dewey describes sermons in hand for New York Sundays and a hand too weary from them to answer friends promptly. Morning light, a green slope under a window, and quiet close one letter. The volume recalls pulpit fame, travel, and a wide circle of notable acquaintance.
betty-s-bright-idea-deacon-pitkin-s-farm:
Harriet Beecher Stowe gathered three New England tales in this illustrated volume of 1875, all turning on Christmas and conscience. Betty's Bright Idea opens in New York as the hallowed season settles over the roaring, rattling life-world of shops and streets. Deacon Pitkin's Farm and The First Christmas of New England follow, moving the holiday back to Puritan times and forward to a farm family's trials.

Faith is tested in small exchanges. A failing mother tells her son that when her strength is gone she asks God for more, and he always gives it. The son begs to swap Bibles: hers, marked and worn, would do him more good. She gives it with a bright flush and a pleased smile. Stowe writes her late manner at its warmest — theology in the kitchen, in dialect and in tears.
britannica-1911-abaris: Abaris is the subject of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a Scythian or Hyperborean priest and prophet of Apollo, said to have visited Greece about 770 B.C., or some centuries later. Legend gives him a golden arrow, the god's gift, on which he rode through the country. He lived without food, healed the sick, foretold events, worked wonders, and freed Sparta from a plague, the entry reports, citing Herodotus and Iamblichus. Works on Scythian oracles bear his name in Suidas.
britannica-1911-abatis: Abatis, also spelled Abattis or Abbattis, is the headword of a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry gives the word as a French term, meaning a heap of material thrown down. In field fortification it names an obstacle built from tree branches. The branches lie in a row with tops pointed toward the enemy, laced or tied with wire. Troops set it alone or paired with wire entanglements and other blocks, the entry states. One tight notice fixes a soldier's word still met in war histories.
britannica-1911-abiogenesis:
Abiogenesis receives a science entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The word names the theory that living things sometimes rise whole from dead matter, once called spontaneous generation. Aristotle taught it as observed fact: plant-lice from dew, fleas from rot, mice from Nile mud in Ross's old gloss.

Redi's screened meat of 1668 began the refutation for visible life: no flies, no maggots. The microscope reopened the question for bacteria, till Pasteur showed that sterilized matter, kept clean, stays barren. Heat-proof spores explained the long doubt. All known life now comes from life, the entry states flatly. Lab-made protoplasm stays a bare possibility, reached by stages if at all, and the verdict binds only known forms.
britannica-1911-acis:
Acis, in Greek mythology, was a beautiful Sicilian shepherd, son of Pan and the nymph Symaethis, and lover of the Nereid Galatea, a sea nymph. The 1911 Britannica entry tells his story in a few lines drawn chiefly from Ovid. His rival was the Cyclops Polyphemus, the one-eyed giant, who surprised the lovers together and crushed Acis to pieces with a rock.

Blood became a river. As Acis's blood gushed out beneath the rock, Galatea changed it into the river that bears his name, now called the Fiume di Jaci. The entry notes that this river was celebrated for the coldness of its waters, a detail Sicilian tradition kept attached to the tale.
britannica-1911-ackerman-francis:
Francis Ackerman (about 1335-1387) was a Flemish soldier and diplomatist born at Ghent who rose during that city's struggle with Louis II, count of Flanders. He helped persuade Philip van Artevelde to lead Ghent in 1382, then scoured the countryside at the head of troops for provisions and saved the city from starvation. Diplomacy won help from Brussels, Louvain, and Liege, and as admiral of the Flemish fleet he gained a promise of aid from Richard II of England.

Leadership followed Artevelde's death. Ackerman won victories, conducted a skilful retreat to Ghent in 1385, and helped conclude peace with Burgundy that December. Trusting the new duke and ignoring warnings, he stayed in Flanders and was murdered at Ghent in 1387.
britannica-1911-acropolis:
Acropolis means, in Greek, the upper part of a town. Early settlers chose high ground for defence. A hill with steep sides made a natural citadel. Great cities later grew around such strongholds. The word began with Greek towns like Athens and Argos. Thebes and Corinth had their own acropolises. Usage soon widened beyond Greece, though.

Writers apply the term to citadels anywhere. Rome and Jerusalem qualify under it. Many towns of Asia Minor qualify too. Even Castle Hill at Edinburgh has been called one. One example outshines all the rest. The Acropolis of Athens carries unmatched historical associations. Its famous buildings crown the rock there. Bare mention of the Acropolis means Athens, the entry says.
britannica-1911-actinomycosis:
Actinomycosis is a chronic infective disease of cattle and man. Older doctors blamed a single ray-fungus for it. Research instead found many parasite species responsible. Their shared genus name is Streptothrix. A London committee recommended Streptotrichosis as the clinical term in 1899. The disease forms grainy tumours in inflamed tissue. These may suppurate, harden, or calcify over time.

Organs show varied damage, the entry explains. Livers develop scattered foci of suppuration. Lungs may mimic consumption almost exactly. Skin lesions are the most characteristic sign. Soft, mottled nodules break into crater-like ulcers. Sticky fluid exudes from the openings. Infection probably spreads through grain the fungus inhabits. Potassium iodide helps, but surgery is usually needed.
britannica-1911-adams-charles-francis:
Charles Francis Adams (1807-1886) was an American diplomatist. He was son of President John Quincy Adams. John Adams was his grandfather in turn. Boston was his birthplace in August 1807. His father took him to Russia in 1809. Eight years abroad gave him perfect French. Harvard graduated him in 1825. Law study and business occupied his Boston years. He edited a party journal, the Boston Whig.

Politics peaked in two crises. The Buffalo Convention of 1848 nominated him for vice-president. He ran on the Free Soil ticket then. Lincoln sent him as minister to Britain in 1861. His mission was preventing British intervention. Sympathy for the South made that task hard. Adams stopped Confederate ironclad rams from sailing. Geneva's Alabama tribunal used his fairness in 1871.
britannica-1911-aegis:
Aegis is a 1911 Britannica article on the shield of Zeus in Greek myth. In Homer, the aegis is the shield or buckler of Zeus. Hephaestus fashioned it for him. It is furnished with tassels and bears the Gorgon's head at its centre.

At first, the text says, it stood for the storm-cloud. The word most likely comes from a root meaning rapid, violent motion. When the god shakes the aegis, Mount Ida is wrapped in clouds. The thunder rolls, and men are struck with fear. He at times lends it to Athene, and rarely to Apollo. A later tale tells a different origin. Zeus is said to have used the skin of the goat Amaltheia as a buckler. That goat suckled him in Crete. He bore it when he went to battle with the giants. Myth readers get one object read as cloud, shield, and goat-skin at once.
britannica-1911-agenais:
Agenais, or Agenois, was a former province of France. In old Gaul it was the land of the Nitiobroges, with Aginnum as its chief town. In the 4th century it was the Civitas Agennensium, part of Aquitania Secunda. It formed the church district of Agen. The land shared the fate of Aquitaine in the ages that came next. It then became a countship that passed by birth, in the part of the land now called Gascony.

In 1038 the dukes of Aquitaine and counts of Poitiers bought that countship. The wedding of Eleanor of Aquitaine to Henry Plantagenet in 1152 brought Agenais under the rule of England. When Richard the Lionheart wed his sister Joan to the count of Toulouse in 1196, Agenais formed part of her dowry. It fell to the crown of France in 1271 with the rest of the last count's lands.
britannica-1911-agis:
Agis is the subject of a kings entry in the 1911 Britannica. The name was borne by four kings of Sparta. The first Agis was son of Eurysthenes in the tale. He founded a royal house of Sparta, the text says. His line was traced back through heroes to Heracles. He belongs more to myth than to firm past. Custom credits him with the taking of a sea town.

The second king of the name took the throne in 427 before Christ. He led Spartan land forces through a long war. That war was the Peloponnesian war with Athens. He won a great rout of foes at Mantinea in 418. That win came after a truce that had shamed him. The entry gives his moves year by year in the war. Later kings of the same name follow in the entry.
britannica-1911-aickin-francis:
Francis Aickin, an Irish actor who died in 1805, earned the stage name Tyrant from his force in grand, fiery parts. London first saw him in 1765 at Drury Lane, playing Dick Amlet in Vanbrugh's The Confederacy. He went on acting at Drury Lane and Covent Garden until 1792, building a list of more than eighty roles.

Two parts stood out above the rest: Jaques in As You Like It, and Hamlet's Ghost. His younger brother James wins a notice too. James played leads in both comic and tragic plays at Edinburgh, then angered his public by standing up for a fellow actor who had been dismissed. London took him in. There he acted for decades, worked as deputy manager, and fought a duel with John Philip Kemble in which no blood was shed.
britannica-1911-aire-pas-de-calais:
Three canals meet at Aire, a town of Pas-de-Calais in northern France that sits low and marshy on the river Lys. Rail puts it twelve miles south-south-east of St Omer, and 4,258 people lived there in 1906. Wet, flat ground shaped the place and its work alike.

St Pierre, the chief church, went up in the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries and boasts a grand tower and rich work inside. Two more landmarks stand out: a town hall of the eighteenth century and the Bailliage, a small house in the Renaissance manner. Mills ground flour, and leather works, oil works, and nail shops gave jobs, beside trade in farm goods. In medieval times the counts of Flanders held Aire and granted a charter in 1188 that still survives. The peace of Utrecht handed the town to France in 1713.
britannica-1911-alais:
Alais is a town of south France, chief town of a district north west of Nimes on a main rail line. It is a key rail junction, the 1911 Britannica entry says, and gives its town count in the early years of the age. The town sits at the foot of a range of hills, on the left bank of a river that half rings it.

Wide streets, walks, and fine plane trees make the town fair to see. Its church is a heavy work of a past age, and its fort serves as barracks and jail. A great scientist did his key work on silk worm disease in the town, and a bust there marks his name. A statue of a famed chemist stands there too. Courts, a trade board, a high school, and a school of mines serve the town, a chief mart for raw silk.
britannica-1911-alcestis:
Alcestis gave her life for her husband, and a hero wrestled her back from the dead. So runs one of the best-loved tales of wifely love in Greek myth. She was the daughter of Pelias and Anaxibia, and she wed Admetus, king of Pherae in Thessaly. The tale turns on a pact with death itself: she agreed to die in Admetus's place, so that he could go on living, and Heracles saved her after.

Euripides built his play Alcestis on the tale. Sophocles wrote an Alcestis too, though only scraps of it last. In our own era Robert Browning took Euripides' telling as the ground for his Balaustion's Adventure. A short notice, then, for a tale that poets have mined for two thousand years and more.
britannica-1911-ampelopsis:
Garden walls are the home ground of Ampelopsis, a plant genus of the vine order and a close kin of the grape-vine. Fast-growing and hardy, these climbers thrive in plain garden soil, spread easily from cuttings, and pull themselves up by tendrils. Their Greek name pairs the words for vine and look, since in habit they copy the grape-vine.

Two kinds get close notice. Virginian creeper, a North American plant brought to Europe early in the seventeenth century, bears hand-shaped leaves of three to five leaflets. A Japanese kind that arrived in 1868, better known as A. Veitchii, has smaller leaves of shifting shape. Suckers at the tips of its branched tendrils let it grip stone or brick, which makes it handy for covering walls.
britannica-1911-angina-pectoris:
Angina pectoris, Latin for pain of the chest, names a violent paroxysm of pain connected almost invariably with disease of the coronary arteries and progressive degeneration of the heart muscle. An attack usually begins suddenly, with pain felt first over the heart, then radiating through the chest and often down the left arm. A sense of constriction and suffocation accompanies it, though actual breathing seldom becomes difficult.

Exertion commonly brings on a seizure, and the sufferer is brought at once to rest, enduring intense agony while it lasts. The face turns pale, the skin cold, and the pulse feeble, yet after rarely more than two or three minutes complete relief follows. Attacks recur on slight exertion, and the first seizure sometimes proves fatal. The entry distinguishes this true angina from a nervous imitation with longer seizures and a good prognosis, treated through its underlying neurosis.
britannica-1911-angoumois: Angoulême, the city on the Charente, gave its name to Angoumois. The old province of France matched, in the entry's day, roughly the present department of Charente, and Angoulême was its capital. For the province's fuller record, the named source is Castaigne's 1845 essay toward a historical library of the Angoumois.
britannica-1911-ankylosis:
Ankylosis means stiffness of a joint. The word comes from a Greek term for bent or crooked. Injury or disease causes the condition. Rigidity may be complete or partial. Inflammation outside the joint can produce it. Muscles and tendons may be the affected structures. Doctors call that form false ankylosis. Disease within the joint produces true ankylosis.

Bone fusion creates the most complete form. Inflamed joint-ends grow together into one mass. Surgeons can sometimes restore movement. Excision of an ankylosed shoulder may free the limb. An elbow may regain usefulness the same way. Anatomists use the term more broadly too. Bones originally distinct may coalesce with age. No motion then remains between them. The entry covers both medical senses compactly.
britannica-1911-ankylostomiasis:
Ankylostomiasis is a disease caused by intestinal worms. Miners' anaemia is another common name. Germany calls it Wurmkrankheit, the worm disease. Mining regions have suffered it heavily. England, France, Germany, and Belgium all report cases. North Queensland in Australia appears too. Ancient Egypt apparently knew the disease. It killed many enslaved people in the West Indies.

Bilharz and Griesinger identified the cause in 1854. Small nematoid worms infest the intestine. They measure a third to half an inch. The worms cling to the intestinal membrane. They draw nourishment from their host. Symptoms include stomach pain and capricious appetite. Dirt-eating, pallor, and weakness follow. Fatal cases bring dysentery and haemorrhages. Sanitation forms the main precaution. Male fern, thymol, and similar remedies are prescribed.
britannica-1911-anubis:
Anubis was one of the most important gods of Egypt, and this 1911 Britannica entry begins by setting him beside a kindred god. Egypt had two kinds of dog-like divinities, led by Anubis and by Ophois, the opener of the ways. Anubis is shown as the animal lying down, while Ophois stands stiffly and is carried on a standard in war and in processions. Both kinds were kindly powers, but those of Anubis guarded the graveyard.

The two sorts match, in some measure, the milder and fiercer sides of the dog tribe. In late days the Greeks reported that dogs were sacred to Anubis and wolves to Ophois. The figure of Anubis is coloured black, as suits a god of funerals and of the night. It is drawn leaner than a greyhound, yet with the bushy tail of the fox or jackal.
britannica-1911-apollinaris:
Apollinaris the Younger was bishop of Laodicea in Syria, died in three ninety. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He worked with his father to recast the Old Testament in Homer verse. They did so when Julian barred Christians from teaching the classics.

Apollinaris is best known as a warm foe of Arianism in debate. His zeal to stress the godhood of Christ led him too far. He denied a rational human soul in the nature of Christ. In its place he set the Logos as the ruling holy force. Church councils condemned that view, most of all at Constantinople in three eighty one.
britannica-1911-apotheosis:
Apotheosis means making a person into a god, from a Greek word for deifying. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica says the idea fits faiths with many gods. Such faiths blur the line between gods and men in several ways. Greek faith honored city founders and heroes after death in this spirit.

Living men at times gained worship as true gods as well. Lysander and Philip of Macedon are named as early cases there. Eastern courts pushed the claim further for their kings in time. Heirs of Alexander all claimed some divine honor for their houses. Rome later made the practice formal for its emperors and kin.
britannica-1911-appendicitis:
Appendicitis is the modern medical term for swelling of the appendix. The 1911 Britannica entry calls that part a section of the intestine. The ill is not new, yet it seems far more common than of old. No clear cause for that rise has yet been found, it admits. Among the germs tied to the ill, no one germ stands out as chief.

Some link the ill to influenza or to the use of preserved foods. Those views have their backers, though proof is still lacking in full. At times a pin, a bristle, or a fish bone lodges in the appendix. Such a thing can set up swelling and rot in that small tube. A hard lump of faeces can burst the wall in grave cases.
britannica-1911-arbois:
Arbois is a town of eastern France. It lies in the department of Jura. The Cuisance river flows through it. Lons-le-Saunier is twenty-nine miles south-west by rail. Population in 1906 was 3,454. The town seats the Poligny arrondissement tribunal. A communal college serves local students. St Just's church dates from the tenth century. Its wood-carving is notably good.

An Ursuline convent houses the town hall. That convent was built in 1764. It also holds the law court. A fourteenth-century church serves as market now. An old Burgundy dukes' château survives too. Red and white wines make Arbois well known. Saw-mills and tanneries operate locally. Market gardens surround the town. Paper, oil, and casks are manufactured there. The entry is a tidy provincial gazetteer notice.
britannica-1911-artois:
Artois is a province article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about an old province in the north of France. It matches most of the modern department of Pas de Calais. The land is rich and well watered. It yields much grain and hops and gives fine pasture for cattle. Its chief town was Arras.

Other key places were Saint-Omer, Bethune, Aire, Hesdin, and Lens. The name Artois comes from the Atrebates, who held the district in the time of Caesar. From the ninth to the twelfth century the counts of Flanders held it. In 1180 it passed to King Philip Augustus of France. It came as the dowry of Isabella of Hainaut, niece of the count of Flanders. At her death in 1190 her kin disputed the land with the French king.
britannica-1911-asbury-francis:
Francis Asbury, who lived from 1745 to 1816, was a church leader who built Methodism in America. The 1911 Britannica entry starts with his poor youth near Birmingham in England. He left school early for work making buckle tongues as a lad of fourteen. Faith came at thirteen, and by sixteen he was a local preacher.

John Wesley sent him as a travelling minister in 1767, and in 1771 he crossed to the colonies. Fewer than three hundred Methodists were there when he landed at Philadelphia. Within a year the flock more than doubled under his drive. He soon held charge of the work in America and kept it through the war years.
britannica-1911-atargatis:
Atargatis was a Syrian goddess, often called the fish-goddess, and an entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica unpacks her name and her cult. The Greeks knew her by a shortened form, Derketo, and the Romans as Dea Syria. Her name joins two divine names, the first akin to Astarte, though the entry warns the two goddesses, of common origin, had distinct cults.

Her home was Syria proper, above all Hierapolis, where she had a great temple, and a temple of hers is also named at Carnion in Gilead. From Syria her worship spread to Greece, Italy, and the far west, carried largely by Syrian merchants. The entry pictures her beggar-priests touring great cities with her image on an ass.
britannica-1911-atlantis:
Atlantis is the subject of a legend entry in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names a famed island in the Atlantic Ocean, first mentioned by Plato in the Timaeus. Plato tells how Egyptian priests described the island to Solon. They said it was larger than Asia Minor and Libya put together.

It lay just beyond the Pillars of Hercules, with lesser islands beyond it. The priests said Atlantis had been a powerful kingdom thousands of years before Solon. Its armies had overrun the lands around the Mediterranean Sea. Athens alone had withstood them with success. At last, the tale says, the sea overwhelmed the island.
britannica-1911-atterbury-francis:
English man of letters Francis Atterbury, born in sixteen sixty two, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He later became a politician and a bishop. His father was rector of the parish where he was born, in Buckinghamshire. He was schooled at Westminster and at Christ Church, Oxford.

At Oxford he became a tutor. In sixteen eighty two he put out a Latin verse version of a famed poem. He did far better in English prose, the entry says. A reply of his to an attack on the Reformation won praise for its force of speech. Its targets were so stung that they charged him with treason. After the Revolution he swore loyalty to the new government, though bred to oppose resistance. He took holy orders and preached in London to great effect.
britannica-1911-attis:
Attis was a god of Phrygia, later worshipped across the Roman empire with the Great Mother of the Gods. The 1911 Britannica article pairs the two as earth and her fruit, like Isis and Osiris in Egypt. Their rites were held each spring in secret ceremonies. Attis was never worshipped alone, though the Mother at times was. He was linked in myth with Pan, Men, and Adonis.

One tale, told by Pausanias, makes Attis a fair youth loved by the being Agdistis. Driven mad on his wedding day, he unmanned himself and died. Agdistis, in grief, won from Zeus the grant that his body would never rot. The article weighs a view that Attis was a Syrian god grafted onto the Phrygian cult. It finds it more likely that he was native to Asia Minor. The Phrygians took him up and mixed him with a god of their own.
britannica-1911-avoirdupois:
Avoirdupois, from the French avoir de pois, goods of weight, is the system of weights used in Great Britain and America for all goods except precious metals, gems, and medicines. Its foundation is the grain: a cubic inch of water weighs a set number of grains, and 7,000 grains now make the pound.

The pound divides into sixteen ounces, and each ounce into sixteen drachms. Building upward, fourteen pounds make a stone, two stones a quarter, four quarters a hundredweight, and twenty hundredweight a ton of 2,240 pounds. The entry prints the full table with grain values for each step, from the drachm up to the ton, giving readers the whole scale at a glance.
britannica-1911-axis:
Axis, the Latin word for axle, carries that plain sense and many extensions built on it. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry lists the main fields where the term does technical work, all turning on one image: a central line.

In its widest use, an axis is the imaginary line about which a body or system turns, or a line about which a form is evenly disposed. Geometry and crystal study use it to fix a figure's orientation. Anatomy applies the name, among other uses, to the second neck vertebra, the bone the head pivots on. In botany, axis simply means the stem of a plant.
britannica-1911-baily-francis:
Baily, Francis (1774-1844), was an English astronomer born at Newbury in Berkshire who toured unsettled North America in 1796-1797, then entered the London Stock Exchange in 1799. Books on leases, interest, and life annuities built him a fortune and a name as a writer on life-contingencies, letting him retire in 1825 for astronomy alone.

Baily helped found the Royal Astronomical Society in 1820 and won its gold medal for a catalogue of 2,881 stars. He drove the reform of the Nautical Almanac, cut down the great star catalogues of Lalande and Lacaille, and supervised the British Association's catalogue of 8,377 stars. His vivid account of the beads of light seen at the 1836 eclipse, named Baily's Beads, launched the modern age of eclipse expeditions.
britannica-1911-bakis:
Bakis was a general name for inspired prophets in Greece. The word means speaker in Greek. Such men dispensed oracles to enquirers. They flourished from the 700s to the 500s B.C. Suidas mentions three of the name.

The Boeotian Bakis was the most famous. Corycian cave nymphs inspired him, men said. His oracles survive in Herodotus and Pausanias. They were written in hexameter verse. Readers judged them strikingly fulfilled. The Arcadian Bakis cured Sparta's women of madness. That cure is his one recorded deed. Many oracles under his name belong elsewhere. Scholars assign several to Onomacritus instead.
britannica-1911-barahona-de-soto-luis:
Luis Barahona de Soto (1535?–1595) was a Spanish poet who trained at Granada and worked as a physician at Cordova. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives his life and judges his verse. His chief poem, the Primera parte de la Angélica of 1586, carries on the story of the Orlando furioso.

The lost second part was long thought gone, yet pieces of it turned up in the Diálogos de la monteria, printed in 1890. That book also holds parts of his poem Los Principios del mundo and many fine lyrics. Cervantes called him one of the best poets not only in Spain but in the whole world. The article grants the praise is warm, then credits his rich fancy and his rare command of Italian forms brought into Spanish verse.
britannica-1911-barham-richard-harris:
Richard Harris Barham (1788–1845) was an English humorist, better known by his pen name Thomas Ingoldsby, born at Canterbury on 6 December 1788. He lost his father at seven and inherited a small estate, part of it the manor of Tappington, often named in his Legends. An accident at school shattered his arm and partly crippled it for life.

Barred from active pursuits, Barham read deeply, went to Brasenose College, Oxford, and entered the church, taking a country curacy in 1813. London followed: minor canon of St Paul's in 1821 and a priest of the Chapel Royal. The 1911 Britannica entry follows his turn to print in Blackwood's Magazine and the grotesque verse tales, The Ingoldsby Legends, begun in Bentley's Miscellany in 1837.
britannica-1911-barye-antoine-louis:
Antoine Louis Barye (1796–1875), a French sculptor born in Paris, is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. Like many Renaissance sculptors he began as a goldsmith. He studied under the sculptor Bosio and the painter Gros and entered the École des Beaux Arts in 1818. His real bent appeared in 1823, when, working for a goldsmith, he watched the wild beasts in the Jardin des Plantes and drew and modelled them with force.

Animals made Barye's art and name. His Tiger devouring a Crocodile (1831) and Lion and Snake (1832) fixed a style of his own. Groups such as Theseus and the Minotaur followed year after year, despite constant money troubles. Larger works include the Lion of the Column of July and the Tuileries lions and tigers. Made a professor in 1854 and elected to the Academy in 1868, he is called the greatest French artist of animal life.
britannica-1911-batthyany-louis:
Louis Batthyány, Count Batthyány (1806–1849), a Hungarian statesman born at Pressburg, is the subject of a long 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica biography. He made up for poor schooling while serving as a hussar officer in Italy, and took up new ideas. From 1839 he led the opposition in Hungary's Upper House, where his rank and firm character gave him weight. 

Prime minister in a storm was his fate. On 31 March 1848 Batthyány became the first constitutional prime minister of Hungary. When the Croats under Jellachich took up arms, he strove to hold the constitution and win the court to his side. His power faded as Kossuth rose. He tried to mediate, then raised a regiment from his own tenants. Arrested in January 1849, he was sentenced to hang at Olmütz. To escape that fate he stabbed himself with a hidden dagger and bled to death on 5 October 1849, by the entry's account.
britannica-1911-bayard-thomas-francis:
Thomas Francis Bayard (1828–1898), an American diplomatist born in Wilmington, Delaware, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His great-grandfather, grandfather, uncle, and father had all sat for Delaware in the Senate. His grandfather helped make the treaty of Ghent. Bayard meant to go into business and took no college course. Instead he read law in his father's office from 1848 and was called to the bar in 1851, practising chiefly in Wilmington.

Office came in full measure. Bayard sat in the Senate for Delaware from 1869 to 1885, leading the Democrats there, and won a high name for his grasp of finance and law. Four times he drew votes for his party's nomination for the presidency. From 1885 to 1889 he was secretary of state under President Cleveland, following a steady, careful course abroad. He ended as ambassador to Great Britain, from 1893 to 1897.
britannica-1911-bazaine-achille-francois:
Achille François Bazaine (1811–1888), marshal of France, was born at Versailles and joined the army as a private in 1831. He won the Legion of Honour in Algeria, served with the Foreign Legion against the Carlists in Spain, and rose by steady active service.
