By 1839 he was a captain, and a decade later a brigadier-general at Tlemçen.

Bazaine fought in Crimea, where he governed Sevastopol after its fall, and in Lombardy, where he was wounded at Melegnano. He led the French in Mexico from 1863 and became marshal and senator. In the Franco-German War he held the Army of the Rhine and surrendered Metz, an act that brought him to trial in 1873.
britannica-1911-beauvais:
Beauvais is a town of northern France and the chief town of the department of Oise. It lies forty-nine miles north of Paris on the Northern railway. It had 17,045 people in 1906. The town sits at the foot of wooded hills on the left bank of the Therain river. Its old walls are gone, and broad roads now run where they stood.

The church of St Pierre is the town's great sight. In some ways it is the boldest work of Gothic building, yet it was never brought to an end. It has only a transept and a choir, with a vault more than 150 feet high. Work began in 1247 and was stopped by falls of the vault in 1284 and of a tall tower in 1573. The transept was built from 1500 to 1548.
britannica-1911-becque-henry-francois:
Henry Francois Becque is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the ninth of April 1837 in Paris, he was a French writer of plays. He wrote the words for an opera in 1867, in the manner of Lord Byron.

The article marks his first weighty play as a dark drama of 1870. Its worth was seen in full when it was revived in 1886. A play of 1882 fixed his place as a maker of new paths in the theatre. His most winning play came in 1885, a tale of Paris life. He wrote little in his last years, but his followers kept his line alive. His full plays were gathered in three books in 1899, the year of his death.
britannica-1911-belleville-illinois:
Belleville is a city and county-seat of St Clair county, Illinois, fourteen miles south-east of St Louis, Missouri. Its people numbered 15,361 in 1890 and 21,122 by 1910. Three railways and wide interurban electric lines serve it, with a belt line joining the Baltimore & Ohio system.

Many residents are of German birth or descent, and two newspapers print in German beside several in English. Stoves, flour, shoes, glass and farm tools come from its works, set in rich farm country with coal mines near by. The first coal shaft was sunk in 1852, and Belleville’s industry dates from that pit.
britannica-1911-belvidere-illinois:
Belvidere is a city and the county-seat of Boone county, Illinois, on the Kishwaukee river, about seventy-eight miles north-west of Chicago. It counted 3,867 people in 1890 and 7,253 by 1910. The Chicago & North-Western railway and a wide interurban electric system serve the town.

Sewing machines head its long list of manufactures, which also runs to boilers, automobiles, bicycles, roller-skates, pianos, gloves, corsets and flour. Dairy goods matter too, since Borden’s condensed milk factory stands in the city. Belvidere was settled in 1836 and was incorporated in 1852 and again in 1881.
britannica-1911-ben-nevis:
Ben Nevis is the highest mountain in the British Isles, in Inverness-shire, Scotland, at 4,406 feet above the sea. From Banavie on the Caledonian Canal it shows as two great masses, one higher than the other. Its top is a plateau of a hundred acres, ending north-east in a sheer fall of more than 1,500 feet.

Snow lasts all year in some of its gorges, and the rock runs from granite and gneiss below to greenstone above. For over twenty years observers kept a summit weather station, opened in 1883 at a cost of £4,000 raised by the public. Their figures show the top far colder and wetter than Fort William in the glen below.
britannica-1911-berthollet-claude-louis:
Claude Louis Berthollet (1748–1822) was a French chemist, born at Talloire in Savoy. He studied at Chambery and at Turin, where he graduated in medicine. He settled in Paris in 1772 as physician to the Duke of Orleans. His chemical work soon won him high repute. In 1780 he entered the Academy of Sciences. In 1785 he joined Lavoisier's school, though not on every point.

The 1911 Britannica entry lists his studies of ammonia, prussic acid, and chlorine. He proposed chlorine as a bleaching agent in 1785. He also made potassium chlorate and tried it in gunpowder. During the Revolution he led the saltpetre supply effort. His stress on the mass of reacting substances shaped later affinity theory. His long dispute with Proust is noted at the close.
britannica-1911-bilbeis:
Bilbeis, also spelled Belbes, is a town of lower Egypt on the eastern arm of the Nile. It lies 36 miles north-north-east of Cairo by rail. Its population in 1907 was 13,485. The Coptic name Phelbes seems to come from Egyptian, the 1911 Britannica entry says. Nothing is known of the place before medieval times, however. Muslims fortified it strongly as the bulwark of the kingdom on that side.

Crusaders under Amalric besieged Bilbeis for three months in 1163 to 1164. Another crusader army captured and pillaged it in 1168. Napoleon ordered its fortifications restored in 1798, but they have decayed again since. The entry ends with a British note from a later war. Bilbeis was the first halt of the English cavalry marching on Cairo after Tel-el-Kebir. That battle was fought on 13 September 1882.
britannica-1911-bilharziosis:
Bilharziosis is a disease of parts of Africa, marked by blood in the urine. A parasite living in the lining of the urinary passages causes it. Bilharz found that parasite in 1852, and it took his name, Bilharzia. Its scientific name is Schistosoma haematobium. The worms and their eggs lodge in the tiny veins of the bladder. They also infest the ureter and the kidney's pelvis, and more rarely other organs.

The 1911 Britannica article describes the damage in plain clinical terms. The bladder lining swells into patches and warty growths, where salts settle. Eggs often form the core of urinary stones. Blocked urine flow can lead to kidney infection and grave illness. Symptoms range from slight discomfort to death in bad cases. Liquid extract of male fern was the one drug used with much success, the article says.
britannica-1911-biogenesis:
Biogenesis is the biology term for the rule that life comes only from life. Each living thing, however simple, arises from a parent organism. Budding, fission, spore-making, and sexual reproduction are the routes it names. The word joins the Greek bios, life, with genesis, birth. The rival idea, abiogenesis, is treated in its own article. The 1911 Britannica entry says no biological rule rests on wider observation.

The entry then turns to a side issue called homogenesis. Parent and offspring are alike, each of the same kind as its parent. Old tales, like barnacles turning to geese, get a brief dismissal. Modern claims for unlike generation shrink to microbes, the entry says. Closer study showed those cases to be parasitism instead. The piece is signed by Peter Chalmers Mitchell.
britannica-1911-bitlis:
Bitlis, or Betlis, is the chief town of a Turkish vilayet of the same name in Asiatic Turkey. It stands 4,700 feet up, in the deep, narrow valley of the Bitlis Chai, a Tigris tributary. The main town and its bazaars crowd along the stream. Suburbs scatter houses among orchards up two side streams. The houses are massive, well built of a soft volcanic tufa stone. Gardens and courtyards climb the hillsides in a striking picture.

At the meeting of two streams stands a fine old castle, now partly ruined. Local tradition puts an Alexander fortress on its site. Arabic inscriptions suggest an Arab building instead, the 1911 Britannica entry notes. The town holds about 35,000 people, some 12,000 Armenians and the rest mostly Kurds. Its vilayet runs from the Mush plain to wild mountains. Iron, lead, copper, and traces of gold are reported there.
britannica-1911-bitter-karl-theodore-fra:
Karl Theodore Francis Bitter (1867– ) was an American sculptor, born in Vienna on 6 December 1867. He studied art in Vienna as a young man. In 1889 he removed to the United States and became naturalized there. In America he won great popularity as a sculptor of public works. In 1906 and 1907 he served as president of the National Sculpture Society in New York. The 1911 Britannica entry is a career note built around his commissions.

His principal works are listed across several famous sites. They include the Astor memorial gates at Trinity Church, New York. His Elements Controlled and Uncontrolled stood on the Chicago Exposition's Administration Building. A large relief, Triumph of Civilization, fills a Philadelphia railway waiting room. He made decorations for the Dewey Naval Arch in New York. Statues and memorials for universities and chambers of commerce round out the list.
britannica-1911-blackburne-francis:
Francis Blackburne (1782–1867) was an Irish judge who twice served as lord chancellor of Ireland. Born at Great Footstown in County Meath, he studied at Trinity College, Dublin, and was called to the English bar in 1805. He later joined the Irish bar in 1822.

Early in his Irish career he enforced the Insurrection Act in Limerick for two years and restored order there. He was attorney-general for Ireland in 1830 and again in 1841, then master of the rolls, chief justice of the queen's bench, and lord chancellor in 1852 and again in 1866. The entry recalls him as the prosecutor of O'Connell and the judge at the trial of Smith O'Brien.
britannica-1911-blomefield-francis:
Francis Blomefield (1705-1752) was an English writer on the history of Norfolk, and this 1911 Britannica entry tells how his great work grew. He was born at Fersfield in Norfolk and left Cambridge in 1727 to take orders. By 1729 he was rector of Hargham and then of Fersfield, his family's living. He had gathered matter for a history of the county since the age of fifteen.

In 1733 he put the plan forward in earnest, and while digging for more matter he found some of the famous Paston Letters. The first volume of his History of Norfolk was finished at the end of 1739, printed on a press he bought for the purpose. A second volume followed in 1745. The entry is frank that he leaned hard on earlier collections.
britannica-1911-bloomington-illinois:
Bloomington is a city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Bloomington is a city in Illinois, the county seat of McLean county. It stands in the central part of the state, south-west of Chicago. Its population reached 25,768 in the census of 1910.

Four railways served the city, along with electric interurban lines. The entry gives much space to its schools. Illinois Wesleyan University, founded in 1850, held colleges of arts, law, and music. It also ran an academy and a school of oratory, with 1350 students in 1907. In the town of Normal, two miles north, stood the state normal university. That school trained teachers and had opened in Bloomington in 1857. The article paints a rail city whose chief pride was education.
britannica-1911-boissonade-de-fontarabie:
Jean François Boissonade de Fontarabie (1774–1857) was a French editor of later Greek writers. Born in Paris, he entered public service in 1792 under Dumouriez, lost his post in 1795, and regained office under Lucien Bonaparte as a prefecture secretary. He then quit office for good and gave himself to Greek study.

Paris made him deputy professor of Greek in 1809 and full professor in 1813. In 1828 he took the Greek chair at the Collège de France, and he also served as royal librarian and as standing secretary of the Académie des Inscriptions. His editions run from Philostratus and Marinus to Babrius's Fables (1844) and Tzetzes (1851), mostly writers of the later Greek world.
britannica-1911-bonivard-francois:
François Bonivard (1493–1570) was a Savoyard prior whose captivity inspired Byron's poem The Prisoner of Chillon. Born at Seyssel of an old family, he succeeded his uncle in 1510 as prior of St Victor, near Geneva. The entry calls him a man of the Renaissance strayed into the Reformation age, and warns that his real life differs from Byron's legend.

He fought the duke of Savoy's claim to lordship over Geneva and paid for it. The duke held him at Gex from 1519 to 1521, took his priory, and in 1530 shut him underground at Chillon for four years. Bernese troops freed him in 1536 when they seized Vaud. He turned Protestant only after release, found his priory destroyed, took a Geneva pension, married four times, and stayed deep in debt.
britannica-1911-borgia-francis:
Francis Borgia (1510–1572) was a Spanish duke who left a court career to lead the Jesuits, and was later made a saint. Born at Gandia in Valencia, he showed deep piety from boyhood and was raised from age twelve at Saragossa by his archbishop uncle. In 1528 his father sent him to the court of Charles V.

There he shone, married Eleanor de Castro, and was made marquis of Lombay and master of horse to the empress. He rode with Charles to Africa in 1535 and Provence in 1536. Escorting the dead empress's body to Granada in 1539 fixed his resolve to quit the court, yet new honours followed, as viceroy of Catalonia. The later pages tell of his secret entry into the Jesuits, his rise to general of the order, and his death in 1572.
britannica-1911-boucher-francois:
François Boucher (1703–1770) was a French painter of graceful, pleasure-loving scenes, nicknamed the Anacreon of painting. Born in Paris, he first made designs and book illustrations for the engraver Jean François Cars. In 1727 he went to Italy and made his name at Rome as a painter.

Back in Paris in 1731 he quickly became a society favourite. His Rinaldo and Armida (1734) is now in the Louvre. He was made inspector of the Gobelins tapestry works in 1755 and court painter in 1765. Madame de Pompadour employed him for her portrait and for decorative schemes. The entry notes that his Watteau-like charm lost favour after his death and was only lately prized again. The Wallace Collection holds some of his finest pictures outside the Louvre.
britannica-1911-brieg-valais:
Brieg, now often spelt Brig, is a small Swiss town in the canton of Valais at the foot of the northern slope of the Simplon Pass. It stands on the right bank of the Saltine stream, just above where that stream joins the Rhone. Older houses look Italian, and its grandest buildings all date from the 17th century.

Castle, former Jesuits' college and Ursuline convent alike owe their building to one generous member of the local Stockalper family. The town's wealth hangs on the Simplon route: it slowly overtook the older village of Naters across the river, became its own parish in 1517. Grew fast once the carriage road opened in 1807 and the tunnel in 1906. In 1900 it held 2182 people, and a new lower town was spreading toward the Rhone.
britannica-1911-britomartis:
Britomartis, whose name is read as sweet maiden, was an old Cretan goddess later merged with Artemis. Callimachus calls her a nymph, daughter of Zeus and Carme and a favourite companion of Artemis. Hunted by Minos, king of Crete, who desired her, she leapt from a rock into the sea to escape him.

Falling into fishermen's nets saved her from drowning, and Artemis made her a goddess under the name Dictynna, from the Greek word for a net. She watched over hunters, fishermen and sailors and served also as a goddess of birth and health. Her worship centred at Cydonia and spread to Sparta, Aegina, where she was known as Aphaea, and Mediterranean islands. Some read her as a moon goddess, her flight and leap standing for the moon's circling and vanishing.
britannica-1911-bronchiectasis:
Bronchiectasis, from Greek words for the bronchial tubes and for stretching, is a widening of the bronchi, the air passages of the lungs, that follows many lung diseases. Acute and chronic bronchitis, chronic pneumonia and phthisis, acute pneumonia and broncho-pneumonia can all leave it behind, its place fixed by the first lesion. Blockage of the windpipe or bronchi, as from an aneurism's pressure or a new growth, can also cause it by force.

Once thought a disease of middle age, it has been shown by Dr Walter Carr to be fairly common in weakened children after measles or whooping cough. The widening is usually tube-shaped, more rarely sack-like, hitting the medium and smaller tubes and commonly one lung only, with emphysema often beside it. Its cough is strongly paroxysmal, severe yet broken by hours of freedom, and posture changes its force in a marked way.
britannica-1911-bronchitis:
Bronchitis is the name for inflammation of the mucous membrane lining the bronchial tubes, the air passages of the lungs. Two main kinds are set apart: specific bronchitis, arising in catching disorders such as diphtheria, influenza, measles and pneumonia from the germs of those diseases. Non-specific, spreading down from above or caused by chemical or mechanical irritation.

For ease the entry then treats it as acute and chronic. Acute bronchitis, like other chest inflammations, generally comes from exposure to cold, above all with damp, or from a sudden move from heated to cool air. Signs vary with the attack's severity and with how far down the tubes the inflammation spreads. It usually opens as a catarrh, a common cold. Feverishness and general disturbance of the system proclaim something more severe at work, the starting point of the long medical account.
britannica-1911-bryaxis:
Bryaxis was a Greek sculptor of the 4th century B.C. He was one of four great sculptors on the mausoleum at Halicarnassus. That tomb was built about 350 B.C. This short 1911 Britannica entry gives what is known of him. His share of the mausoleum work cannot be split from his companions' work.

A signed basis was found at Athens. It bears his name and figures of horsemen in relief. He also made a great statue of Apollo. That statue stood at Daphne, near Antioch. A claim credits him with a statue of Serapis for Sinope. The entry notes grave historic doubts about that claim. It points readers to Gardner's Handbook of Greek Sculpture. The whole notice is brief, and it sticks to these few works.
britannica-1911-budweis:
Budweis is a town in Bohemia in Austria, south west of Prague by rail. Its count of folk in nineteen hundred was near forty thousand. It stands where two streams join, and the main stream bears ships from that point. A fair square with arch front builds is its pride, led by the town hall.

A great church with a lone tower and a church with fine walks are named. Work runs wide, from soaps to matches, paper, gear, and the famed black lead sticks. The town is the trade hub of the south tract. Its first rail line, for horse cars, was the first in the realm.
britannica-1911-bugis:
The Bugis are a people of Malayan stock, first at home in the kingdom of Boni. Boni lies in the south west peninsula of the island of Celebes. From that district they spread over the whole island in time. They founded settlements throughout the whole Malay Archipelago as well. They are of middle size and robust, with a lighter skin than most Malays.

In temper the Bugis are brave, haughty, and fierce by the entry's account. They speak a tongue allied to that of the Macassars, with like letters. They farm more than the tribes near them and make cotton cloth for export. They trade in gold dust, shell, pearls, nutmegs, and camphor from Boni. Their love of the sea gives them near a monopoly of trade round Celebes.
britannica-1911-burckhardt-john-lewis:
John Lewis Burckhardt (1784-1817) was a Swiss traveller and scholar of the East. He was born at Lausanne on 24 November 1784. After study at Leipzig and Gottingen he came to England in the summer of 1806. He bore a letter from the naturalist Blumenbach to Sir Joseph Banks. Banks and the African Association took up his offer to explore the inner parts of Africa.

Burckhardt read in London and Cambridge and hardened himself to all kinds of hardship and want. In March 1809 he left England for Malta, and in the autumn he went on to Aleppo. To learn the life of the East at first hand, he dressed as a Muslim. He took the name of Sheikh Ibrahim Ibn Abdallah. After two years in the Levant he had a full command of Arabic. His grasp of the Koran stood the test of the most learned men there.
britannica-1911-burdett-sir-francis:
Sir Francis Burdett, an English lawmaker for reform, opens a fight life in the 1911 Britannica. Born in seventeen seventy, he learned at Westminster School and at Oxford. Trips to France and Switzerland came next in his youth. He stood in Paris in the first days of its great revolt. Back home he wed a banker child and gained a vast sum in that match.

He bought a seat in the diet in seventeen ninety six at high cost. There he hit Pitt and the war with France in sharp speech. Rights of the folk were his chief theme from the start. Crowds made him their idol in short time for that stand. A probe of a harsh jail made the state bar him from all jails.
britannica-1911-burton-sir-richard-franc:
Richard Francis Burton is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Burton was a British consul, explorer, and scholar of the East. He lived from 1821 to 1890 and was born in Hertfordshire. His childhood was spent in France and Italy with little control. That loose schooling fed a love of free wandering. It also gave him rare skill in the tongues of the continent.

The article tells how Oxford sent him down for wild conduct. He joined a Bombay regiment in 1842, though he hated all discipline. Service in India let him study eastern life and languages. He learned Gujarati, Marathi, and other tongues with great speed. He also mastered Persian and Arabic. Work on the Sind survey let him mix with the people in disguise. The text notes that his pilgrimage to Mecca in 1853 made him famous.
britannica-1911-cappel-louis:
Louis Cappel (1585–1658) was a French Protestant divine and scholar. This 1911 Britannica entry gives his life and his bold theories. He was born at St Elier, near Sedan, in 1585. He studied theology at Sedan and at Saumur. He spent two years at Oxford on Arabic. At twenty-eight he took the chair of Hebrew at Saumur. Twenty years later he held its theology chair.

Cappel made the Hebrew text of the Bible his special study. He held its vowel points were not original. The Massorete Jews of Tiberias added them, he argued. That was in the 5th century A.D. He also held the square Hebrew letters to be Aramaic. The Samaritan letters, he said, were the originals. Johannes Buxtorf attacked these views with heat. His Critica Sacra caused equal offence in theology. He finished it in 1634 but could not print it until 1650. His son helped him publish it at Paris.
britannica-1911-cary-henry-francis:
Henry Francis Cary (1772–1844) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an English author and translator born at Gibraltar, the son of an army captain. He was schooled at Rugby, Sutton Coldfield, and Birmingham, then at Christ Church, Oxford. He took holy orders and in 1797 received the vicarage of Abbott's Bromley in Staffordshire, which he held for life. At school he already wrote for the Gentleman's Magazine and published sonnets and odes.

Cary's fame rests on his translation of Dante. At Oxford he gave much time to French and Italian literature, and the Inferno appeared in 1805 with the original text. The whole Divina Commedia followed in 1814, printed at his own expense after his publisher refused the risk. Thomas Moore brought the work to Samuel Rogers, whose notice helped its standing. The entry ties the classic English Dante of its day to a country clergyman who financed it himself.
britannica-1911-catalysis:
Catalysis is a chemistry article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica on changes brought about by a substance that is itself left whole at the end. That substance is called the catalyst. The name comes from Greek words for down and to loosen. Berzelius brought the term in after first studying such changes.

The article splits these actions into two groups. In one, the catalyst first joins with one part of the mix to form a new compound. That compound then acts on the rest, and the catalyst is freed to work again. In the other group the catalyst seems to act by mere touch. A known case makes the point: heat a mix of potassium chlorate and manganese dioxide, and oxygen flows off at a steady rate. The dioxide comes out just as it went in.
britannica-1911-catherine-of-valois:
Catherine of Valois, queen of Henry the Fifth of England, born in fourteen hundred and one, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. She was the daughter of Charles the Sixth of France. She was born in Paris in October of that year. The ill mind of her father was a hard draw back for the girl.

Her sole school years were spent in a house of nuns at Poissy. A match with the prince of Wales was first put in words when she was a child. That prince, as king, put the plan once more. With her hand he asked a vast gift in coin and in lands. When those terms were said no to, war broke out. When peace was made at Troyes, the two were bound at last.
britannica-1911-caulaincourt-armand-loui:
Armand Augustin Louis, Marquis de Caulaincourt (1773–1827), is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French general and diplomatist. He came from a noble family and entered the army young. He stayed in France through the revolution. In 1793 he lost his captain's grade and served in the ranks. With Hoche's protection he regained his rank in 1795. By 1799 he was colonel in the Army of the Rhine.

After the peace of Lunéville in 1801, he went to St Petersburg. His task was to settle an understanding between Russia and France. On his return he became aide de camp to the First Consul. In 1804 he was sent to seize English agents in Baden. That mission led to a charge over the arrest of the duc d'Enghien. He never stopped denying it. Napoleon later made him duke of Vicenza and ambassador to Russia. There he worked to hold the Tilsit alliance together.
britannica-1911-caylus-anne-claude-de-le:
Anne Claude de Lévis, Count de Caylus, who lived from 1692 to 1765, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French student of old remains and a man of letters, born at Paris. His mother wrote noted memoirs of the court of Louis the Fourteenth. As a young man he served in French army campaigns from 1709 to 1714.

After the peace, Caylus travelled widely and gave his time to old objects and their study. He joined both the academy of painting and the academy of inscriptions. His chief work was a six-volume set on Egyptian, Greek, Roman, and Gallic remains, issued in the 1750s. The article also praises him as a fine engraver who copied the works of great masters. A dispute over who truly found the old wax painting method is noted too.
britannica-1911-chalcis:
Chalcis is a town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about the chief town of the island of Euboea in Greece. It stands on the strait of the Euripus at its narrowest point. The name comes down from old times and links to the Greek word for copper or bronze.

The article tells of a town quick to trade and to plant new towns. In the 700s and 600s before Christ it founded thirty towns on one mainland point. More towns rose from its stock in Sicily. Its metal work, purple dye, and pots sold all round the inland sea. War with Athens in the early 500s broke its power. In later ages it served as a fort for kings who sought to hold Greece. The modern town holds about 10,000 people.
britannica-1911-champollion-jean-francoi:
Jean Francois Champollion, a French scholar of Egypt born in seventeen ninety, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was called the Young to set him apart from his elder brother. Born at Figeac, he was taught at home by that brother. He then won a state place at a new school.

His first work, in eighteen hundred and four, held a bold claim. He said the giants of the Bible and of Greek tale were signs for the forces of nature in man form. At age sixteen he read a paper at Grenoble. In it he held that the Coptic tongue was the old tongue of Egypt. He moved to Paris soon after. At age nineteen he held a chair of past study at Grenoble.
britannica-1911-charles-count-of-valois:
Charles, count of Valois, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He lived from 1270 to 1325 in France. He was the third son of King Philip the Third. He was born in March 1270. By his father will he took four lordships. Those lands formed the countship of Valois as one whole. A pope once offered him the throne of Aragon.

His father failed to place him on that throne. In 1290 he wed a princess of Naples. He then gave up his claim to Aragon. Wars took him to Guienne and to Flanders in turn. He crossed the Alps to aid the pope in Italy. Claims to an eastern throne came through his second wife. Those claims came to naught in the end. His eldest son took the French throne in 1328.
britannica-1911-chasseloup-laubat-franco:
François, marquis de Chasseloup-Laubat, a French general and engineer who lived from 1754 to 1833, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at St Sernin of a noble family, he joined the French engineers in 1774. He was still a junior officer when the Revolution came, and made captain in 1791. His skill showed fast in the campaigns of 1792 and 1793.

He ran the siege works at Mainz in 1796, then served in Italy under Bonaparte. As chief of engineers in Italy in 1799 his work stood out, and he was made general of division. His crowning work was the fortress of Alessandria. In 1806 Napoleon called him to the Grande Armée for sieges at Colberg and Danzig. His last campaign was the Russia march of 1812, and he later refused to join Napoleon in the Hundred Days.
britannica-1911-chassis:
Chassis is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French word for a frame. It comes from the late Latin capsum, an enclosed space. Properly, a chassis is a window frame. The English word “sash” derives from it. The term also names the movable traversing frame of a gun.

Its chief modern sense belongs to the motor vehicle. There the chassis is the part made of the wheels, the frame, and the machinery. The body, or carriage part, rests on it. The entry thus moves from windows to guns to motor cars in a few lines. Each sense holds to the root idea of a frame that carries something else. For a reference work of 1911, the motor sense marks how fast the new machine had claimed an old word.
britannica-1911-chatteris:
Chatteris is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a market town in Cambridgeshire, England. It stands in the Wisbech parliamentary division, 25 and a half miles north by west of Cambridge by rail. Its urban district counted 4711 people in 1901. The town lies in the middle of the flat Fen country. The church of St Peter is mainly in the Decorated style.

Fragments survive of a Benedictine convent founded in the tenth century. It was rebuilt after a fire in the first half of the fourteenth. The town has breweries, and works for engineering and rope making. To the north runs the great Forty Foot Drain. It is also called Vermuyden's Drain, after the Dutch engineer tied to the fen drainage works of the mid seventeenth century. The short entry joins the town's church, its lost convent, and the drained fen that defines its landscape.
britannica-1911-chauvelin-bernard-franco:
Bernard François, Marquis de Chauvelin (1766–1832), is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a French diplomatist and administrator. He was master of the king's wardrobe in 1789, yet he joined the Revolution. After service in the army of Flanders he was sent to London in February 1792. His task was to keep England neutral in the coming war. After the execution of Louis XVI in January 1793, England gave him eight days to leave.

An embassy in Tuscany failed, and the Terror imprisoned him as a suspect. He was freed after the 9th Thermidor. Under Napoleon he joined the council of state. From 1812 to 1814 he governed Catalonia as intendant general, charged with winning the Catalans for King Joseph. He sat as deputy from 1816 and spoke for press liberty and a wider franchise. He resigned his seat in 1829.
britannica-1911-chemotaxis:
Chemotaxis is a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry defining a biological term. The word joins the stem of “chemistry” with the Greek taxis, arrangement. It names the attraction that chemical substances exercise on living or growing organisms, or on parts of them. The pull can act on a whole plant or animal, or on a single cell within one.

The entry gives one clear example. The male cells of ferns and mosses are drawn toward an organic acid or a sugar solution. That movement, toward the chemical rather than away from it, is the point of the term. In a few lines the entry gives the word's two roots, its sense, and its standard case. Readers who meet chemotaxis in a biology text get exactly what the phenomenon is, and one living instance of it.
britannica-1911-child-sir-francis:
Child, Sir Francis (1642–1713) was an English banker, a Wiltshire man apprenticed to a goldsmith who became a London goldsmith himself in 1664. In 1671 he married Elizabeth Wheeler and, with her stepfather Robert Blanchard, took over the Wheeler goldsmith business. That takeover was the beginning of Child's Bank, the entry says. Child soon gave up goldsmith work and kept only to banking, in which he grew rich and successful.

He was jeweller to the king and lent large sums to the government, and city honours followed in a long line. He joined the common council in 1681, became alderman and knight in 1689, served as sheriff in 1691 and as lord mayor in 1699. Parliament seats at Devizes and London came between 1698 and 1710, and he died on 4 October 1713. The bank passed in time to his sons and is still owned by his descendants.
britannica-1911-choiseul-etienne-francoi:
Étienne François, Duc de Choiseul, a French statesman who lived from 1719 to 1785, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the eldest son of the marquis de Stainville and bore that title in early life. Born in June 1719, he entered the army. During the War of the Austrian Succession he served in Bohemia and in Italy. He stood out at the battle of Coni in 1744.

Choiseul then served in the Low Countries and rose to lieutenant-general. In 1750 he married an heiress who brought him a large fortune. He won the favour of Madame de Pompadour, and in 1753 he was sent as ambassador to Rome. There he handled talks over the unrest caused by the bull Unigenitus with skill. In 1757 he moved to Vienna to cement the new alliance between France and Austria. His success there opened the way to higher office.
britannica-1911-chopin-frederic-francois:
Frederic Francois Chopin is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Chopin was a Polish composer and piano player who lived from 1810 to 1849. He was born near Warsaw. His father was of French origin, and his mother was Polish. A Czech teacher gave him his first music lessons, and a Warsaw college gave him sound schooling.

The article tells how his gift opened the best homes of Polish society to him. He had full training in music theory at Warsaw. In 1829 he left for Vienna, where he first played in public as a formed artist. His style was his own from the start. In 1831 he reached Paris and settled there for life. He soon became the music hero of Paris society. His link with the writer George Sand is noted as a key part of his life.
britannica-1911-clematis:
Clematis is a genus of plants of the buttercup order. It holds near two hundred kinds, spread wide over the world. In England it is known by Clematis Vitalba, called old man's beard or traveller's joy. That plant is common on chalk or light soil. The plants are shrubby climbers with leaves that stand in pairs. The leaf stalk is quick to feel touch, like a tendril, and twists round props to hold the plant up.

The flowers stand in clusters at the leaf axils or at the stem ends. They have no petals, but white or coloured sepals, at times very large. They hold no honey, and insects come to them for their rich store of pollen. The fruit is a head of achenes. Each fruit bears a long, bearded style that stays on it. That feathery tail helps the wind to spread the seed far.
britannica-1911-clement-francois:
Clément, François (1714–1793) was a French historian, born at Bèze near Dijon and educated at the Jesuit College at Dijon. At seventeen he entered the Benedictines of Saint Maur and worked with such intense application that at twenty-five he was forced into a long rest. In Paris he wrote the 11th and 12th volumes of the Histoire littéraire de la France. He also edited, with Dom Brial, volumes of the Recueil des historiens des Gaules.

The king placed him on the committee publishing charters, diplomas and other documents of French history. The Academy of Inscriptions chose him as a member in 1785, the entry records. He revised the Art de vérifier les dates, with three indexed volumes appearing from 1783 to 1792. Another volume, covering the period before the Christian era, was in preparation when he died. Death came suddenly, by apoplexy, at sixty-nine.
britannica-1911-clermont-en-beauvaisis:
Clermont-en-Beauvaisis, or Clermont-de-l'Oise, is a town of northern France, capital of an arrondissement in Oise, on the right bank of the Brèche. It lies 41 miles north of Paris on the Northern railway to Amiens, with 4,014 people in 1906. A 14th century keep crowns the hill on which the town is built, relic of a fortress. Part of that fortress site is now occupied by a large penitentiary for women.

The church dates from the 14th to 16th centuries, and the hôtel-de-ville, built by Charles IV who was born here in 1294, is the oldest in northern France. The Promenade du Châtellier on the old ramparts is the town's most attractive feature. Felt and corset making, with trade in horses, cattle and grain, support it. It was probably founded in Norman invasion times.
britannica-1911-clouet-francois:
Clouet, François was a French miniature painter, son of Jean Clouet, whom he followed very closely in the science of his art. A document of December 1541, where the king renounced his father's escheated estate in the son's favour, is the earliest reference to him. Like his father he held the office of groom of the chamber and painter in ordinary to the king. His salary started where his father's left off, the document shows.

Attributions remain uncertain, since no original attestations of his works survive, yet an ancient and unbroken tradition ascribes many pictures to him. Portraits of Francis I at the Uffizi and the Louvre are attributed to him, as is a chalk portrait of Mary, queen of Scots. His portrait of Elizabeth of Austria in the Louvre is perhaps his masterpiece. He prepared the death masks of Francis I and Henry II, and died on 22 December 1572.
britannica-1911-coghlan-charles-francis:
Charles Francis Coghlan (1841–1899) was an Irish actor born in Paris. He was trained for the law, not the stage. His first London appearance came in 1860. He rose to lead the company at the Prince of Wales's theatre. In 1876 he crossed to America and stayed there for the rest of his life.

In America he acted first with Augustin Daly's company. He then joined the Union Square stock company for a long run of The Celebrated Case. He played beside his sister and in support of Mrs Langtry and Mrs Fiske. In 1898 he staged his own version of Dumas's Kean, called The Royal Box. He starred in it through his last years. He died at Galveston, Texas, on 27 November 1899. His sister Rose gains a full note as well.
britannica-1911-colchis:
Colchis, in old geography a district at the east end of the Black Sea, is surveyed in an entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The Caucasus hills bound it on the north, Iberia on the east, and the sea on the west. Its ground matches much the later province of Kutais. The name first shows up in Aeschylus and in Pindar.

Many tribes lived along its shore, among them the Lazi, the Moschi and the Suani. They struck their neighbours as so unlike in tongue and looks that old writers spun tales to explain them. Herodotus linked them to Egypt, as heirs of the army of Sesostris, and noted a shared rite with Egyptians and Ethiopians. The entry also cites a claim that Egyptian settlers in Colchis kept wooden tablets that mapped seas and roads with care. Such tales, it warns, won few firm backers, then or since.
britannica-1911-collin-d-harleville-jean:
Jean François Collin d'Harleville (1755–1806) was a French dramatist born at Mévoisins, near Maintenon, on 30 May 1755. His first stage success was L'Inconstant, a comedy. The Comédie Française took it in 1780 but did not stage it until six years later. Other houses played it in 1784. Two more comedies followed in quick order.

L'Optimiste came in 1788 and Châteaux en Espagne in 1789. His best play, Le Vieux Célibataire, appeared in 1793. Later works run to 1803 and include Les Artistes and Les Mœurs du jour. Collin was one of the first members of the Institute of France. He died in Paris on 24 February 1806. Editions of his theatre appeared in 1822, 1876 and 1882. The first holds a notice by his friend Andrieux.
britannica-1911-combinatorial-analysis:
Combinatorial analysis is a branch of mathematics about grouping and ordering things. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica quotes a clear account from Nicholson in 1818. The field lists all ways a set of things can be joined or mixed. Writers long saw it as key to algebra and to chance theory alike.

Early results appear in the first algebra works, the entry notes. Abraham De Moivre is named as the true pioneer of modern study. His 1697 paper gave a law for terms in a raised series. Euler then linked the splitting of numbers to algebra in a deep way. His work tied adding whole numbers to multiplying forms.
britannica-1911-crawford-william-harris:
William Harris Crawford (1772–1834) was an American statesman born in Amherst county, Virginia, on 24 February 1772. At seven he moved with his parents to Edgefield district in South Carolina. Four years later the family moved on to Columbus county in Georgia. His father's death in 1788 left the house in reduced means. William taught school for six years to make what he could.

He then studied two years at Carmel Academy and ran a large school at Augusta. In 1798 he was admitted to the bar in Georgia. From 1800 to 1802 he helped prepare a digest of the laws of Georgia. He sat in the state house from 1803 to 1807. In that time he rose to lead one of two bitter personal factions in Georgia politics. Two duels came out of that strife. He killed his man in one and took a wound in the wrist in the other. The Senate took him in 1807.
britannica-1911-crevier-jean-baptiste-lo: Jean Baptiste Louis Crevier lived from 1693 to 1765 and was a French author. The brief 1911 Britannica note places his birth in Paris, where his father was a printer. He studied under Rollin and taught speech at the college of Beauvais for twenty years. He brought Rollin's Roman history to its end with six more volumes. His own works include a history of the Roman emperors and a history of the University of Paris, plus two editions of Livy with notes.
britannica-1911-cropsey-jasper-francis:
Jasper Francis Cropsey (1823–1900) was an American landscape painter born at Rossville, Staten Island, on 18 February 1823. He practised architecture for several years before turning to painting. He studied in Italy from 1847 to 1850 and joined the National Academy of Design in 1851. From 1857 to 1863 he kept a studio in London. After his return to America he won a wide vogue.

Cropsey was best known for vivid autumn scenes in the manner of the Hudson River school. He was one of the original members of the American Water Color Society. He stayed active in his profession until a few days before his death. He died at Hastings-on-Hudson, New York, on 22 June 1900. The entry adds a second trade to the painter's name, for Cropsey drew the designs for the stations of the elevated railways in New York City.
britannica-1911-dais:
Dais was at first the raised part of the floor at the end of a hall in the old age. The lord sat there at the high table with his friends. His men and staff sat low in the main hall. A deep bay window often stood at one end or both ends of the raised floor.

The entry notes a shift in sense in France, where the word came to mean a cloth roof hung over a seat of rank. That use may have grown from the rich seats of great men. In plain use now, the word means any raised stage in a room. The piece is brief and clear.
britannica-1911-damiens-robert-francois:
Robert François Damiens (1715–1757) was a Frenchman who won lasting notoriety for attacking Louis XV. Born in a village near Arras, he served in the army, then worked as a menial at the Jesuit college in Paris. Dismissals for misconduct followed him from post to post, and men called him Robert le Diable. Church quarrels over the Jansenists heated his mind. He thought the king's death would restore peace.

On 5 January 1757 Damiens rushed at the king as he entered his carriage and stabbed him, dealing only a slight wound. He made no try to escape and was seized at once. Condemned as a regicide, he was tortured with red-hot pincers and molten matter poured into his wounds. Horses then tore his body apart in the Place de Grève. His house was razed, his kin renamed by order, and his father, wife, and daughter banished from France.
britannica-1911-danby-francis:
Francis Danby (1793–1861) was an English painter born in the south of Ireland on 16 November 1793. His father's death moved the family to Dublin while he was still at school. He learned drawing at the Royal Dublin Society's schools and began landscape painting under a young artist named O'Connor. With George Petrie he set out for London in 1813 on scant funds. The trip failed, and the party walked home, pausing at Bristol.

At Bristol Danby sold water-colours, then won notice with large oils sent to London. The Upas Tree in 1820 and The Delivery of the Israelites in 1825 gained him election as an associate of the Royal Academy. His Opening of the Sixth Seal took a prize of 200 guineas in 1828. Then domestic trouble and a quarrel with the Academy drove him abroad for over a decade by the Lake of Geneva. He returned in 1841 and died at Exmouth on 9 February 1861.
britannica-1911-daphnis:
Daphnis, in the 1911 Britannica, is a myth entry on the hero of the shepherds of Sicily. He is held the inventor of bucolic, or shepherd, poetry. The chief sources for his tale are Diodorus, Aelian, and Theocritus. By the tale, he was the son of Hermes and a Sicilian nymph, found by shepherds in a grove of laurels, from which his name came.

Raised by nymphs, he kept flocks and played the syrinx. A nymph bound him to be true to her alone, on pain of blindness. He broke the vow, lost his sight, and soon died. Sicilians gave offerings at the spring his father caused to flow at that spot. Theocritus tells the tale with no blindness, but with a hopeless love and a death that all nature mourns.
britannica-1911-decapolis:
Decapolis is set out in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica as a league of ten cities with their lands. The Greek name means just that, ten cities. All but one lay east of the upper Jordan and the Sea of Tiberias. As a league of cities, it has no firm edge that can be drawn on a map.

The names of the first ten are given by Pliny. Damascus heads the list and is the sole one that keeps its old weight now. One town west of the river is still lived in as a small place. The ruins of three more towns stand to this day. The rest are lost or in doubt. The west town held the roads to the sea, which made it the chief town of the league.
britannica-1911-declaration-of-paris:
Declaration of Paris, a set of rules of law between nations, was adopted on 16 April 1856 and is set out in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It closed the talks that made the treaty of Paris. Count Walewski, the French envoy, put the plan forward. Sea law in time of war had long bred grim disputes, the text says.

Doubt on rights and duties at sea set neutrals and fighters at odds. Such gaps could spark grave trouble and even open conflict. Fixed and uniform rules were thus held to be a clear need. Four rules were adopted by the envoys. Privateering is abolished for good. A neutral flag shields foe goods, save for contraband of war. Neutral goods are safe from seizure under a foe flag, with the same bar. A blockade binds only if a real force upholds it.
britannica-1911-delolme-jean-louis:
Jean Louis Delolme (1740–1806) was a Swiss jurist and writer on state rule. He was born at Geneva in 1740 and studied for the bar. He had begun to work as a lawyer when a pamphlet of his gave offence to the heads of the town. He was forced to flee and took shelter in England. There he lived for years on the small, unsure pay of pieces for journals. In 1775 he had to take aid from a fund for the poor to get home.

Delolme died at Sewen, in the canton of Schwyz, on 16 July 1806. In his long exile in England he made a close study of the English constitution. He set out the fruit of that study in his Constitution de l'Angleterre, printed at Amsterdam in 1771.
britannica-1911-elgin-illinois:
Elgin is a city in Kane County, Illinois, northwest of Chicago. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica gives its growth from under nine thousand people in 1880 to near twenty six thousand in 1910. Rail lines and electric lines linked it to Chicago and nearby towns. Schools, a large library, and wide parks served the city.

Dairy farms around Elgin made it a key butter market. Its shops made watches, watch cases, canned corn, and dairy goods. The Elgin National Watch works and the Borden milk works won fame across the country. A lasting settlement began in 1835, and city status came in 1854.
britannica-1911-emmet-thomas-addis:
Emmet, Thomas Addis (1764–1827), was an Irish lawyer and politician, the second son of Robert Emmet and elder brother of Robert Emmet the rebel. Born at Cork on 24 April 1764, he studied at Trinity College, Dublin, and at Edinburgh, where he read medicine and philosophy under Dugald Stewart. He toured the chief medical schools of the continent and returned to Ireland in 1788.

The sudden death of his elder brother Christopher turned Emmet from medicine to the law, and he was called to the Irish bar in 1790. He soon practised chiefly for prisoners charged with political offences and advised the leading United Irishmen. Arrested in 1798, he was held at Fort George until 1802. After his brother's failed rising of July 1803 he emigrated to the United States, joined the New York bar, and served as attorney-general of New York in 1812 to 1813.
britannica-1911-ennis:
Ennis is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in Ireland. It is the county town of County Clare. The name comes from a Gaelic word for an island. The town stands on the river Fergus. Limerick lies to the south east by rail. A count from 1901 gives the urban district 5093 people. It is the junction for the West Clare rail line. Brewing, distilling, and flour milling go on there.

Limestone is quarried in the country near the town. The Catholic church serves as pro-cathedral of Killaloe diocese. The parish church was formed from a Franciscan abbey's ruins. That abbey was founded in 1240 by an O'Brien chief. The abbey, though much harmed, is full of fine detail. It holds a lofty tower and a marble screen. A chapter house, fine tombs, and a notable east window survive. An Erasmus Smith school stands among the town's buildings.
britannica-1911-ephemeris:
Ephemeris, a Greek word for a “diary,” is a table giving, for set times, the apparent position and other figures for a heavenly body. The entry is short and practical. Such tables tell where a body will appear in the sky and supply figures that go with it. They serve both the astronomer and the navigator.

The Astronomical Ephemeris, familiarly known as the “Nautical Almanac,” is a national yearly book. It holds the ephemerides of the main heavenly bodies, the elements and other data of eclipses, and further matter of use to astronomers and sailors. The entry names the governments that publish such annuals. They are the United Kingdom, the United States, France, Germany, and Spain. The notice thus does no more than define the tool and point to the official books that carry it, leaving the tables themselves to those yearly volumes.
britannica-1911-eucharis:
Eucharis, in botany, is a small genus of the order Amaryllidaceae, native to Columbia. The best known kind is Eucharis amazonica, also called grandiflora. It grows from a bulb, with broad stalked leaves. Its upright stalk, a foot and a half to 2 feet long, carries an umbel of three to ten large white flowers. Each flower bears a central cup like a daffodil's, sometimes tinged with green.

Growers raise it from offsets taken off in spring and potted singly. It wants good loamy soil kept open with sand, plus plenty of water. Night heat of 65 to 70 degrees suits it, with a rise by day. A cooler rest after growth brings on flowering around the turn of the year. A stock worked in succession can flower all year. The entry also records the Eucharis mite, a bulb disease that resisted most remedies, and a hybrid with Urceolina named Urceocharis.
britannica-1911-eupolis:
Eupolis was an Athenian poet of the Old Comedy who thrived in the years of a great war. The 1911 Britannica entry says nothing at all is known of his own life tale. One tale claims a famed leader he had mocked threw him into the sea. It is more likely, the entry says, that he died in arms for his city.

A famed Roman poet ranks him with the two great names of his school. The entry praises his quick rich fancy joined to sound sense in life. He matched one peer in pure fine speech and the other in sharp irony. First friends with his great rival, they fell out and charged each other with theft of ideas. Of his plays, which won first prize seven times, scraps alone stand.
britannica-1911-fain-agathon-jean-franco:
Agathon Jean François Fain, a French writer on his own times, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Paris in 1778. He rose through state offices to become secretary and keeper of the records for Napoleon. He rode with the emperor on campaigns and trips. In 1809 he was made a baron of the empire.

The entry lists his year-by-year accounts of the last phase of Napoleon's reign. These books are praised for their truth and wide grasp of fact. His memoirs, printed long after his death in 1908, show Napoleon at work on his letters. Under King Louis Philippe, Fain again served as first secretary of the cabinet.
britannica-1911-fawkes-francis:
Francis Fawkes (1720-1777), English poet and divine, was born at Warmsworth near Doncaster in Yorkshire, where his father was rector, and was baptized on 4 April 1720. He studied at Jesus College, Cambridge, took his M.A. in 1745, and held a string of livings: curate of Bramham and of Croydon, vicar of Orpington, rector of Hayes, and finally chaplain to the princess of Wales.

His first publication is said to have been Bramham Park, a Poem, in 1745, followed by a volume of poems and translations in 1761 and Partridge Shooting, an eclogue, in 1764. His translations of Anacreon, Sappho, Bion, Moschus, Musaeus, Theocritus and Apollonius won him considerable fame. Yet the entry judges his song Dear Tom, this brown jug more likely to be remembered. Fawkes died on 26 August 1777.
britannica-1911-felix-of-valois:
Felix of Valois (1127-1212) was one of the founders of the Trinitarians, or Redemptionists, an order devoted to freeing Christian captives. Born in the Valois district of France on 19 April 1127, he became a hermit in the forest of Galeresse in early manhood. He stayed there until his sixty-first year. Then his disciple Jean de Matha proposed an order of monks who would give their lives to ransoming Christians held by the Saracens.

The two men went to Rome late in 1197 and won the pope's sanction. Back in France they founded the monastery of Cerfroi in Picardy. Felix stayed to govern and spread the order while Jean de Matha ran its journeys abroad. He also founded a Paris house near a chapel of St Mathurin, whence his monks were called Mathurins. Felix died at Cerfroi on 4 November 1212 and was canonized.
britannica-1911-florianopolis:
Florianopolis is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a city and port of Brazil. It is the capital of the state of Santa Catharina there. It stands on the inside shore of a large island of that name. The count for 1890 is 11,400, with many Germans among them.

The harbour forms where the strait between isle and mainland widens out. Small forts guard the narrow ways in from north and south. The isle is hilly and wooded, and shields the port from east storms. The town itself is called poorly built and plain to the eye. A palace, arsenal, school, and hospital are among its halls. German farm colonies up the coast send their goods to its market.
britannica-1911-forde-francis:
Francis Forde, who died in 1770, was a British soldier in India. He first appears in the army list as a captain in the 39th Foot in 1746, the first king's regiment to serve in India. He was on duty there when he became major in 1755. At Clive's own invitation, Forde resigned his king's commission to serve as second in command of the East India Company's troops in Bengal. Soon after Plassey he was sent against the French at Masulipatam.

Forde beat the French at Condore and stormed Masulipatam itself in January 1759, losing a third of his men in a brilliant success. The Company still refused to confirm his rank, leaving him junior to his old subaltern Eyre Coote. He beat the Dutch at Chinsurah that November. In 1769 he sailed to investigate Indian administration with full powers. His ship was never heard of after leaving the Cape of Good Hope on 27 December.
britannica-1911-foullon-joseph-francois:
Joseph Francois Foullon (1717-1789), French administrator, was born at Saumur. During the Seven Years' War he was intendant-general of the armies, and intendant of the army and navy under Marshal de Belle-Isle. In 1771 he became intendant of finances. In 1789, when Necker was dismissed, Foullon was made minister of the king's household. The reactionary party thought of him as Necker's replacement.

Foullon was hated on all sides, the entry says. The farmers-general detested his severity, and Parisians his wealth, gathered in cold indifference to the poor. He was reported, probably without foundation, to have said that if the people could not get bread, they might eat hay. After the Bastille fell on 14 July he hid at his estate at Vitry and spread news of his own death. He was recognized and seized, and killed by the Paris crowd.
britannica-1911-fourcroy-antoine-francoi:
Antoine Francois, comte de Fourcroy (1755-1809), French chemist, was the son of an apothecary in the household of the duke of Orleans. He was born at Paris on 15 June 1755. On the advice of the anatomist Vicq d'Azyr he took up medical studies. Lack of money made the road hard, but in 1780 he won his doctor's diploma at last. The chemistry lectures of Bucquet at the Paris Medical School turned his mind to chemistry for good.

In 1784 Fourcroy succeeded Macquer as lecturer in chemistry at the college of the Jardin du Roi, and his lectures drew great crowds. He was among the earliest converts to the views of Lavoisier. His copious writings spread the new chemistry across France. The entry follows his work in chemistry, physiology and pathology, and his public career through the Revolution, in which the lecture room and the state both claimed him.
britannica-1911-francais-francois-louis:
Francois Louis Francais (1814-1897), French painter, was born at Plombieres in the Vosges. At fifteen he was put as office-boy with a bookseller. After years of hard struggle, living sparely by drawing on stone and designing woodcut vignettes for books, he studied painting under Gigoux. Afterwards he worked under Corot, whose influence stayed decisive on his landscape style for the whole of his career as a painter of the French countryside.

Francais found his subjects in the country near Paris. He never matched Corot's lightness of touch or the lyric poetry of his master's work. Yet he is counted among the leading landscape painters of his country and time. He first exhibited at the Salon in 1837 and entered the Academie des Beaux-Arts in 1890. Few of his pictures stand in public galleries. The entry names his painting of an Italian evening among the works by which he is best judged.
britannica-1911-frederick-louis:
Frederick Louis (1707-1751), prince of Wales, eldest son of George II, was born at Hanover on 20 January 1707. After his grandfather took the British throne in 1714 he was styled duke of Gloucester and made a knight of the Garter. A planned match with a Prussian princess collapsed because George II and Frederick William I disliked each other.

Frederick settled in England in 1727 and was created prince of Wales in 1729, but father and son quarrelled without cure. The king kept his allowance short, and the prince made his court the centre of opposition and worked for the ruin of Walpole. He married Augusta of Saxe-Gotha in April 1736, yet a fight over money drove them further apart, and in 1737 he was ordered out of St James Palace. Barred from command against the Jacobites in 1745, he died in London in March 1751, leaving a son who reigned as George III.
britannica-1911-fustel-de-coulanges-numa:
Fustel de Coulanges, Numa Denis (1830–1889), a French historian, was born in Paris on the 18th of March 1830. After the École Normale he was sent to the French school at Athens in 1853. From 1860 to 1870 he taught history at Strassburg, and there he published La Cité antique in 1864. That book made religion the key to the growth of Greece and Rome, and its style ranks among the masterpieces of French prose.

From Strassburg he passed to the École Normale in 1870 and to the Sorbonne, where a chair of medieval history was created for him in 1878. His Histoire des institutions politiques (1874) argued that the invasions were slow, not violent, and that Merovingian institutions owed as much to Roman law as to German custom. Attacked in Germany and France, he rewrote the work, expanding six volumes that reached the Carolingian period. He died at Massy on the 12th of September 1889.
britannica-1911-galena-illinois:
Galena is a city of Illinois and the county-seat of Jo Daviess county, on the Galena river near its junction with the Mississippi, some 165 miles west-north-west of Chicago. Its people numbered 5005 in 1900 and 4835 in 1910. The city climbs rocky limestone bluffs, its parallel streets at different levels joined by flights of steps. Grant Park holds a statue of General Grant, who lived at Galena when the Civil War broke out. The neighbourhood holds the state's richest deposits of zinc and lead, and the city takes its name from the galena ore first worked there.

Galena began as a trading post the French called La Pointe and the English Fever River. It was laid out as a town in 1826 and incorporated in 1835. Its manufactures include mining pumps and machinery, flour, woollen goods, lumber and furniture, and the river gives water power.
britannica-1911-garnier-marie-joseph-fra:
Marie Joseph François Garnier, a French officer and explorer who lived from 1839 to 1873, gets a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. Born at St Étienne, he entered the navy and served in Brazil and the Pacific. By 1862 he was inspector of the natives in Cochin-China. It was his idea to send a mission up the Mekong valley.

Too young to lead it, he served under Captain Lagrée. From Kratie to Shanghai the party crossed 5,392 miles, and Garnier took near all the star fixes himself. When Lagrée died, Garnier led the party safe home. In 1873 he took Hanoi for a French protectorate in Tongking, and a month later he was slain in a fight with the Black Flags.
britannica-1911-garnier-pages-etienne-jo:
Étienne Joseph Louis Garnier-Pagès, a French politician who lived from 1801 to 1841, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Marseilles, son of a naval surgeon who died soon after. His mother remarried a college professor named Pagès. The two boys of the blended house took the double name Garnier-Pagès.

Étienne worked first in trade at Marseilles and then in insurance at Paris. He studied law from 1825 and made a mark as an advocate. A keen foe of the Restoration, he joined democratic societies and fought in the July revolution of 1830. In 1831 he entered the chamber of deputies for Isère. He spoke for universal suffrage and helped frame a famous report of 1832. His grasp of business and finance gave him weight with all parties. He died at Paris in June 1841.
britannica-1911-gastritis:
Gastritis, in the 1911 Britannica, is inflammation of the stomach, above all catarrh of its inner lining. The entry takes the acute and chronic forms in turn. Acute attacks are blamed on corrosive poisons, other poisons, fevers such as diphtheria and typhus, and food that has begun to spoil or cannot be digested.

An acute attack brings loss of appetite, nausea, headache, a furred tongue and pain about the stomach, and often ends in vomiting. Treatment is plain: remove the cause, suck ice, and use soothing drugs such as bismuth with a light milk diet. The chronic form, tied to disease of other organs and to heavy drinking, thickens the stomach wall and spoils digestion. Its treatment turns on strict diet, washing out the stomach, and drugs such as bismuth, arsenic and pepsin preparations.
britannica-1911-gerard-francois:
Francois Gerard (1770-1837), baron and French painter, was born at Rome on 4 May 1770, where his father served in the French ambassador's house. The 1911 Britannica entry brings him to Paris at twelve, through the sculptor Pajou's studio and the painter Brenet's, to David. Poverty forced him to work for pay, and David took his help.

His Belisaire of 1795 and Psyche et l'Amour of 1797 raised him, and his portrait of Madame Bonaparte in 1799 set him among the first portrait-painters of the day. Honours followed: baron of the empire, member of the Institute, first painter to the king. The entry's verdict is that he is best remembered by his portraits, and above all by his drawings of women. He died on 11 January 1837, after three days of fever.
britannica-1911-ginguene-pierre-louis:
Pierre Louis Ginguene (1748-1815), a French author, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Rennes in Brittany, he was schooled at a Jesuit college in his home town. He came to Paris in 1772 and wrote criticism for the Mercure de France. A comic opera and two satires followed in the years after.

The article says one slight piece, claimed by six or seven authors, brought him great success. His defence of the composer Piccini against the fans of Gluck made his name wider still. He hailed the first signs of the Revolution and helped run a weekly paper addressed to the villages of France. He also wrote letters in defence of the life and views of Rousseau. Held in prison during the Terror, he escaped death only by the fall of Robespierre.
britannica-1911-giraldus-cambrensis:
Giraldus Cambrensis (about 1146-1220), also called Gerald de Barri, was a medieval historian born in Pembrokeshire. The 1911 Britannica entry makes him the son of William de Barri and a granddaughter of the Welsh princess Nesta. Drawn to the church by his uncle, the bishop of St David's, he studied at Paris and was made archdeacon in 1172.

Henry II blocked his election as bishop of St David's in 1176, fearing his strong Welsh ties. As a king's chaplain from 1184 he went with Prince John to Ireland. There he wrote the Topographia Hibernica and the Expugnatio Hibernica, a strongly prejudiced history of the conquest, which he read to applause at Oxford in 1186. In 1188 he crossed Wales with Archbishop Baldwin, preaching the Third Crusade. The entry follows his long fight for St David's thereafter.
britannica-1911-girardon-francois:
Francois Girardon (1628-1715) was a French sculptor, born at Troyes on 17 March 1628. The 1911 Britannica entry has him trained by a wood-carver, then spotted by Chancellor Seguier, sent to Paris under Anguier, and on to Rome. Back in France by 1652, he attached himself to the court painter Le Brun.

Much of his work was made from Le Brun's designs, with that manner's pomp and large treatment of form. Versailles took an immense quantity of it. Academy posts rose to chancellor in 1695, and in 1690 he became inspector-general of works of sculpture. His bronze equestrian statue of Louis XIV of 1699 was melted down in the Revolution. The Tomb of Richelieu at the Sorbonne survives as a capital example of his style. He died at Paris in 1715. Note: this record's hosted file is a shared page chunk; his entry stands complete within it.
britannica-1911-girodet-de-roussy-anne-l:
Anne Louis Girodet de Roussy (1767-1824), better known as Girodet-Trioson, was a French painter born at Montargis on 5 January 1767. The 1911 Britannica entry has him orphaned young and raised by his guardian Trioson, who later adopted him. After early study he entered David's school and won the Prix de Rome at twenty-two.

At Rome he painted the Endymion, hailed at the Salon of 1792. The entry makes him a herald of the romantic movement trapped in classical training: firm forms and cold colour sit ill with his literary, sentimental subjects. His Fingal of 1802 is judged harshly, but the Scene de Deluge of 1806 won the decennial prize against David's Sabines, and Atala au Tombeau won wide popularity. Night work ruined his health, and his powers faded. He died on 9 December 1824.
britannica-1911-glacis:
Glacis, in the 1911 Britannica, is a term of military engineering, sent to the articles on fortification and siegecraft for full treatment. It names an artificial slope of earth built in front of a work. Its purpose is to keep an attacker under the defenders' fire to the last possible moment.

The reasoning is simple. On flat ground, troops close under a high work are sheltered from its fire. Raising the ground into a glacis removes that shelter, since the slope is swept by fire from the parapet above. More loosely, the entry adds, the word covers any slope, natural or artificial, that does the same job. The notice is short and purely definitional, with the geometry of attack and defence as its whole content.
britannica-1911-glamis:
Glamis is a village and parish of Forfarshire, Scotland, five and three-quarter miles west by south of Forfar. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the parish 1,351 people in 1901. The name, sometimes spelled Glammis with a silent i, comes from Gaelic words for a wide gap or vale.

The chief sight is Glamis Castle, seat of the earl of Strathmore and Kinghorne, about a mile from the station. In its present form it is mostly 17th century, in Scottish Baronial style. But the first structure stood in the 11th century, when Macbeth was Thane of Glamis. The entry tells its history. Robert II gave the thanedom to John Lyon, founder of the present family. Janet Douglas was burned as a witch in 1537, before her innocence was shown. Sir Walter Scott's night in the castle is also recalled.
britannica-1911-godet-frederic-louis:
Frederic Louis Godet is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Godet was a Swiss Protestant theologian, born at Neuchatel in 1812. He studied theology at Neuchatel, Bonn, and Berlin. In 1850 he became professor of theology at Neuchatel.

For fifteen years he also held a pastorate alongside his chair. In 1873 he helped found the free Evangelical Church of Neuchatel. He taught in its theological faculty until his death in 1900. The article calls him a conservative scholar of high standing. His fame rests on his French commentaries on the Bible. They cover the Gospel of John, the Gospel of Luke, and the Epistle to the Romans. A commentary on Corinthians completes the set. English translations carried his work abroad, and the entry lists their many editions.
britannica-1911-goldsmith-lewis:
Lewis Goldsmith is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Goldsmith was an Anglo French public writer who lived from about 1763 to 1846. He was born near London. In 1801 he printed an attack on the war policy of Pitt. The next year he moved from England to Paris. There Napoleon set him to run an English paper that took the French view.

The article tells of secret missions he claims he was given. One tale has him sent to seek a royal claim given up for the throne of Poland. He says he was told to seize the prince, but warned him instead. He served Napoleon on secret work until 1807. He came back to England in 1809 and was held in prison for a time. He then turned hard against the French revolt. His later paper attacked Napoleon with great heat.
britannica-1911-gounod-charles-francois:
Charles François Gounod, a French composer who lived from 1818 to 1893, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born in Paris in June 1818. His father was a talented painter. Gounod entered the Paris Conservatoire in 1836. He studied under Reicha, Halévy, and Lesueur.

In 1839 he won the Grand Prix de Rome. While living in that city, he gave much time to sacred music. He studied above all the works of Palestrina and Bach. In 1843 he went to Vienna, where a requiem of his was performed. On his return to Paris, he tried in vain to find a publisher for songs written in Rome. He became organist to a chapel of foreign missions. His thoughts then turned toward religious music. At that time he even weighed the idea of the priesthood. The article opens the making of a composer torn between altar and stage.
britannica-1911-grant-sir-francis:
Sir Francis Grant, a painter in fashion, is drawn in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Edinburgh in 1803, he was a Perthshire laird's son. He trained for the bar, then turned to art at twenty-four. A course of study in Edinburgh set his hand on its path. By 1843 his work hung at the Royal Academy in London.

Hunt scenes of hounds and horsemen first made his early name. High birth sitters then drew him to portrait work in fashion. His drapery and dress detail won praise for its true touch. Women of rank sat to him with marked success in town. Scott, Macaulay, and Disraeli all sat for his brush in time. He rose to lead the Royal Academy in later years.
britannica-1911-gresset-jean-baptiste-lo:
Jean Baptiste Louis Gresset (1709-1777) was a French poet and dramatist, born at Amiens on 29 August 1709. The 1911 Britannica entry says his poem Vert Vert is his main title to fame. Yet he spent his last twenty-five years regretting the frivolity that produced it. Jesuit-educated, he became a novice at sixteen.

Vert Vert, published at Rouen in 1734, tells of a convent parrot who learns swearing from bad company on a journey. The entry insists the story is nothing and the treatment everything: the nuns' tiny jealousies and trifles make the poem unrivalled among French verse tales. Complaints of licentiousness got Gresset expelled from the order. In Paris his comedy Le Mechant, Brunetiere judged the best verse comedy of the French 18th-century stage. He died at Amiens on 16 June 1777, deep in remorse.
britannica-1911-haggis: Haggis is a dish made from the heart, liver, and lungs of a calf or sheep, sometimes with the smaller intestines too, says a short entry from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The meat is chopped fine with suet and oatmeal, seasoned with pepper, salt, and onions, and boiled in the animal's stomach. The dish is counted as peculiarly Scottish, though it was common in England until the eighteenth century. The entry finds the word's origin obscure, and suggests a link with a verb meaning to cut in small pieces.
britannica-1911-hanriot-francois:
François Hanriot (1761–1794) was a French revolutionist born at Nanterre. Poor parentage and early dishonesty marked his start. He lost a lawyer's clerk post for dishonesty. The Paris octroi dismissed him in July 1789. He had abandoned his post when crowds burned the barriers. Hand-to-mouth living followed for a time. Then he became an orator of the sans-culottes section. He commanded its armed force in August 1792.

The September massacres also saw him in command. Prominence came on 30–31 May 1793. The Commune made him provisional commander of Paris' armed forces. He led the forces that purged the Girondists on 2 June. From 1 July he held the command permanently. That post gave him enormous power. At Thermidor he tried to rescue Robespierre. He sounded the tocsin and rushed to the Hôtel de Ville. Arrested next day, he was guillotined on 28 July 1794.
britannica-1911-hemsterhuis-francois:
François Hemsterhuis (1721–1790) was a Dutch writer on aesthetics and morals. He was born at Franeker on 27 December 1721. Tiberius Hemsterhuis, the philologist, was his father. Leiden university educated him, and Plato was his study. Failing a professorship, he entered state service. For many years he served as secretary to the state council. He died at the Hague on 7 July 1790. Goethe, Herder and Jacobi were among his acquaintances.

His philosophy is Socratic in content, Platonic in form. Self-knowledge and truth, unfettered by any system, were its foundation. His best work lies in aesthetics, the analysis of feeling. His writings all appeared in French. The Lettre sur la sculpture of 1769 defines beauty famously. Beauty gives the greatest number of ideas in the shortest time. Sopyle attacks materialism in dialogue form. Aristée is his theodicy on God and man. Elegance of form and refined sentiment mark everything.
britannica-1911-henault-charles-jean-fra:
Charles Jean Francois Henault is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a French writer on the past born in Paris in sixteen eighty five. His father farmed the royal taxes and loved books and verse. The boy was schooled at a Jesuit college in the city.

The entry tells how pulpit fire first drew him toward a church life. Wealth and charm soon pulled him back to the world of courts. Light verse and stage works won him a seat in the French Academy. Grave posts in law courts showed his more solid side in time. He ended as chief of the queen household staff in France.
britannica-1911-hersent-louis:
Louis Hersent, a French painter who lived from 1777 to 1860, has a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Paris on 10 March 1777, he became a pupil of David in his youth. He obtained the Prix de Rome in 1797 at age twenty. In the Salon of 1802 his Metamorphosis of Narcissus appeared before the public.

Hersent continued to exhibit with rare breaks up to the year 1831. His most considerable works under the empire were Achilles Parting from Briseis and Atala Dying in the Arms of Chactas. His typical works belong to the period of the Restoration in France. Louis the Sixteenth Relieving the Afflicted and Daphnis and Chloe were both in the Salon of 1817. The Abdication of Gustavus Vasa in 1819 brought him a medal of honour from the judges.
britannica-1911-hincks-sir-francis:
