Sir Francis Hincks is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Hincks was a Canadian statesman, born at Cork, Ireland, in 1807. He was the son of a Presbyterian minister. In 1832 he went into business in Toronto and fell in with reform circles.

An inquiry into the Welland Canal accounts turned him toward politics. In 1838 he founded the Examiner, a weekly paper on the Liberal side. He entered parliament in 1841 and soon held the finance post of inspector-general. He resigned with Baldwin in 1843 over responsible government, then returned to office in 1848. On the Baldwin ministry's fall in 1851, Hincks became premier of Canada. The article follows a man who moved from ledgers and newspapers to the head of a government.
britannica-1911-hippias-of-elis:
Hippias of Elis, a Greek sophist of the fifth century before Christ, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a younger fellow of Protagoras and of Socrates. His home city trusted him so much that it sent him on key embassies to many towns. At Athens he met Socrates and other lead thinkers of the day.

Hippias claimed skill in all fields and taught for high fees with success. Poetry, grammar, history, maths, and the stars all fell in his range. He boasted he could speak at Olympia on any topic with no notice. He also boasted that he wore nothing he had not made by hand. The entry grants his real ability but calls his learning shallow. His aim was to arm pupils for debate, not to give them true knowledge. Two dialogues of Plato expose his methods.
britannica-1911-hotman-francois:
François Hotman (1524–1590) was a French publicist, eldest son of Pierre Hotman, born at Paris on the 23rd of August 1524, his family of Silesian origin. His Catholic father, a counsellor of the Paris parlement, meant him for the law and sent him to Orleans at fifteen. He took his doctorate in three years and became a pleader at Paris. But the barrister's arts were not to his taste.

Hotman turned to jurisprudence and letters, and in 1546 lectured on Roman law at Paris. The courage of Anne Dubourg under torture won him to the Reform. In 1547 he left for Lyons, then Geneva and Lausanne, where Calvin's backing made him professor of belles-lettres and history. In 1555 he lectured on law at Strassburg, becoming professor there in 1556. His fame drew offers from Prussia, Hesse and Elizabeth of England. He also ran secret missions for the Huguenot leaders.
britannica-1911-howard-oliver-otis:
Oliver Otis Howard (1830–1909) was an American soldier, born in Leeds, Maine, on the 8th of November 1830. He graduated at Bowdoin College in 1850 and at the U.S. Military Academy in 1854. In 1857 he served in Florida against the Seminole Indians, then taught mathematics at West Point until 1861. At the Civil War's opening he resigned to command the 3rd Maine volunteers.

At the first battle of Bull Run Howard led a brigade, and in September 1861 he became brigadier-general of volunteers. In the Peninsular campaign, at Seven Pines, he was twice wounded and lost his right arm. Back in service by August 1862, he fought through the Virginian campaigns and took over Sedgwick's division at Antietam. In March 1863 he became major-general of volunteers. The account follows him to Chancellorsville and beyond, through the war and his later work for the freedmen and for education.
britannica-1911-huber-francois:
François Huber (1750–1831) was a Swiss naturalist, born at Geneva on the 2nd of July 1750. His family had already marked itself in letters and science. His great-aunt Marie Huber wrote widely on religion, and his father Jean Huber, a soldier of Ferney's circle, wrote on the flight of birds. At fifteen François began to suffer an eye disease that ended in total blindness.

Blind, Huber still worked, through the eyes of his wife, Marie Aimée Lullin, and his servant, François Burnens. Their observations laid the foundations of scientific knowledge of the honey-bee's life. His Nouvelles Observations sur les abeilles appeared at Geneva in 1792, in English in 1806. He also wrote on the origin of wax and on dangers that threaten bees. He died at Lausanne on the 22nd of December 1831. His son Pierre followed him, turning from bees to the ants of his famous Recherches of 1810.
britannica-1911-huc-evariste-regis:
Évariste Régis Huc (1813–1860) was a French missionary-traveller, born at Toulouse on the 1st of August 1813. At twenty-four he entered the Lazarist congregation at Paris, and soon after his ordination in 1839 he sailed for China. At Macao he spent some eighteen months in the Lazarist seminary, preparing for mission work. He learned the Chinese tongue and took to Chinese dress.

From Canton Huc first ran a mission in the southern provinces, then passed to Peking to perfect his language. He settled at last in the Valley of Black Waters, just inside Mongolia, beyond the Great Wall. From there grew the great journey: in 1845 he and Gabet reached the Tibetan boundary at Tang-Kiul. Rather than face four months alone to Lhasa, they waited eight months for a Tibetan embassy returning from Peking. His Souvenirs of that journey made him famous in Europe.
britannica-1911-hugues-clovis:
Clovis Hugues, French poet and socialist born at Menerbes in Vaucluse on 3 November 1851, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He studied for the priesthood but did not take orders in the end. Fiery pieces in the local papers of Marseilles cost him dear in 1871. A court gave him three years in prison and a fine of 6000 francs.

In 1877 he fought a duel and killed his foe, a rival journalist. Voters at Marseilles sent him to the chamber in 1881 as a deputy. He was then the sole voice of the Socialist party in that house. Paris chose him as a deputy in 1893, and he held that seat till 1906. His poems, novels, and comedies brim with wit and rich life. Poems written in prison stand among his chief works.
britannica-1911-hunt-william-morris:
Hunt, William Morris, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an American painter. Born at Brattleboro in Vermont on the 31st of March 1824, he came of land-rich folk. He spent a short time at Harvard in the year 1840. His true schooling began on a trip to Europe with his kin.

In Paris he studied with Couture, then fell under Millet's sway. That bond with Millet shaped his style for all his life. He brought the Barbizon school to America more than any other man. Back home in 1855 he painted some of his best loved works. The crowd then called for portraits from his hand instead. A great Boston fire in 1872 burned many of his works.
britannica-1911-hypochondriasis:
Hypochondriasis is a medical term for a false belief of ill health. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica takes it from the Greek for the soft parts under the breastbone. The ancients tied it to disorders of the belly organs. Cullen classed it among nervous diseases in 1777. Falret later framed it as low spirits joined to false beliefs about health. Its subjects often come from families with weak nervous stock.

In its common form the mind is sound but for the one belief. Society called its mild cases the vapours or the spleen. Such folk insist they are unwell though no cause can be found. In sharper forms, pain is fixed by the patient on one region. The entry treats it as kin to the broader insanity of a family line.
britannica-1911-hypostasis:
Hypostasis is a theology article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a term that looms large in the Trinitarian debates of the fourth and fifth centuries. By one account, Gnostic writers first brought it into theology. In the earliest church use it meant much the same as the Greek word for substance, as it had among the Stoics.

Dionysius of Rome condemned the attempt to split the Godhead into three separate hypostases and three gods. The Nicene Creed, in its curses, speaks in the same mixed way. Yet alongside that loose use ran a wish to split the terms apart. Men wanted to keep hypostasis for the divine persons alone. That push began at Alexandria. The article tracks it by setting the early writings of Athanasius against his later ones.
britannica-1911-iblis:
Iblis, the devil of Moslem myth, is set out in a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He stands as the match of the devil of Jews and Christians. In the Koran he shows more often under the name Shaitan. Iblis is named eleven times there, Shaitan eighty-seven times. He is chief of the spirits of evil in that faith.

His shape was modelled on the devil of the Jewish tale. Iblis rose against Allah and was cast out of Paradise. The Koran tale makes his fall a price for one refusal. He would not bow and worship Adam as he was bid. Sentenced to death, he won a stay till the day of judgment.
britannica-1911-in-antis: In antis is a term from classical building, used for temples whose entrance part was formed in a set way. Two columns stood in the entrance, placed between the antae, the pilaster-like ends of the side walls. The entry is a single short sentence and gives only that definition, with a cross reference to the article on the temple for the wider subject. It records the name, the type of building it applies to, and the exact placing of the two columns that marks the form.
britannica-1911-indianapolis:
Indianapolis is the capital and largest city of Indiana, set near the exact centre of the state. The 1911 Britannica article places it on the west fork of the White river. Its count in 1910 was 233,650, up from 169,164 in 1900. The city stands 824 miles west of New York by rail and 183 miles south-east of Chicago. Its land takes in some thirty square miles.

Since the first rail line reached it in 1847, the city has grown as a great rail hub. More than 150 trains a day use its Union Station, with more than 30,000 riders. A belt line rings the city and moves over a million freight cars a year. Electric interurban lines fan out to the whole state. In 1908 twenty-five such lines ran some four hundred cars a day into the city.
britannica-1911-jones-sir-alfred-lewis:
Sir Alfred Lewis Jones is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a British shipowner. He lived from 1845 to 1909. He was born in Carmarthenshire in Wales. At twelve he was apprenticed to managers of the African Steamship Company. He made several voyages to the west coast of Africa. By twenty six he had risen to manage the business.

The post gave him too little scope for his ambition. He borrowed money and bought two or three small sailing ships. The venture did well and his fleet grew over time. He saw that steamers would soon replace sailing ships. So he sold his vessels while trade was still good. In 1891 Elder Dempster bought the old African firm. They offered him a manager's post, which he took. He took it on terms that gave him many shares.
britannica-1911-killis:
Killis is a town of north Syria in the province of Aleppo. The 1911 Britannica entry sets it 60 miles north of Aleppo city. It sits in a plain of great richness, ringed by olive groves. Oil from those groves is held the finest in all Syria. A coach road from Aleppo to Aintab gives the town its trade weight.

Some 20,000 folk live there, of Circassian, Turkoman, and Arab stock. The town lies on the north rim of Arab lands in that region. A planned rail junction near the town may raise its rank in time. Lines for Baghdad and for Beirut were set to meet close by. That cross point would bring new trade and growth to Killis.
britannica-1911-lagrange-joseph-louis:
Joseph Louis Lagrange (1736–1813), French mathematician, was born at Turin on the 25th of January 1736. His great-grandfather, a French cavalry captain, had passed into Sardinian service and settled at Turin. His father, treasurer at war, had ample means from his post and his wife's fortune, then lost them in rash speculations. Lagrange counted that loss his own good fortune: had he been rich, he said, he might never have known mathematics.

His first tastes were literary. At the college of Turin he learned the rudiments of geometry without difficulty but without distinction, until reading a tract by Halley fired him for the analytical method. Working unaided, he rose in two years to the level of the greatest of his contemporaries. At nineteen he sent Euler his idea of a general method for the problems Euler was treating. His abstract way of regarding functions opened a new development of higher analysis.
britannica-1911-lagrenee-louis-jean-fran:
Louis Jean François Lagrenée (1724–1805), French painter, was born at Paris on the 30th of December 1724 and was a pupil of Carle Vanloo. In 1755 he became a member of the Royal Academy, presenting as his diploma picture the "Rape of Deianira," now in the Louvre. He visited St Petersburg at the call of the empress Elizabeth. On his return he was named in 1781 director of the French Academy at Rome, where he painted the "Indian Widow," one of his best-known works.

In 1804 Napoleon conferred on him the cross of the Legion of Honour. He died on the 19th of June 1805 in the Louvre, of which he was honorary keeper.
britannica-1911-lais:
Two Greek women named Lais are distinguished in a short 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. Both were courtesans of old Greece. The elder was a native of Corinth, born about four eighty before Christ. She was famed for greed and a hard heart, which won her the name the Axe.

Among her lovers were men of thought and a noted runner. In old age she drank too much, the entry says. Her grave near Corinth bore a lioness tearing a ram. The younger Lais was born in Sicily about four twenty. She was taken to Corinth as a girl. A painter used her as a model, struck by her looks as she drew water.
britannica-1911-lambert-francis:
Francis Lambert (c. 1486–1530), Protestant reformer, was the son of a papal official at Avignon, where he was born. At fifteen he entered the Franciscan monastery, and after 1517 preached through France, Italy and Switzerland. Study of the Scriptures shook his faith in Roman Catholic theology, and by 1522 he had left his order. He identified himself with neither Zwinglianism nor Lutheranism. He disputed with Zwingli at Zürich in 1522, married at Wittenberg in 1523 and settled at Strassburg in 1524 to spread the Reformation among French-speaking people.

Distrusted by the Germans, he saw his work prohibited by Strassburg in 1526, Jacob Sturm befriended him and recommended him to the Landgraf Philip of Hesse. With Philip's encouragement he drafted his scheme of church reform. It was democratic and congregational, with the church governed by a synod, pastors elected by the congregation, and canon law repudiated. Philip submitted the scheme to a synod at Homburg.
britannica-1911-lathrop-francis:
Lathrop, Francis, is the subject of a 1911 Britannica life of an American artist. Born at sea near Hawaii on the 22nd of June 1849, he came of a noted line. He was a pupil of Farrar in New York as a youth. He read art at the Royal Academy at Dresden in Germany.

From 1870 to 1873 he was in England for more study and work. There he learned from Ford Madox Brown and Burne-Jones as masters. In the school of William Morris he gave his care to stained glass. Back in America he won fame as an illustrator and portrait man. Later he kept to decorative work for church and college halls. His stained glass window at Princeton chapel is named as his mark.
britannica-1911-laurent-francois:
François Laurent, a Belgian historian and legal thinker who lived from 1810 to 1887, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Luxemburg in July 1810. He held a high post in the ministry of justice. In 1836 he became professor of civil law at the university of Ghent.

His defence of liberal and anti-clerical ideas made him bitter foes. He spoke for them from his chair and in the press. Yet he kept his post until his death in February 1887. He treated the ties of church and state in a three-volume work. The same theme filled much of his chief work of history. That work, on the history of mankind, ran to eighteen volumes. It came out at Ghent and Brussels over fifteen years. The article shows a scholar whose views shaped both law and public debate.
britannica-1911-laya-jean-louis:
Jean Louis Laya, who lived from 1761 to 1833, was a French dramatist born in Paris. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the fourth of December 1761. His first comedy, written with a partner in 1785, was taken by the Comédie Française but never staged. In 1789 he wrote a verse tragedy in plea for religious tolerance. A play on the perils of public opinion came the next year.

His fame rests on the Friend of the Laws of 1793, a bold blow at mob rule. Its masked portraits of Robespierre and Marat were plain to all. The play came out nineteen days before the death of Louis the Sixteenth. Banned in ten days, it was played again while 30,000 Parisians guarded the hall. Men were guillotined for the crime of owning a copy. Laya hid till the Terror passed.
britannica-1911-lebrun-charles-francois:
Charles Francois Lebrun is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lebrun was a French statesman, born in 1739 at St-Sauveur-Lendelin. He began as a lawyer at Paris in 1762. He served the crown in legal and financial posts and advised the chancellor Maupeou.

After Maupeou fell, Lebrun turned to letters and translated Tasso and the Iliad. The Revolution brought him back to public life as a deputy. After the coup of 1799 he became third consul under Napoleon. He helped rebuild French finance and the rule of the departments. Later he governed Liguria and then Holland for the empire. The entry follows him through the Restoration to his death in 1824.
britannica-1911-legendre-louis:
Louis Legendre, who lived from 1752 to 1797, was a French revolutionary born at Versailles. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born on the twenty-second of May 1752. When the Revolution broke out, he kept a butcher's shop in Paris. He backed its ideas with zeal, joined the Jacobin Club, and helped found the Cordeliers. Though his speech was rough, he had a true gift to stir a crowd.

Legendre took a lead part in the storming of the Bastille in 1789. He was there too at the Champ de Mars killings and at the attack on the Tuileries. As a deputy he voted for the death of Louis the Sixteenth. He helped bring down the Girondists. After the fall of Robespierre he shut the Jacobin Club and rose to lead the Convention. He died in December 1797.
britannica-1911-lenormant-francois:
Francois Lenormant is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Lenormant was a French scholar of old lands and coins who was born in Paris in 1837. His father was a noted scholar of Egypt and old art. The boy learned Greek from age six and wrote on Greek tablets at age fourteen.

The article tells of his trips to Greece and south Italy for field research. His father died of fever on one such trip to Athens. Lenormant served in the war of 1870 and was wounded at Paris. Later he taught at the National Library and helped found a journal on old art. He was an early reader of wedge shaped writing from Assyria. He died in Paris in 1883.
britannica-1911-leptis:
Leptis names two old towns on the African coast. Leptis Magna, now Lebda, stood in Tripolitana at the mouth of the Cinyps. Leptis Parva, now Lamta, was a small port of Byzacena. Magna takes most of the space here.

Magna ranked among the oldest Phoenician trade posts on that coast. Sidon founded it and Tyre later joined. Tribute of a talent a day went to Carthage. Rome gained its trust in the Jugurthine War. Caesar laid a yearly charge of 300,000 measures of oil on it. Trajan made it a colony. Septimius Severus, born there, raised its rights and beauty. Trade fell as the harbour silted. Desert raids wore it down. Justinian tried in vain to rebuild it.
britannica-1911-long-john-davis:
John Davis Long is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Long was an American lawyer and political leader, born in Maine in 1838. He graduated at Harvard in 1857 and was admitted to the bar in 1861. He practised in Boston and soon entered politics as a Republican.

The article lists his climb through public office. He sat in the Massachusetts House and served as its speaker. He was lieutenant-governor in 1879 and governor from 1880 to 1882. Six years in the national House of Representatives followed. From 1897 to 1902 he was secretary of the navy, under Presidents McKinley and Roosevelt. He then led Harvard's Board of Overseers. His books included a version of the Aeneid and a work on the new American navy.
britannica-1911-loubet-emile-francois:
Emile Francois Loubet is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born on the thirtieth of December 1838, he was the seventh president of the French republic. He was the son of a small landowner who served more than once as mayor of their town.

The article follows his climb through French public life. He joined the Paris bar in 1862 and settled to practice in a small town. As mayor in the crisis of 1870 he backed Gambetta's line. He won a seat in the lower house in 1876. There he fought for free, forced, and church free schooling for all. He rose to head the Senate in 1896. In February 1899 he was chosen president, with 483 votes to 279 for his one strong rival.
britannica-1911-lyte-henry-francis:
Henry Francis Lyte was an Anglican divine and writer of church hymns. He lived from seventeen ninety three to eighteen forty seven. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born near Kelso, he was schooled at Enniskillen and at Trinity College, Dublin.

Lyte took orders in eighteen fifteen and held a curacy near Wexford first. Weak health drove him to England, and he settled at Brixham in eighteen twenty three. In eighteen forty four his health at last gave way for good. He died at Nice on the twentieth of November eighteen forty seven. His best known hymns are Abide With Me and Praise My Soul.
britannica-1911-maimbourg-louis:
Louis Maimbourg is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a French Jesuit and writer from 1610 to 1686. He was born at Nancy in France. He joined the Society of Jesus at age sixteen. After study at Rome he taught classics at Rouen. He then turned to preaching with fair success at best. Small disputes drew him in before a great one came.

He threw his force into a clash over Gallican rights. A work of 1682 on the rights of Rome cost him his place. The pope ordered him out of his order for it. The king of France gave him a home and a pension. He died in Paris in August of that year 1686. His many works retold church past in lively style. The entry calls those works loose and not to be trusted.
britannica-1911-mareotis: Mareotis, in Arabic Mariut, is the lake that lies farthest west in the Delta of Egypt. A thin strip of land parts the lake from the Mediterranean sea. The city of Alexandria is built on that strip. The article is a cross note only, and it points the reader to the main texts on Egypt and on Alexandria for the full account of the lake and its shore.
britannica-1911-marguerite-de-valois:
Marguerite de Valois is a house entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It deals with three princesses of one French royal house who shared a name. All three left their mark on the court and on books of the age. The first and last of the three count for most in the tale.

The first bore four names in her life from birth and two wed matches. She was a king sister and the most strong woman in the realm in her prime. Her first match brought her scant joy, and she was left a widow young. Court craft and verse both bear her stamp in French annals. The entry takes care to part her tale from her kin of like name.
britannica-1911-mariette-auguste-ferdina:
Auguste Ferdinand François Mariette, a French Egyptologist who lived from 1821 to 1881, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Boulogne in February 1821, where his father was town clerk, he did well at the town college and showed artistic talent. At eighteen he went to England to teach French and drawing at Stratford-on-Avon. A year later he was designing patterns for a ribbon maker at Coventry.

Poorly paid and homesick, Mariette went back to Boulogne and took a degree at Douai in 1841. He taught at his old college and wrote on history for local papers. Sorting the papers of his cousin Nestor L'Hôte turned him toward Egyptology. He studied hieroglyphs and Coptic with passion. In 1847 he published a catalogue of the Egyptian gallery at Boulogne. In 1849 he took a post at the Louvre and left for Egypt the next year.
britannica-1911-matthew-of-paris:
Matthew of Paris (died 1259) was an English monk and chronicler known only through his writings, as this 1911 Britannica article presents him. Despite his surname, his stance toward foreigners shows he was English by birth. The first fact he records of himself is his entry as a monk at St Albans in 1217.

His life was spent mainly in that house, apart from a mission to Norway in 1248, carrying a message from Louis IX of France to its king. At St Albans he reworked the histories of earlier monks and continued them in his Chronica majora from 1235. He drew much from letters, and more from talks with eye witnesses. Among them was Henry III, who in 1257 kept him close for a week and guided his pen.
britannica-1911-mclane-louis:
Louis McLane (1786-1857), an American political leader, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Smyrna in Delaware, he was the son of a well known soldier of the Revolution. He was admitted to the bar in 1807. He entered politics as a Democrat and sat in the House of Representatives for ten years, then in the Senate for two.

The article lists a long run of high posts. He was minister to England, then secretary of the treasury in the cabinet of President Jackson. In that post he argued for the United States Bank. In 1833 he moved to head the state department, and left the cabinet the next year. He later ran the Baltimore and Ohio railway for ten years and served again as minister to England. He died at Baltimore in 1857.
britannica-1911-meletius-of-lycopolis:
Meletius of Lycopolis lived in the 300s and founded a sect in Egypt. The 1911 Britannica entry names that sect the Meletians after him. Some called it the Church of the Martyrs in the Thebes district. With Peter of Alexandria he was jailed in the Diocletian purge of Christians. His fame rests on a hard line toward lapsed Christians in that purge.

He refused to take back those who had renounced the faith in fear. At least till the purge had ceased, he would not grant pardon. That refusal split him from Peter and from other bishops in Egypt. Those bishops would grant pardon to men who did penance for the lapse. Free again, Meletius held his ground and drew a crowd of backers.
britannica-1911-meningitis:
Meningitis is a term in medicine for swelling of the membranes of the brain. The 1911 Britannica entry takes the word from a Greek term for membrane. The swelling may strike the brain, the spinal cord, or both at once. One grave form is tubercular meningitis of the brain in youth. A tubercle bacillus in the membranes brings that form on in full.

That form strikes most oft in children under ten years of age. Adults may take it too, though less oft than the young. A weak frame from birth raises the risk of the ill, it says. Foul air, poor food, and strain of mind play their part as well. It may also follow ills of childhood such as measles in some cases.
britannica-1911-mieris:
Mieris is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a family of Dutch artists. The family practised painting at Leiden for three generations. Their work spans the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The first named is Frans van Mieris, the elder. He lived from about 1635 to 1681. His father Jan was a goldsmith and diamond setter. Frans was born at Leiden in April 1635, by one account.

His father wished to train him to the goldsmith's trade. Frans preferred drawing to chasing metal, and chose art. He took service with a glazier who kept a school of design. In his father's shop he learned the ways of fine folk. Their dress and manners became familiar to him there. The sheen of jewels and stained glass caught his eye. He soon moved to the teaching of Gerard Douw. His manner gained the finish of the Dutch school at its most refined.
britannica-1911-mignet-francois-auguste-:
François Auguste Alexis Mignet, who lived from 1796 to 1884, was a French historian. The 1911 Britannica article says he was born at Aix in Provence on the eighth of May 1796. His father was a locksmith who loved the ideas of the French Revolution. Mignet shone at school in Avignon and then read law at Aix. He was called to the bar in 1818, but chose the life of a writer instead.

Early prize essays on Charles the Seventh and on Saint Louis brought him notice. He moved to Paris and wrote for a liberal paper against the restored kings. With Thiers he wrote a history of the French Revolution in 1824, done in four months. In 1830 the two men helped found the National, a paper that backed the July revolt.
britannica-1911-molina-luis:
Luis Molina, a Spanish Jesuit who lived from 1535 to 1600, is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Cuenca, he joined the Society of Jesus at age eighteen. He studied at Coimbra and then taught at the university in Evora in Portugal. After twenty years there he moved to a chair in Madrid, where he died.

Molina is known most for a book that sought to join free will with grace and with the foreknowledge of God. He held that people are free to act or not to act. God, he argued, knows how each person will use that freedom. This view, built on what he called middle knowledge, drew sharp debate. Dominican critics pushed back, and Pope Clement the Eighth had to step in.
britannica-1911-monmouth-illinois:
Monmouth is a city article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Monmouth is a city in Illinois, the county seat of Warren county. It stands in the western part of the state, south of Rock Island. Its population grew from 5936 in 1890 to 9128 in 1910.

The entry notes the city's rail links and its college. Monmouth College, a United Presbyterian school founded in 1856, had 454 students in 1908. Public buildings included a court-house, a federal building, a hospital, and a county library. The city sits in good farming country where cattle, swine, and ponies are raised. It also had varied manufactures. A brief civic record closes the piece: settled about 1824, a village in 1836, a city in 1852. Readers get a compact portrait of a small prairie city.
britannica-1911-mont-cenis:
Mont Cenis is a pass in Savoy, France, at six thousand eight hundred ninety three feet. Its pass entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The pass marks the line between the Cottian and Graian Alps. Napoleon built a carriage road across it from eighteen o three to eighteen ten.

A light rail line named for Fell opened beside the road in eighteen sixty eight. That line was torn up when a long tunnel opened in eighteen seventy one. The tunnel runs eight miles and links Modane with Bardonneche in Italy. Roads and rails then follow river valleys down toward Turin in Italy. A smaller pass near by may be the route Hannibal once used.
britannica-1911-monteil-amans-alexis:
Amans Alexis Monteil is the subject of a life entry in the 1911 Britannica. He was a French writer on the past who lived from 1769 to 1850. He was born at Rodez and died at Cely. He taught his subject at Rodez and at two other schools. He held that kings and chiefs had been given far too much weight. In his view the life of the plain folk mattered more.

His chief work set out to show the ranks and trades of France. It ran to ten books and came out from 1828 to 1844. He built a large store of old hand writ texts to back the work. He sold that store in 1835. The entry credits him as one of the first in France to stress how folk live.
britannica-1911-montreuil-sous-bois: Montreuil-sous-Bois is the subject of a short town article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The town lies in northern France, in the Seine district east of Paris. It stands on the slope and top of a hill, north of Vincennes. In 1906 its people numbered near thirty six thousand. The town is noted most for its wide peach orchards. Its works make paint, oils and varnish, glass, and chemical goods.
britannica-1911-morris:
Morris is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city in Illinois. It is the county seat of Grundy county. It stands on the north bank of the Illinois river. Chicago lies about sixty two miles to the north east. Counts give it 4273 people in 1900 and 4563 in 1910. The Chicago, Rock Island and Pacific railway serves the city. The Illinois and Michigan canal also serves it. Electric power comes from the river at Marseilles.

The city was named in honour of Isaac Morris. He was a commissioner of the Illinois and Michigan canal. Morris was first settled in the year 1834. It was chartered as a city in 1857. The entry is brief, but it fixes the place well. River, canal, and rail mark its means of trade. Its growth in the decade shown was slow and steady.
britannica-1911-morris-sir-lewis:
Sir Lewis Morris, a British poet who lived from 1833 to 1907, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Penbryn, the eldest son in a Welsh family of note. His great grandfather was a known Welsh poet and antiquary. Morris was schooled at Sherborne and at Jesus College, Oxford, where he took first class honours in classics.

He was called to the bar in 1861 and worked for twenty years as a conveyancing counsel. He gave much energy to schooling causes in Wales, but failed to win a Welsh seat in Parliament. Knighted in 1896, he turned late to verse as well. His Songs of Two Worlds, in three sets from 1872 to 1875, won him wide favour. The Epic of Hades, in 1876 and 1877, retold Greek myths in a modern, moral key and holds his best verse.
britannica-1911-mount-vernon-illinois: Mount Vernon is a city in Illinois, described in a brief place entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of Jefferson county, east of Saint Louis. The count rose from about three thousand in 1890 to about eight thousand in 1910. Four rail lines serve the city, and it is the base of a state appeal court district. Settlers came in 1819, and it gained a city charter in 1872. A storm in 1888 wrecked many buildings.
britannica-1911-nicolas-sir-nicholas-har:
Nicholas Harris Nicolas is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Nicolas was an English scholar of old families and records who lived from 1799 to 1848. He was born at Dartmouth. He served in the navy from 1812 to 1816, then read law. He was called to the bar in 1825. His law work dealt mainly with peerage cases before the House of Lords.

The article says his time went chiefly to family and history studies. He won high knightly honours in the eighteen thirties. He attacked the running of the Society of Antiquaries and then resigned from it. He also attacked the Record Commission as too costly. Those fights led to a formal inquiry into the public records in 1836. Money troubles forced him to leave England, and he died near Boulogne. His chief work is a history of the orders of knighthood.
britannica-1911-orderic-vitalis:
Orderic Vitalis (1075-about 1142) was a chronicler, the son of a French priest in the service of Roger Montgomery, earl of Shrewsbury. This 1911 Britannica article tells how his parents sent him at five to learn letters from an English priest at Shrewsbury. At eleven he was entered as a novice in the Norman monastery of St Evroul, at a cost of thirty marks.

The boy felt like Joseph in a strange land, knowing no French when he arrived. His superiors renamed him Vitalis, since they found his birth name hard to say, but he kept the old name before the new in the title of his Ecclesiastical History. He became a deacon in 1093 and a priest in 1107. His cloistered life was quiet, though he travelled at times to Croyland, Worcester, Cambrai, and Cluny, and he turned early to writing.
britannica-1911-orleanais: Orleanais was one of the old provinces of France before the Revolution. It was the land around Orleans, on both banks of the Loire river. For church use it formed the diocese of Orleans. The Capet family held it before Hugh Capet took the French throne in nine eighty seven. In thirteen forty four Philip the Sixth gave it, with a duke's title, to his younger son Philip. The name is still used for the region near Orleans, though that area is a bit smaller than the old province.
britannica-1911-palgrave-sir-francis:
Sir Francis Palgrave, an English historian who lived from 1788 to 1861, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was the son of Meyer Cohen, a Jewish stockbroker, and was born in London in July 1788. He was taught privately and was so forward a boy that he translated a Latin tale into French at eight. In 1803 he was articled to a firm of solicitors.

Palgrave was called to the bar at the Middle Temple in 1827. On his marriage in 1823 he had become a Christian and taken his present name. He edited great record works for the Record Commission, on writs, rolls, and calendars. In 1831 he published a history of the Anglo-Saxon period. His Rise and Progress of the English Commonwealth of 1832 was called a memorable book. He was knighted in 1832.
britannica-1911-palingenesis:
Palingenesis, a Greek term that means birth again, is explained in a thought entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. In philosophy it names the view that the soul does not die with the body. The soul is instead born again in new lives. In that broad sense it is the same as the passing of souls from body to body.

Schopenhauer gave the term a tighter sense in his system. For him the will itself does not die, but shows itself afresh in new persons. He thus rejects the claim that the same soul comes back in a new body. The Stoics used the word for the fresh making of the world after its fall into the Creator. In the New Testament the word takes a sense of spiritual rebirth, though it shows just twice. In modern biology it names the exact copying of ancestral traits by descent.
britannica-1911-panyasis:
Panyasis of Halicarnassus was a Greek epic poet, kin to the famed writer Herodotus. He flourished about five hundred years before Christ, and was put to death by a tyrant some years later. The 1911 Britannica entry names his two chief poems and their themes.

One poem, in fourteen books, told the deeds of Heracles in many lands. The other, in paired line verse, told how the Ionian towns of Asia Minor were founded and settled. His own age, cool toward epic verse, held him in low regard. Later judges ranked him high, some next to Homer alone. The scraps that stand show rich speech and smooth rhythm, and the entry closes with the books where they can be read.
britannica-1911-parenthesis: Parenthesis, from a Greek word that means put in alongside, is a grammar term in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names the act of placing a word, phrase, or full sentence inside other words. The added part does not break the build of the host sentence. It serves to qualify, explain, or add a point. In print such parts are marked off by commas or dashes. Brackets, round or square, are the more usual marks.
britannica-1911-paris-illinois:
Paris is a city and the county seat of Edgar county, Illinois. Its city entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. It lies in the east part of the state, north west of Terre Haute. Counts rose from about forty nine hundred in eighteen ninety to seventy six hundred.

Two rail systems serve Paris, and their lines cross inside the city. The city is a transfer point for traffic in all four directions. Rich farm land surrounds it, with corn and oats as chief crops. That farm wealth gives the city a large and steady trade base. Paris was founded in about eighteen twenty five and chartered in eighteen fifty three.
britannica-1911-parkman-francis:
Francis Parkman, American historian, was born in Boston on 16 September 1823 and is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. His line held Harvard men, merchants, and clergy. His father was a noted Boston clergyman and friend of Channing. His mother traced her line back to John Cotton.

The boy was the eldest of six children, and his health was frail. He spent much time at his grandfather Hall home in Medford. That home stood on the edge of the Middlesex Fells. The fells held 4000 acres of rough and rocky woods, wild as old forest. There he spent free hours gathering eggs and insects. The wild ground near the city helped shape the man who would write of the frontier.
britannica-1911-partonopeus-de-blois:
Partonopeus de Blois is the subject of a tale entry in the 1911 Britannica. Partonopeus is the hero of a French romance. The tale dates from the 1200s in France. It has been tied to a writer named Denis Piramus. At its core it reworks the tale of Cupid and Psyche. The hero is set in the days of King Clovis. He was seized while hunting in the Ardennes.

He was borne to a strange castle with unseen folk. An empress came to him at night in secret. She barred him from trying to see her for years. He fought foes led by a king of Denmark. He then broke the spell with a charmed lantern. Woes followed, but the tale ends in joy. A sequel tells of the kin of his foe. Notes on the name and on print forms close the entry.
britannica-1911-pas-de-calais:
Pas de Calais, a coastal department in the north of France, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It was formed in 1790 from most of Artois and the north shore part of Picardy. The Straits of Dover bound it on the north, and the English Channel on the west. Just over a million people lived there at the count in the entry.

Most of the shore is sand dunes, with ports at Calais and Boulogne. Cape Blanc Nez and Cape Gris Nez are the noted headlands. Gris Nez is the point of France closest to England. Broad plains fill most of the land and are rich and well farmed. Low fen land in the north has been drained by canals into fine soil. Wheat and other grains give good yields. The air is damp and changeable but free of harsh heat or cold.
britannica-1911-pelham-henry-francis:
Henry Francis Pelham, an English scholar and historian who lived from 1846 to 1907, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. Born at Berg Apton in Norfolk in September 1846, he was the son of the bishop of Norwich. He was taught at Harrow and at Trinity College, Oxford. There he took a first class in classics in 1869. He was a tutor of Exeter College for twenty years.

In 1887 Pelham became university reader in ancient history, and two years later Camden professor. He was curator of the Bodleian from 1892 and president of Trinity College from 1897. His chief gift to ancient history was a long article on Roman history, reprinted as the Outlines of Roman History in 1890. His death in 1907 left much of his work unpublished.
britannica-1911-peritonitis:
Peritonitis, a swelling of the skin that lines the belly, is set out in a health entry in the 1911 Britannica. That skin wraps the gut and the parts that lie in the belly. The ill may come in sharp or slow form, and in one spot or spread wide. Cold, wet, wounds, and sick parts near by can all bring it on. A burst gut or a burst sore can spill its cause into the space.

Signs start with a chill shake, sick gut, and sharp pain in the belly. The sick man lies on his back with knees drawn up for ease. Breath comes fast and short from the chest with no belly move. The belly swells with trapped wind as the ill grows worse. Skin runs hot and the pulse runs small, hard, and fast.
britannica-1911-persis:
Persis was the south western part of Iran, named for its folk, whose name the Greeks reshaped into the form still used in the west. The 1911 Britannica entry leans on an old sea captain who sailed with Alexander the Great for a close account of the land. It splits the region into three zones, each with its own heat, soil, and way of life.

The coast is drawn as sandy, hot, and thinly peopled, with few good ports and date palms for its main crop. Inland vales lie high, cool, and well watered, rich in crops and herds, and these formed the true heart of old Persis. The north is higher still, rough and cold in winter, and fades toward desert in the east.
britannica-1911-peru-illinois:
Peru is a city in La Salle County, Illinois, on the Illinois river. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it just west of La Salle town, near a canal end. Its people neared eight thousand in 1910 by the count given. Two rail lines served the bluff built city on the river bank.

Saint Bede College, run by Benedictine fathers, opened there in 1891. A bronze monument in a park honors local Civil War dead. Coal mines in the area round the city fed its trade. Varied factory work added to that base over time. First settlement came about 1827, with town status in 1845.
britannica-1911-pervigilium-veneris:
Pervigilium Veneris is a poem article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a short Latin poem, the Vigil of Venus. Its author, its date, and its place of writing are all unknown. The poem most likely belongs to the second or third century. One writer in 1905 gave it to Sidonius Apollinaris, of the fifth century.

It was written, by its own claim, in early spring, on the eve of a three-night feast of Venus. In verse it tells of the yearly waking of the plant and animal world through the goddess. The poem holds ninety-three lines in a trochaic measure. Strophes of uneven length are parted by a refrain in Latin: tomorrow let him love who has never loved, and let him who has loved, love tomorrow. The article lists its early printings and its English verse translations.
britannica-1911-peter-of-blois:
Peter of Blois is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica life of a French writer. He was born at Blois to noble Breton parents. His dates are given as about 1135 to about 1205. He studied law at Bologna and theology in Paris. In 1167 he went to Sicily to teach the young king. There he also kept the royal seal.

Peter made foes in Sicily and soon left by his own request. Back in France, he taught in Paris for a time. He served an archbishop of Rouen as secretary. He then joined the court of Henry the Second of England. He became archdeacon of Bath in time. He also served two archbishops of Canterbury as chancellor. Twice he pled their cause before the pope in Italy.
britannica-1911-petitot-jean-louis:
Jean Louis Petitot, a French painter in enamel who lived from 1652 to about 1730, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was the eldest son of Jean Petitot, the master of that art. His father taught him the craft in full. Some of his works match his father's so close that the two hands can scarce be told apart.

He was, the entry says, the one true rival his father ever had. For a time he settled in London and painted enamel portraits of Charles the Second. In 1682 he went back to Paris, then in 1695 to London once more. He stayed in that city till his death. His own portrait by Mignard hangs in a museum at Geneva. A self-made enamel likeness is also kept in a peer's collection.
britannica-1911-philemon-and-baucis:
Philemon and Baucis is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a tale told by Ovid. The two are hero and heroine of that tale. Zeus came to earth in human form with Hermes. Tired and weary, the gods sought shelter for the night. All shut their doors against the two travellers. One aged couple in a humble cottage took them in.

Before leaving, the gods revealed who they truly were. They bade their hosts climb a mountain with them. A flood was set to punish the rest of the land. The country was drowned, but the cottage stood alone. That cottage was changed into a great temple. The gods made the pair its priest and priestess. They granted the pair's prayer to die together one day. After many years they were changed into trees. Philemon became an oak, and Baucis a lime tree.
britannica-1911-phlebitis:
Phlebitis is swelling and soreness of a vein. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica explains its risks and care. The word comes from a Greek term for a vein. When a vein swells, the blood in it tends to clot.

A loose clot can travel toward the heart as an embolus. It may lodge in the lungs or pass on to the brain. Gout, joint ills, and slow blood flow can all start a clot. A swollen vein near the skin feels like a hard cord. The limb turns dusky and sore along its course. Strict rest in bed is the first rule of care. Surgery may tie off the vein and cut out the clotted part.
britannica-1911-piron-alexis:
Alexis Piron, a French writer of epigrams and plays who lived from 1689 to 1773, is the subject of a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Dijon, the son of an apothecary who wrote verse in the Burgundian dialect. Alexis began as a banker's clerk, then studied law. In 1719, near thirty, he went to Paris to seek his fortune.

An edict had cut the fair theatres down to a single character on the stage, and no regular writer would attempt a one man drama. Piron did, and his Arlequin Deucalion was a great success with the public. In 1728 he produced a comedy at the Comedie Francaise that later bore the name The School for Fathers. He tried tragedy three times without success, then returned to comedy. His La Metromanie of 1738, whose hero suffers from a mania for verse, restored his standing.
britannica-1911-plaster-of-paris: Plaster of Paris is a kind of burnt gypsum used as a hard cement. A brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica states what the substance is. In chemical terms it is calcium sulphate that has been calcined. Mixed with water, it sets into a hard mass. The name comes from its place of making. The substance was largely manufactured in the neighborhood of Paris. For fuller detail on how such cements work, the entry points readers to the article on cement in the same work.
britannica-1911-pneumatolysis:
Pneumatolysis, a word built from Greek terms for vapour and for setting free, is a rock science term explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It means the discharge of vapours from molten rock masses below the earth, and the effects those vapours work on the rocks around them. In all eruptions of volcanoes, such gases are strong agents.

Lava lumps thrown from a crater are so full of gas that they cool like spongy bread. Streams of lava run under white clouds of steam, and a dark hood of vapour hangs over the mouth. Most writers of the day laid the blasts of volcanoes to steam set free from the molten mass. The chief gases are water vapour and carbonic acid. Tests at small side vents also found hydrogen, nitrogen and sour gases, and fresh lava acts like a great vent, laying down minerals in its cracks.
britannica-1911-ponsard-francois:
Francois Ponsard, who lived from 1814 to 1867, was a French playwright. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica marks his place in stage history. He was born at Vienne in June 1814 and trained as a lawyer. His first print work was a rendering of a Byron poem.

His tragedy Lucrece reached the Paris stage in April 1843. That night marked a turn away from wild romantic drama. Ponsard kept some freedom in time and place. But his verse went back to a sober older style. The great actress Rachel fit his method well and spread his fame. Later hits dealt with honor, money, and the revolt years. He joined the French Academy in 1855 and died in 1867.
britannica-1911-pythis: Pythis, also called Pythius, was one of the most noted Greek architects of the later age. He worked in the Ionic style of building in his craft. In that style he built the temple of Athena at Priene. A stone inscription for that temple is held in the British Museum. It records that Alexander the Great was the founder of the temple. Pythis also made a great marble chariot group for a tomb. That work, drawn by four horses, crowned the top of the Mausoleum.
britannica-1911-quincy-illinois:
Quincy, a city on the Mississippi river in Illinois, is described at length in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is the county seat of Adams county in the west of the state. About thirty six thousand people lived there at the counts in the entry. Three rail lines and river steamers serve the city. Quincy Bay gives steamers a fine harbour.

The city stands on river bluffs with wide views, and holds a park with old Indian mounds. Its free public library dates back to a founding in 1837. A state home for soldiers and sailors covers more than two hundred acres. Schools include a Catholic college and a boys school, and two hospitals serve the town. Quincy is the trade and factory centre of a large region. Stoves, wagons, and flour lead its long list of goods.
britannica-1911-rabelais-francois:
Francois Rabelais, a French humorist who lived from about 1490 to 1553, is profiled in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born at Chinon on the Vienne, in the province of Touraine. The date of his birth is wholly uncertain, the entry stresses at the start. Tradition and later writers have put it at 1483, 1490, and 1495.

Nothing in the firm facts of his life rules any of those dates out, the article says. Most writers of the seventeenth century give the earliest year. Against it stands his age at known points, such as his entry at Montpellier. For the middle date there is a witness of some merit, not too far removed in time. The entry promises only one new point on the dispute, weighing how each date fits the rest of his life.
britannica-1911-regnard-jean-francois:
Jean Francois Regnard lived from 1655 to 1709 and was a French writer of comic plays. The Britannica life of 1911 opens in Paris, where he was born. His father was a rich shop keeper who died when Regnard was young. The youth came into a large fortune at about age twenty. He set off at once for Italy and a life of travel.

His wild trips took him as far north as Lapland. He came home by way of Poland, Turkey, and Germany in 1683. Back in Paris he bought a post as treasurer of France. At his estate of Grillon he hunted, feasted, and wrote plays. His first piece, Le Divorce, reached the stage in 1688.
britannica-1911-renard-alphonse-francois:
Alphonse François Renard, a Belgian geologist who lived from 1842 to 1903, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. He was born at Renaix, in Eastern Flanders, in September 1842. He was educated for the church of Rome. From 1866 to 1869 he was superintendent at a college at Namur.

In 1870 he entered the Jesuit training college at Maria Laach, in the Eifel. There, while he studied philosophy and science, geology drew him in. The volcanic rocks of the district caught his eye above all. From then on he worked at chemistry and mineralogy. He fitted himself for the study of rocks, the field that made his name. In 1874 he became professor of chemistry and geology. He taught in the college of the Belgian Jesuits at Louvain. The article follows a church scholar turned rock scientist by the stones at his door.
britannica-1911-reybaud-marie-roch-louis:
Marie Roch Louis Reybaud (1799–1879) was a French writer, economist, and politician, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica lists his works. He was born at Marseilles on the fifteenth of August 1799. After travels in the Levant and in India, he settled in Paris in 1829. He wrote for the Radical press of that city.

Reybaud edited a ten volume history of the French expedition to Egypt, issued from 1830 to 1836. He also edited the voyage account of Dumont d’Urville in 1833. In 1840 his studies of modern reformers and socialists won wide notice. That work gained him a prize in 1841 and a seat in an academy in 1850. In 1843 he published Jérôme Paturot, a clever social satire. That book had a prodigious success with the public.
britannica-1911-riel-louis:
Louis Riel, a Canadian agitator who lived from 1844 to 1885, is profiled in this 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica article. He was born at St Boniface in October 1844, by his own account. Known as a Métis, his blood was mainly French. From 1866 he worked two years in Minnesota, then returned to St Vital.

In 1869 the transfer of Hudson's Bay Company rights to Canada caused great unease among the Métis. A party led by Riel turned back the new Canadian governor at the frontier. In November they captured Fort Garry and passed a bill of rights. In December a provisional government was set up with Riel as president. The article then faults Riel as flighty, vain, and mystical. His killing of Thomas Scott in March 1870 roused English-speaking Canada against him.
britannica-1911-rome-de-l-isle-jean-bapt:
Jean Baptiste Louis Romé de l'Isle, a French student of minerals who lived from 1736 to 1790, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Gray in Haute-Saône. As secretary to a company of gunners he went to the East Indies. In 1761 the English took him prisoner, and he stayed a captive for three years.

His fame rests on his work with minerals and with the shapes of crystals. His Essay on Crystallography came out in 1772. A far larger form of that work, in three volumes with an atlas, came out in 1783. The entry treats that book as his chief work. He died at Paris in March 1790, with his name fixed in the science he helped to found.
britannica-1911-roubiliac-louis-francois:
Louis Francois Roubiliac, who lived from 1695 to 1762, was a French sculptor who worked in England. The 1911 Britannica entry gives his birth at Lyons and training under Balthasar and Coustou. Tales put his London move near 1720, yet a Paris prize in 1730 casts doubt on that. Walpole backed him at once, and he soon led his field in England.

He passed the Fleming Rysbraeck and Scheemakers in public favour in short order. Portrait statues, busts, and tomb monuments formed the bulk of his commissions there. Westminster Abbey holds his monuments to Handel, Wade, and the duke of Argyll. He died in January 1762 and rests at Saint Martin in the Fields.
britannica-1911-rouelle-guillaume-franco:
Guillaume Francois Rouelle (1703-1770), a French chemist, is the subject of an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Mathieu near Caen, he began as an apothecary. In 1742 he was made the man who showed the trials in chemistry at the royal garden in Paris. There he won great fame as a teacher, and Lavoisier sat among his pupils.

The article delights in tales of his lectures. He spoke with such fire that, lost in thought, he would walk out of the room in search of a tool and go on talking to pupils who could not hear him. His rages at men he disagreed with often ended in one sharp word for a thief of ideas. His chief feat was to fix the meaning of salts, a word once used in the loosest way. He set them out as the compounds formed when acids and bases join.
britannica-1911-rude-francois:
Francois Rude, a French carver in stone born in seventeen eighty four, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Dijon, he worked at his father stove trade till age sixteen. In eighteen hundred and nine he went to Paris from the Dijon art school. He won the Grand Prix in eighteen twelve.

When the old royal house came back, he left for Brussels. There he cut nine low relief works for a palace. He wed a French girl there whose kin had helped him much. In time he came back to Paris. In eighteen twenty seven two works won wide note. One was a Virgin for a church. One was a swift god tying his shoes, now in the Louvre. His great fame dates from eighteen thirty three.
britannica-1911-saarlouis:
Saarlouis is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town of Germany. It was once a fortress town of some note. It lies in the Prussian Rhine Province in rich land. The Saar river runs by its left bank site. A railway links it to Saarbrucken and to Trier. A count from 1905 gives the town 8313 people. The town is well laid out with wide streets. 

The town holds a Catholic and a Protestant church. Its council chamber walls hang with Gobelin tapestries. Those tapestries were a gift of Louis the Fourteenth. Coal mines lie near the town on all sides. Local works make porcelain, enamel wares, and leather. A brisk trade runs in cattle and grain. Louis the Fourteenth founded the town in 1681. Vauban built its forts, which were pulled down in 1889. Marshal Ney was born in the town.
britannica-1911-san-luis:
San Luis is the subject of a province article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. San Luis is a province of Argentina. Its area is over twenty eight thousand square miles. By 1904 its people were put at near ninety seven thousand. Part of the land is dry pampa, and part is the foothills of the Andes. The text calls it one of the least important provinces, for its dry soil and few resources.

The article notes a mild, dry, and healthful climate in the rough north. Streams there allow some watering of rich soil. The south is a great dry salt plain where few can live. Farming and grazing go on in the north but lack water. The hills hold rich minerals, and gold mines have opened. Exports include cattle, hides, wool, and feathers. The capital, also called San Luis, sits on a high plateau.
britannica-1911-semois:
The Semois is a river of Belgium and France, and a short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica follows its course. The river rises near Arlon in Belgium and runs a little under 120 miles. It flows into the Meuse near Monthermé in France. About one hundred miles of its course lie in Belgium.

The entry praises the scenery along the river, the finest in Belgium. Its course winds so much that 120 miles of river cover only 47 miles in a straight line. Bouillon is the only town on its banks. The river cannot be sailed, and that fact has kept factories away. Its valley thus keeps a wooded calm and a medieval quiet. Readers get a portrait of a river valued for its beauty, not its trade.
britannica-1911-senlis:
Senlis is a town of northern France, in the department of Oise, described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the right bank of the Nonette, a stream that feeds the Oise, thirty-four miles north of Paris by rail. Its people numbered 6,074 in 1906. Three great forests lie round it, and its old stones draw much interest.

Its Gallo-Roman walls are among the most perfect in France. They stand twenty-three feet high and run in an oval round the old town, with towers at their angles. The Roman city had two gates, and the town now has five. On the site of the Roman hall rose a castle used at times by the kings of France from Clovis to Henry the Fourth. Near the town the base of a Roman theatre ground has been found.
britannica-1911-sepsis:
Sepsis means infection of a wound by germs or their poisons, as a 1911 Britannica medical entry explains. The Greek root points to rot, and the term covers three unlike states of the blood. They are sapraemia, septicaemia, and pyaemia, each with its own cause and course. The entry takes care to keep the three apart from the start.

Sapraemia is a poisoning by toxins soaked up from dead tissue near a wound. No germs enter the blood itself in that state, so blood tests act unlike true blood infection. Deep, badly drained wounds with trapped rot are the chief risk in surgery. Dirt on skin or foreign matter in a wound can bring the same harm.
britannica-1911-simon-jules-francois:
Jules François Simon (1814–1896) was a French statesman and philosopher, and a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica starts with his family. He was born at Lorient on the twenty seventh of December 1814. His father was a linen draper from Lorraine. The family name was Suisse, and Simon dropped it for his third given name.

At some cost, the family sent him to a seminary at Vannes. He served a short time as an usher in a school. In 1833 he entered the École Normale in Paris as a student. There he came under Victor Cousin, who sent him to teach philosophy at Caen and Versailles. Simon helped Cousin with translations from Plato, without public credit. His own rise in French letters and politics followed from that hard start.
britannica-1911-smith-morgan-lewis:
Morgan Lewis Smith was an American general who lived from eighteen twenty two to eighteen seventy four. His life entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Oswego county, New York, he settled in Indiana in eighteen forty three. He gained army service before the Civil War broke out in America.

At the war start Smith raised the Eighth Missouri regiment of foot. He led a brigade at the capture of Fort Donelson in that war. Good service at Shiloh won him a brigadier general rank in eighteen sixty two. A grave wound at Chickasaw Bayou kept him out till Chattanooga campaign. Sherman called him one of the bravest men he ever knew.
britannica-1911-stas-jean-servais:
Jean Servais Stas, a Belgian chemist who lived from 1813 to 1891, is covered in a 1911 Britannica life story. He was born at Louvain on August 21, 1813. He trained for medicine and took his degree, then turned to chemistry. In 1835 he gained a place in the Paris lab of Dumas.

In 1840 Stas took the chemistry chair at the Royal Military School in Brussels. He held it for more than twenty five years, till a speech ill forced him out. His name is best known for his measures of the weights of the atoms of key elements. His care was extreme, and his results varied by a hair. His data led him to drop a famed claim that all such weights are whole numbers.
britannica-1911-sterling-illinois:
Sterling, a city in Whiteside county in Illinois, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the north bank of Rock river, 109 miles west of Chicago by rail. Its people numbered 6,309 in 1900 and 7,467 in 1910. Two rail lines and an electric line to Dixon served it. Across the river lies Rock Falls, in practice a suburb.

The article points to the river as the source of its strength. A canal feeder joins there, giving a direct water route to Chicago and St Louis. Two great dams give good water power. The city held large ironworks and many other factories, and its public library held 12,000 books in 1910. Sterling was formed in 1839 by the joining of two towns founded a few years before, and it won a city charter in 1857.
britannica-1911-steyn-martinus-theunis:
Martinus Theunis Steyn, last head of the Orange Free State, born in eighteen fifty seven, is profiled in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born at Winburg in that state, he studied in Holland and then in England. He was called to the English bar in November of eighteen eighty two. He came home to work at law in Bloemfontein.

In eighteen eighty nine he was made state law man of the Free State. Months later he rose to a judge seat, and in time to a high court post. His rulings won him a name for skill and sound sense. When the head of state quit, Steyn stood for the post for the Dutch side. He won by a clear count in February of eighteen ninety six. As head he bound his state to the Transvaal, a path that led to the end of the republic.
britannica-1911-sturm-jacques-charles-fr:
Jacques Charles Francois Sturm was a French man of sums who lived from eighteen three to eighteen fifty-five. He was born at Geneva, of German stock. He first taught the son of a famed host in Paris. With a school friend he then sought his luck in that town and found press work.

In eighteen twenty-nine he found the rule that bears his name. It counts the true roots of a sum task that lie past set bounds. A chair of sums came the next year. He rose to top posts at the great schools of Paris. His class books came out past his death and fixed his name.
britannica-1911-sybaris:
Sybaris is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a city of Magna Graecia. The city stood on the Gulf of Tarentum. It lay between two rivers, the Crathis and the Sybaris. It was the oldest Greek colony in that region. Settlers from Achaea founded it about 720 years before Christ. Men from Troezen joined them but were later cast out. The land was rich, though the entry calls it unhealthy.

The city let in new citizens from all quarters freely. That open policy helped it grow great and rich. It held a vast subject land and planted colonies of its own. Some of those stood even on the far sea coast. The wealth of the Sybarites became a byword in Greece. At its peak, no Greek city could match its splendour. Strife between democrats and oligarchs then broke its peace. That strife led to war with Crotona.
britannica-1911-tonsillitis:
Tonsillitis is a medical article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about acute swelling of the tonsils, also called quinsy. It comes from germs that reach the tonsil through the mouth or by the blood. At times an attack follows breathing sewer gas. House surgeons and nurses, who spend their days in hospitals, often suffer it.

The illness may start with a chill or a fit of shivering. Then come swelling in the throat, pain, and hard swallowing. If both tonsils are inflamed, even fluids may not go down, and breathing can be badly checked. The body heat can rise several degrees, with pain about the ear and jaw. The article warns that the attack often runs on to an abscess. It is a plain, close account of a common and nasty throat illness.
britannica-1911-topelius-zakris:
Zakris Topelius, the Finnish author, is traced in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in 1818 at Kuddnäs, near Nykarleby. His father, a doctor, was the first great collector of Finnish folk songs. The son entered the school at Helsingfors in 1833. He rose to a professor's chair in 1863 and won each honour the school could give.

Topelius first won fame with lyric verse in Heather Blossoms. His first tale of old Finland, The Duchess of Finland, came in 1850. He ran the Helsingfors Gazette as chief editor for near twenty years. His best loved work was a set of tales of a barber-surgeon. They retold Finnish past times in the manner of Walter Scott.
britannica-1911-trachis:
Trachis is a place article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city of ancient Greece. It stood at the head of the Malian Gulf, in a small plain between the rivers Asopus and Melas. The wall of Mount Oeta shut it in. The Trachinian Cliffs let it command the main road from Thessaly.

That post made Trachis a strong point against invaders from the north. It also guarded the road up the Asopus gorge into the Cephissus valley. Oddly, the article notes, no record tells what part it played at Thermopylae against Xerxes. In 427 before Christ the Spartans sent a garrison to hold the plain. They built a citadel by the gorge and gave it a new name, Heraclea. The Spartans failed to hold the place against the hill tribes and the Thessalians.
britannica-1911-tunis:
Tunis is the capital of Tunisia and the largest city in North Africa outside Egypt. A 1911 Britannica entry sets it on a neck of land between two salt lakes. A deep cut channel through the lake has made the old inland town a seaport. Hills with forts command the city from the north west and south west.

The town rises like an amphitheatre with the kasbah citadel at its top point. The old Medina lies between two suburbs that once had walls of their own. Gates are what chiefly remain of those rings of defence in the modern town. The entry opens a full survey of a port with deep Arab and French layers.
britannica-1911-tupis:
Tupis are a tribe and stock of South American Indians of Brazil. The 1911 Britannica article says they call all other peoples Tapuyas, a word for foreigners. Their first home is thought to have been on the Amazon. From the mouth of that river they spread far south along the coast of Brazil. When the Portuguese pressed them hard, they fell back toward the Andes.

One scholar gives the Tupi nation a vast range, from the Atlantic to the Andes, and from Paraguay to the Amazon. Tribes of this stock include the Omaguas and Cocomas of Peru. Another scholar places the Tupis in the Guarani stock. The trade tongue used between Portuguese and Amazon Indians is a bent form of the Tupi speech. The entry gives these views side by side, as the bounds of the stock were still in debate.
britannica-1911-turris-libisonis:
Turris Libisonis was an old seaport town of Sardinia, now Porto Torres, in a 1911 Britannica entry. It stood at the north west tip of the island on the coast road. Two roads linked it south to Carales, one inland and one by the west shore. Roman origin is likely, with Julius Caesar held as its founder in the account.

It bore the title Colonia Julia and was the sole colony in Pliny Sardinia. Odd for a colony, it belonged to one of the urban tribes at Rome. A seven arch Roman bridge and temple ruins mark the ancient site. An inscription dates temple repairs to the years 247 to 249 after Christ.
britannica-1911-tyndaris:
Tyndaris is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on an ancient city of Sicily. It stood on the north coast, west of Mylae in that island. Dionysius the Elder founded it in the year 395 before Christ. He settled six hundred Messenians from the Peloponnese on the site.

It was near the last Greek city founded in Sicily, the entry says. It was one of the first friends of Timoleon in his wars. In the First Punic War it was held by Carthage as a post. In 254 its folk drove out the garrison and joined Rome. Under Rome the town seems to have thrived for a time. Cicero calls it a most noble city in his works.
britannica-1911-uselis:
Uselis, an ancient town of Sardinia, is described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stood in the hills south-east of Oristano, nine hundred feet above the sea. Its modern name is Usellus. The chief record of the place is a bronze tablet dated to the year 158.

That tablet sets out that a local notable, Balbinus, took up the post of patron of the town. It names the town a colony with grand titles tied to Augustus. Yet Pliny states that only one Sardinian town was a colony in his day. The article weighs that clash and sides with a grant of civic rights from Augustus. A church now marks the ancient site, and old remains have been found there. The bishop's seat moved to Ales in the twelfth century. The old name, though, is still kept in official use.
britannica-1911-valais:
Valais is a canton of southern Switzerland, also called Wallis and Vallese. Its canton entry appears in the nineteen eleven Encyclopaedia Britannica. The region is the upper valley of the Rhone from its glacier source. It runs down to the gorge of Saint Maurice and Lake Geneva.

The canton covers just over two thousand square miles in total area. Less than half that land counts as fruitful for farms and woods. Glaciers cover three hundred seventy five square miles, the most in Switzerland. That harsh land makes Valais one of the poorest cantons overall. Fine wines and summer travellers bring in much of its income each year.
britannica-1911-vere-sir-francis:
Sir Francis Vere, an English soldier who lived from 1560 to 1609, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was a nephew of the earl of Oxford and first saw war in 1585. He went with Leicester to the Low Countries, where a hard war raged. At the siege of Sluys he won great credit under older captains.

By 1589 he rose to lead the English troops in that war. He held the post through fifteen campaigns with near full success. Side by side with Maurice of Nassau he won the land back step by step. His camp became the school of the best young soldiers of the day. His crown came at Nieuwport in 1600, where Spanish veterans were crushed. Then came his famed defense of Ostend across a long siege.
britannica-1911-wallace-lewis:
Lewis Wallace is the subject of a life story in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Wallace was an American soldier and author, born at Brookville, Indiana, in 1827. He gave up the study of law to recruit a company for the Mexican War. He served in that war in 1846 and 1847 as a young lieutenant.

Back at the law, he rose again when the Civil War began. He became colonel of the Eleventh Indiana Infantry and fought in West Virginia. In September 1861 he was made a brigadier-general. The capture of Fort Donelson in February 1862 brought him promotion to major-general. He was engaged at the battle of Shiloh soon after. The entry opens the record of a man whose pen would later match his sword, though the head dwells on the soldier's rise.
britannica-1911-wayland-francis:
Francis Wayland, an American educationist who lived from 1796 to 1865, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in New York City, the son of a Baptist pastor, he graduated from Union College in 1813. He studied medicine, then turned to theology at Andover. Lack of funds cut that course short.

After posts as tutor and as a Boston pastor, Wayland became president of Brown University in 1827. In twenty eight years he built the college up step by step. He raised standards of discipline, formed a library, and gave science a larger place. His books on the college system urged reforms such as work based courses. Those reforms came in part only in his lifetime. He backed temperance and the anti slavery cause, and worked for prison reform. Rhode Island called him its first citizen.
britannica-1911-wharton-francis:
Francis Wharton lived from 1820 to 1889 and was an American legal writer. The 1911 Britannica life opens in Philadelphia, where he was born in March 1820. He graduated at Yale in 1839 and was admitted to the bar in 1843. He rose in Pennsylvania politics as a Democrat in that state. In Philadelphia he edited the North American and United States Gazette.

From 1856 he taught English history and letters at Kenyon College, Ohio. In 1862 he took orders in the Protestant Episcopal church in America. From 1863 he served as rector of St Paul's at Brookline. From 1871 he taught church law at the seminary in Cambridge. He also lectured on the conflict of laws at Boston University then.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-diss:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Disentis describes a Benedictine monastery in the Grisons of eastern Switzerland, named for Our Lady of Mercy. Tradition credits Sts. Placid and Sigebert with its foundation in 614, though Mabillon dates it two years earlier.

Avars destroyed the house in 670, martyring its abbot and thirty monks, and Charles Martel with Abbot Pirminius rebuilt it in 711. Charlemagne visited in 800 and heaped benefactions on it, and Abbot Udalric the First became a prince of the empire, a dignity later abbots also held. After a thousand years of independence Disentis joined the new Swiss Congregation in 1617, and St. Charles Borromeo's visit in 1581 crowns its later history.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-sain:
The Catholic Encyclopedia entry on Saint-Denis describes the abbey in the town of the same name, four miles north of Paris. Paris' first bishop Denis and his companions, killed in 270, were buried there, and the small chapel over the spot became a famous pilgrimage place in the fifth and sixth centuries.

Dagobert founded a Benedictine abbey there in 630, replacing the chapel with a large basilica, and he and his successors enriched it with gifts and privileges.
